Part 1: Key decisions and facts

Go/no-go gates. NO at an early gate costs the least.

# Question Threshold Evidence If NO
1 Are the Danish host MoU signed (Month 1), the Kenyan partner agreement signed (Month 3), and the independent gate panel chartered with at least 3 conflict-free members and a written funder commitment to publish any deviation (Month 1.5)? Danish MoU signed by Month 1; panel of 3-5 conflict-free members and Gate Authority Charter by Month 1.5; Kenyan agreement by Month 3; no Danish host with protected lab space by Month 4 means halt Phase One spend beyond committed items. Signed MoUs, signed charter, panel conflict-of-interest statements and the funder's written deviation-publication commitment (Months 1-3). DELAY: pause new commitments to facility setup (EUR 2.0M planned), open parallel talks with a second host or partner, and escalate to the funder. Do not let work continue by momentum without an independent panel.
2 Does the Month 4 evidence show a primary and a legally clean backup strain that are lawful for commercial use, redistribution, modification and import into Kenya, with written Kenyan biosafety feedback, and a Kenyan site baseline that meets the fixed operating envelope? At least 2 strains confirmed lawful (research, commercial, redistribution, modification, derived) with Kenyan import; written Kenyan biosafety feedback; baseline report with >=4 unplanned outages/month, mean >=2 h, >=1 outage/quarter >8 h, spares lead time <=2-4 weeks from >=2 suppliers. Strain Feasibility Report and signed Kenyan Site Baseline Report (Month 4; internal draft Month 3). Hard tripwire at Month 6. DELAY or SWITCH: absorb a strain switch in the EUR 0.30M earmark and re-select the site rather than lowering the envelope. If no strain is lawfully importable for commercial use by Month 6, stop or pivot to Research Only.
3 By Month 7, is a gap-funding route committed in writing and have at least 2 named adopters signed with auditable cost data, on thresholds that the modeled cost can plausibly meet? Written funder or adopter commitment covering the EUR 274,820/yr gap (or EUR 3.0M capex grant); >=2 signed adopters by Month 7; modeled full cost below EUR 15/kg at Month 6 (tripwire). Scenario B (EUR 10/kg) is below opex-only EUR 11.59/kg, so a grant alone cannot meet it. Funder gap-funding decision document, signed adopter commitments with cost-basis data, cost-reduction study results (Months 6-7); locks time-stamped at Month 9. DOWNSIZE or STOP: the Phase One gate cannot pass with fewer than 2 signed adopters. Recommend Research Only, or a reduced Phase Three (Danish unit plus documentation-based replication), instead of locking unreachable scenarios.
4 At the Phase One gate, does measured bench productivity within the pre-registered safety limits, with the HAZOP complete, justify releasing Phase Two funding? Productivity >=90% of the published C. necator H2 benchmark = pass; 70% to <90% = panel decision; <70% = fail; measurement uncertainty above 30% means the panel cannot declare a pass. HAZOP complete; reactor chosen by the pre-registered rule; O2 <4% in H2-rich stream and H2 inventory <0.5 m3 held. Triplicate matched-reactor results audited externally (results about Month 6), evidence freeze Month 9, panel meeting Month 10, release decision by Month 12. MODIFY or STOP: below 70% inside the safety limits, stop or pivot to Research Only. Do not relax safety limits ad hoc; a revised envelope needs an independent ATEX review. The 70-90% band is a panel decision, not automatic continuation.
5 At the Phase Two gate, are the scale-up, stability, downstream and documentation criteria met and the cost chain closed enough to release the EUR 4.0M reference-unit hardware? kLa decline bench to pilot <=25%; 16-week strain-stability run with <10% variation; nucleic acid <=2% of dry matter (or category limit) with the downstream train validated; composition and digestibility confirm the category; defects 0 safety-critical, <=3 critical, <=10 minor; modeled cost <=EUR 14/kg (proposed threshold, pre- or post-subsidy basis unresolved) AND a committed gap-funding route. Pre-registered disproof experiments, stability run, pilot downstream data, early replication defect log and auditor readiness assessment (Month 26), panel decision at Month 30. DOWNSIZE or STOP: withhold the EUR 4.0M hardware and recommend a reduced Phase Three (Danish unit plus documentation-based replication) or Research Only. A failed gate needs an explicit funder decision, never automatic continuation.
6 At the Phase Three gate (evidence freeze Month 57, decision by Month 60), has the independent replication met every Go criterion, with hypotheses A and B reported separately? On-spec biomass from documentation alone; 100% of safety-critical fault injections reach a safe state; >=90% of other fault tests recovered; six consecutive months uptime >=90% (and the chosen scenario's own requirement); operator practical safety pass >=90%; assistance log with developer troubleshooting <=4 h/month flagged; at least one locked scenario met; credible regulatory pathway and scale-up route. Failure of A or B excludes Go. Danish 6-month run (Months 40-46), Kenyan production (Months 48-54), fault-injection results (Months 50-56), audited assistance log, panel recommendation. MODIFY (correctable weaknesses, including a first documentation-traced failure), RESEARCH ONLY (technology works but no scenario or scale-up route), or STOP (repeated replication failure or fundamental safety, legal or reproducibility failure). Findings are published as open knowledge either way.

What you need to decide, and by when.

5 open decisions: 4 high and 1 medium severity. The most urgent decisions are the hardware-release cost rule, which is needed by Month 1.5 (2026-11-24) for the Gate Authority Charter, and the Kenyan envelope rule, which is needed by Month 1 (2026-11-09). The gap-funding route, the Scenario B decision and the meaning of 'scenario met' follow by Months 6-9 (2027-04-09 to 2027-07-09). Until these are made, the plan can safely run the landscape review, strain rights work, HAZOP and bench work, and the panel and host setup. It should not make hardware or scenario-locking commitments.

1. Gap-funding route (🔴 High)

Decision: Which route closes the EUR 274,820/yr deployment gap: adopter grant (EUR 3.0M capex), operating subsidy, or cost reduction?

Why it is open: Gap is not covered by the programme budget. Full cost EUR 19.93/kg vs EUR 12 cap. A EUR 3.0M capex grant leaves a EUR 14,180/yr surplus. The route is undecided.

Option Consequences What changes in the plan
A. Capex grant of EUR 3.0M from funder or adopter. Removes debt service; operating margin EUR 14,180/yr. Reaches Scenario A and probably C, but not B (opex EUR 11.59/kg). Needs written commitment by Month 7 (2027-05-09). deployment_financing, gap_funding_open_decision, Month 7 (2027-05-09) gate evidence.
B. Annual operating subsidy of about EUR 274,820/yr. Creates a recurring obligation beyond the programme. Needs a named payer with auditable terms. deployment_chain_gap, adopter agreements, steward funding.
C. Rely on cost reduction alone (electricity, downstream energy). No new funding. High risk at Month 6 (2027-04-09) (tripwire EUR 15/kg). May lead to Research Only or a reduced Phase Three. energy_per_kg, TEA model, construction_spend_recommendation.
  • If nobody decides: No gap route is committed by Month 7 (2027-05-09), so the Phase One gate cannot pass. Recommend Research Only or a reduced Phase Three.
  • Owner: Funder (release authority), with the Steering Committee and adopters.
  • Decide by: Month 7 (2027-05-09): written commitment is needed before scenarios lock at Month 9 (2027-07-09).
  • Blocks: Month 7 (2027-05-09) gate check, scenario locking at Month 9 (2027-07-09), and release of EUR 4.0M hardware at the Phase Two gate.

2. Hardware-release cost rule (🔴 High)

Decision: What single cost rule (value, and pre- or post-subsidy basis) releases the EUR 4.0M hardware, kept separate from the Phase Three success test?

Why it is open: The release trigger is EUR 14/kg. Failure is stated as both 14 and 15. 'EUR 12-14 enables a scenario' conflicts with caps of 12, 10 and 15. The subsidy basis is not stated.

Option Consequences What changes in the plan
A. EUR 14/kg (proposed threshold) judged after the committed grant or subsidy, per scenario. Aligns with the gap route. Needs a committed route at the Phase Two gate (Month 30 = 2029-04-09). Gate Authority Charter, phase2_gate_criteria, KPI 1, premortem FM1.
B. EUR 14/kg judged before any subsidy. Stricter. Raises the chance of a reduced Phase Three or Research Only. Same documents; the capex grant no longer counts.
C. Set the release trigger equal to each scenario's cap. Strictest. Ties release to caps of EUR 12, 10 or 15. Scenario B would likely fail. Remove the generic 14 trigger; revise KPI 1.
  • If nobody decides: The Charter is chartered with an ambiguous rule, which invites post-hoc interpretation at Month 30 (2029-04-09).
  • Owner: Funder, before the Gate Authority Charter.
  • Decide by: Month 1.5 (2026-11-24): the Charter and KPI framework lock then.
  • Blocks: Gate Authority Charter and KPI framework (Month 1.5 = 2026-11-24); the Phase Two hardware release.

3. Scenario B: re-price, drop or keep (🔴 High)

Decision: Is Scenario B (EUR 10/kg) re-priced, dropped, or kept with an explicit need for cost reduction below opex?

Why it is open: Opex alone is EUR 11.59/kg, so no grant can reach EUR 10. The gap is sized only against the EUR 12 cap. Scenario C has a different gap.

Option Consequences What changes in the plan
A. Drop Scenario B and lock A and C. Simpler gate. Removes the 500 kg/day requirement. scenario_b_thresholds, KPI 1, pitch.
B. Re-price B, for example to at least opex plus margin, with the adopter's agreement. Keeps a feed-producer case. Must be agreed before Month 9 (2027-07-09). scenario_b_thresholds, gap per scenario.
C. Keep B at EUR 10/kg, reachable only by cost reduction. Probably unreachable, so it adds little to Go. Document the per-scenario gap; remove 'enables B'.
  • If nobody decides: B is locked at EUR 10 and cannot be met, which weakens the scenario set.
  • Owner: Steering Committee with the named adopters; funder ratifies.
  • Decide by: Month 6 (2027-04-09): scenario profiles are due then, before signing at Month 7 (2027-05-09).
  • Blocks: Scenario profiles (Month 6 = 2027-04-09), signed adopters (Month 7 = 2027-05-09), locking (Month 9 = 2027-07-09).

4. Meaning of 'scenario met' (🔴 High)

Decision: Is 'scenario met' measured on the 10 kg/day reference unit plus modeled scale-up, or does it need a funded deployment-scale unit?

Why it is open: Reference units give about 10 kg usable protein/day. Scenario floors are 50-500 kg/day. Deployment-scale units are modeled only and not programme-funded.

Option Consequences What changes in the plan
A. Measured cost, uptime and energy on the reference unit, plus an uncertainty-bounded model to scenario capacity. Fits the EUR 50M ceiling. Capacity is not demonstrated. phase3_gate_criteria, KPI 3, project plan 'Measurable'.
B. A funded deployment-scale unit with a named financier. Strong evidence, but a large cost beyond the programme (modeled EUR 3.0M each). Delays beyond Month 60 (2031-10-09) are likely. programme_financed_units, budget, schedule.
C. Accept either route, chosen per scenario and written in the lock document. Flexible, but needs written rules at Month 9 (2027-07-09). scenario locking document.
  • If nobody decides: The Phase Three Go test cannot be applied consistently, because capacity floors exceed built capacity.
  • Owner: Funder with the Independent Gate-Review Panel.
  • Decide by: Month 9 (2027-07-09): scenarios lock then.
  • Blocks: Scenario locking (Month 9 = 2027-07-09) and the Phase Three Go decision (Month 60 = 2031-10-09).

5. Kenyan site baseline and fixed envelope (🟡 Medium)

Decision: Will the Kenyan envelope stay fixed, with the site changed if it fails, and what does the Month 4 (2027-02-09) baseline contain?

Why it is open: The partner is signed at Month 3 (2027-01-09), leaving about 4 weeks before the Month 4 (2027-02-09) baseline. Some documents allow renegotiating the envelope downward, which conflicts with the rule that the envelope is fixed.

Option Consequences What changes in the plan
A. Fix the envelope and change the site if it fails. Month 4 (2027-02-09) holds historical records plus spot samples; water sampling continues. Start the site study before signing. Keeps the test honest. Costs a possible site switch and uses part of the reserve. kenya_envelope_baseline, Review 8 and 9, site study start date.
B. Allow a documented downward envelope revision with panel consent. Easier siting, but weakens the hypothesis B test. kenya_envelope_baseline, hypothesis B claims.
  • If nobody decides: The site is chosen by convenience and the envelope is eased after the fact.
  • Owner: Steering Committee with the Kenyan co-development partner; the panel advises.
  • Decide by: Month 1 (2026-11-09): the independent site study must start before the partner agreement (Month 3 = 2027-01-09).
  • Blocks: Month 4 (2027-02-09) baseline report and the strain and site gate check.

deployment_chain_gap Operating margin EUR 14,180/yr (416,100 - 401,920); DSCR 0.05; shortfall EUR 274,820/yr; full cost EUR 19.93/kg vs EUR 12 cap (gap EUR 7.93/kg) estimate Recomputed: DSCR 14,180/289,000 = 0.049; shortfall 289,000 - 14,180 = 274,820; total annual cost 401,920 + 289,000 = 690,920 over 34,675 kg = 19.93. On these estimates Scenario A fails the proposed cap by a factor of 1.66 (19.93/12). At the EUR 3.0M debt level, even zero non-electric opex would need <=22.9 kWh/kg dry biomass to break even ((416,100 - 289,000)/0.08/69,350).

Only the panel may add a harsher scenario later, never relax one.

Example range EUR 8-12 narrowed to 10.

kenya_envelope_baseline Site envelope (baseline report Month 4 = 2027-02-09): >=4 unplanned outages/month, mean duration >=2 h, >=1 outage/quarter >8 h; spares lead time <=2-4 weeks from >=2 suppliers; 2-3 locally available technicians per trade; drift >20% triggers added outage stressors proposed threshold The assumptions' '>=1 outage/week' and the review's '>=4/month' are about equal; the review's stricter version is used. Site selection is by an independent consultant, not the Kenyan partner.

resupply_autonomy_targets Production continues >=60 days without resupply for each process input (N source, minerals, chemicals) and >=90 days for critical spares; tested by a 60-90 day simulated cutoff in Phase Three; local/regional share >=60% of input cost proposed threshold The risk register gives a 3-6 month spares stock and a 2-3 month cutoff test; the 60 and 90 day figures and 60% share are the plan's own proposals, to be locked in the KPI protocol.
safety_design_limits Preliminary: no operation above 2 bar(g) without independent overpressure relief; gas inventory <0.5 m3 H2 and <0.2 m3 O2; O2 <4% in H2-rich stream; ignition target <1 per 100,000 operating hours proposed threshold From the assumptions' 2-3 bar choice (lower end taken). Pending independent HAZOP/LOPA at Months 1-3 (2026-11-09 to 2027-01-09); the ignition target is a placeholder and LOPA may tighten it. Interlocks may never be bypassed manually.

Focus and Context

A EUR 50 million, five-year infrastructure programme to deliver an open-source, independently replicable hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria protein process for food-supply disruptions. The central claim is that critical food technology can be designed openly, legally implementable in multiple countries, and maintainable by local technicians without vendor lock-in. Three deployment scenarios (reserve agency, regional feed producer, humanitarian logistics) anchor the evidence threshold. The core risk is that the deployment cost chain shows a EUR 7.93/kg gap to affordability, and the gap-funding route is undecided.

Purpose and Goals

Demonstrate that hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria can produce food-grade protein at a cost and reliability sufficient for food-supply disruption scenarios, using a design that is openly published, independently replicable under difficult infrastructure (Kenyan conditions), and maintainable by locally trained technicians. Success means at least one locked deployment scenario achieves its cost, capacity and uptime targets. Hypotheses A (local technician operation) and B (decentralized modules) are tested separately; failure of either excludes a Go decision.

Key Deliverables and Outcomes

Phase One: strain rights document, safety design basis, matched-reactor productivity comparison, Kenyan site baseline, signed adopter scenarios, blueprint v0.1. Phase Two: pilot-scale validation of mass transfer and strain stability, downstream train proof, scale-up disproof-experiment results, documentation readiness audit. Phase Three: two reference units (Danish and Kenyan) with 6-month production runs, fault-injection test results, on-spec biomass reproducibility, operator competency assessment, final Go/Modify/Research-Only/Stop decision with evidence.

Timeline and Budget

60 months total (Month 0 = 2026-10-09 to Month 60 = 2031-10-09). Phase One Months 0–12 (2026-10-09 to 2027-10-09) (EUR 5.5M planned, EUR 6M ceiling user constraint). Phase Two Months 12–30 (2027-10-09 to 2029-04-09) (EUR 13M planned). Phase Three Months 30–60 (2029-04-09 to 2031-10-09) (EUR 22M planned). Programme reserve EUR 4M. Total EUR 50M provisional ceiling (user constraint). Hardware (EUR 4M) is released only at the Phase Two gate.

Risks and Mitigations

Critical: strain rights barriers (mitigation: complete feasibility report by Month 4 = 2027-02-09 with backup strain). Deployment cost gap EUR 7.93/kg (mitigation: lock gap-funding route by Month 7 = 2027-05-09 or recommend Research Only). Independent gate-review panel governance weak (mitigation: sign Gate Authority Charter by Month 1.5 = 2026-11-24 with binding authority). Secondary: hydrogen-oxygen explosion hazard (mitigation: independent HAZOP and design basis by Month 2.5 = 2026-12-24), documentation defects found late (mitigation: live defect tracker by Month 11 = 2027-09-09 and early replication Months 14–24 = 2027-12-09 to 2028-10-09).

Audience Tailoring

This summary is tailored for government funders, multilateral organizations and institutional decision-makers responsible for food-security resilience. The tone emphasizes gated evidence, risk-driven mitigation and transparent governance over technical enthusiasm. Budget and timeline constraints are highlighted as user-imposed boundaries, not aspirations.

Action Orientation

By Month 1 (2026-11-09): sign Danish host MoU and commission HAZOP consultant; engage Kenyan partner (partner and site secured by Month 3 = 2027-01-09). By Month 1.5 (2026-11-24): charter independent gate panel (3–5 members, separate EUR 0.30M funding) and lock KPI framework. By Month 4 (2027-02-09): deliver Strain Feasibility Report and Kenyan Site Baseline Report. By Month 7 (2027-05-09): lock gap-funding route and obtain signed adopter commitments. By Month 9 (2027-07-09): lock deployment scenarios and publish blueprint v0.1.

Overall Takeaway

The programme is a high-risk, high-value infrastructure investment requiring rigorous governance and early risk resolution. Success depends on settling strain rights, safety design, adopter scenarios and gap-funding by Month 7 (2027-05-09), and locking an independent gate-review panel with binding authority by Month 1.5 (2026-11-24). If these foundational steps are executed as specified, the evidence-driven gate structure protects the EUR 50M investment from momentum-driven continuation despite weak evidence. If not, the project risks wasting EUR 20–30M on a failed business case or technical success with no deployment pathway.

Part 2: Supporting analysis

Persuasive elevator pitch.

Open Protein Module: A Five-Year Programme for Open-Source, Resilient Food Production

Project Overview

When the next global food crisis hits, will your nation have to depend on imports that may never arrive? The Open Protein Module turns electricity, water, CO₂ and a nitrogen source into protein through hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria—a process no single company owns, that any independent team can build and repair, and that works even when supply chains fail.

Over five years, this EUR 50 million programme will deliver a complete open-source engineering package, tested in Denmark and independently replicated in Kenya under difficult infrastructure, with an independently reviewed safety design. Current modeled full cost is EUR 19.93/kg (estimate); a route to the EUR 12/kg cap is a hypothesis to be tested, closable only by cost reduction or a funded gap route. It aims to show that critical food technology can be genuinely open, locally repairable, and ready before crisis strikes.

The technology converts hydrogen gas and oxygen (from water electrolysis) into single-cell protein using naturally occurring bacteria. The process is vendor-independent, can be documented openly, and requires no proprietary strains or closed-source designs. A reference unit will produce approximately 20 kg of dry biomass per day (~10 kg usable protein/day) at an estimated 33 kW average electrical load.

Target Audience

Primary: Government ministries and multilateral funders responsible for food security, disaster resilience, and food-supply independence (e.g. EU, bilateral development agencies, African Union, WFP).

Secondary: Impact investors, open-hardware advocates and academic institutions seeking high-risk, high-value research with clear public benefit.

Tertiary: Prospective adopters (reserve agencies, regional feed producers, humanitarian logistics organizations) who will lock in deployment scenarios and help validate thresholds.

The pitch avoids venture-capital language and speaks to institutional risk tolerance and public-good mandates.

Project Phases and Timeline

The programme spans 60 months (Month 0 = 2026-10-09 through Month 60 = 2031-10-09) across three phases:

  • Phase One (Months 0–12 = 2026-10-09 to 2027-10-09): Settle foundational decisions on reactor concept, strain rights, safety design, deployment scenarios and replication governance. Budget: EUR 6 million provisional ceiling (EUR 5.5M planned).
  • Phase Two (Months 12–30 = 2027-10-09 to 2029-04-09): Scale from bench to pilot, validate cost chain, confirm regulatory pathways and early independent replication. Budget: EUR 13 million planned.
  • Phase Three (Months 30–60 = 2029-04-09 to 2031-10-09): Commission two reference units (Denmark and Kenya), conduct safety and fault testing, evaluate against the locked adopter thresholds and publish final open-source documentation. Budget: EUR 22 million planned.
  • Programme reserve: EUR 4 million (EUR 3.5M technical/scheduling contingency + EUR 0.5M currency fund).
  • Unreleased headroom: EUR 5.5 million.

Total provisional ceiling: EUR 50 million.

Risks and Mitigation Strategies

Hydrogen-Oxygen Explosion Hazard

Mitigation: Independent HAZOP analysis by Month 2 (2026-12-09), inherent safety limits locked before reactor selection, and layered interlocks independently reviewed before any pressurized build.

Strain Rights or Biosafety Blocking Replication

Mitigation: A Strain Feasibility Report (Month 4, 2027-02-09) naming a primary and a legally clean backup strain with written Kenyan biosafety feedback. All strain rights documented for research, commercial use, redistribution, modification, and derived strains.

Scale-Up Failure and Cost-Chain Gap

Mitigation: Pre-registered disproof experiments on mass transfer, matched reactor comparisons, and techno-economic sensitivity analysis by Month 9 (2027-07-09). If the EUR 7.93/kg gap persists, recommend Research Only outcome rather than forced deployment. (Current gap: full production cost modeled at EUR 19.93/kg vs. EUR 12/kg target; gap-funding route is an open decision.)

Documentation Gaps Found Only at Replication

Mitigation: An early paper-and-bench replication (Months 14–24, 2027-12-09 to 2028-10-09) with a live defect tracker and auditor assessment before full-scale build. Defect tracker goes live by Month 11 (2027-09-09). EUR 0.15M and 8 weeks reserved for documentation fixes.

Metrics for Success

Technical

  • On-spec biomass (protein ≥60%, nucleic acid ≤2% of dry matter, moisture ≤8%) reproducible from documentation alone in the Kenyan unit.
  • 100% of safety-critical fault injections reach a safe state.
  • ≥90% of operational fault tests recover within pre-set limits.

Operational

  • Six consecutive months uptime ≥90%.
  • ≥8 h outage survived with safe shutdown within 30 s and restart within 2 h.
  • Resupply autonomy ≥60 days per input (nitrogen source, minerals, chemicals); ≥90 days for critical spares.

Evidence Quality

  • Zero unresolved safety-critical documentation defects.
  • Independent replication defects logged and resolved.
  • Gate-panel independence verified.
  • At least one locked scenario met (cost, capacity, reliability).

Adoption

  • Confirmation that at least one prospective adopter can lawfully obtain strain, secure permits, and proceed within 12 months of release.

Economic

  • Cost trajectory toward the EUR 12/kg cap (current modeled full cost EUR 19.93/kg, estimate); a route to the cap remains a hypothesis to be tested.
  • Gap-funding source identified or justified as Research Only.

Stakeholder Benefits

Governments and Multilateral Funders

Demonstrable resilience infrastructure with zero vendor lock-in, replicable by any nation or region facing supply disruptions. Peer-reviewed science on hydrogen-based protein production.

Adopters (Reserve Agencies, Feed Producers)

A complete, independently safety-reviewed, open design they can build and service locally without licensing fees or dependency on a single company. Operator training and competency frameworks included.

Researchers and Open-Hardware Communities

Published, audited process data; peer-reviewed studies on scale-up, safety and replication; open data and analysis code; collaboration agreements with academic institutions.

Independent Technicians in Kenya and Beyond

Demonstrated path to skilled, local employment in protein production with clear competency boundaries and pre-assessed change rights.

Strain Custodians and Culture Collections

Defined chain of custody for cryo-stocks; reciprocal licensing ensures improvements feed back to the global research community.

Ethical Considerations

This project commits to democratic governance: an independent gate-review panel (not the developer team) controls continue/modify/research-only/stop decisions at each phase, with written public justification for any funder deviation. The panel will be composed of 3–5 members, recruited and chartered by Month 1.5 (2026-11-24), funded and managed by the funder (not the host). The funder holds release authority, and any deviation from the panel's recommendation requires published written justification.

Strain choice privileges lawful access over proprietary performance, so independent implementers in Kenya and other nations can build without vendor approval.

Safety decisions prioritize local adopter protection: the Adopter Change Boundary is pre-assessed in detail, and safety-critical modifications require hazard re-analysis, not unilateral builder choice. We acknowledge that hydrogen-oxygen systems carry intrinsic hazard; we manage it through layered, independently reviewed protection and tight inventory limits (no operation above 2 bar(g) without independent overpressure relief; gas inventory <0.5 m³ H₂ and <0.2 m³ O₂; O₂ <4% in H₂-rich stream), not through black-box automation that disempowers local technicians.

Commercialization is not prohibited, but reciprocal open licences prevent closed forks and require improvements to be shared back.

The project will not claim success if replication fails or adopters cannot lawfully operate the design; we treat failure discovery as evidence-based progress, not a defeat.

Collaboration Opportunities

  • With commercial hydrogen-protein producers (e.g. Solar Foods): Public benchmark exchange on productivity, energy, nucleic acid handling and novel-food authorization timelines (not proprietary margins).
  • With existing open-hardware gas-fermentation research (e.g. AMYBO): Co-authored scale-up methodology; joint KPI framework; candidate design evaluation.
  • With Kenyan food-technology and feed-regulation bodies (e.g. icipe, Kenya Bureau of Standards, Ministry of Agriculture): Co-hosted regulatory pre-submission dialogue; Kenyan site and partner identification; adopter engagement and scenario validation.
  • With independent ATEX and safety consultants: Joint hazard analyses; interlock-design review; published safety-case methodology.
  • With non-profit steward entities (e.g. Open Source Ecology, OSHWA): Licence-stack and certification frameworks; defect-tracking and community governance models.
  • With academic institutions: Phase One reactor benchmark collaborative agreements; peer review and co-publication of scale-up and replication findings.

Open invitations to all groups to engage at Month 1.5 (2026-11-24) when the independent panel is chartered.

Long-term Vision

By Month 60 (2031-10-09), a complete open-source protein process will exist, independently replicated under difficult infrastructure, with zero vendor lock-in and publicly documented safety and economic limits.

Within two years post-release, the aspiration is at least three independent deployments in Africa, Asia or elsewhere, each training local technicians and reporting real cost and uptime data.

Within five years, the open design will have become a reference point for food-resilience policy in jurisdictions facing supply risk. Regulators in Denmark, the EU, Kenya and other nations will have confirmed product-safety pathways for open-source biological processes.

A non-profit steward entity will be managing version releases, processing adopter feedback and enforcing reciprocal open licences indefinitely.

The project's greatest legacy is not the protein output, but the proof that critical infrastructure can be designed for independence, published openly, and replicated rigorously—setting a precedent for open-source medicine, water treatment and energy systems in under-resourced regions.

Call to Action

Commit EUR 6 million to Phase One (Months 0–12 = 2026-10-09 to 2027-10-09) to settle the five foundational decisions: reactor concept, strain rights, safety design basis, deployment scenarios and replication governance.

By Month 12 (2027-10-09), you will hold:

  • An independent gate recommendation.
  • Measured evidence of which reactor concept beats the cost-simplicity trade-off.
  • Confirmed legal clearance for Kenyan replication.
  • Locked adopter thresholds.

A single decision point at Month 12 (2027-10-09) will show whether to advance to a EUR 13 million Phase Two with confidence.

  • Commit EUR 6 million Phase One budget (EUR 5.5M planned spend, EUR 0.65M contingency).
  • Recruit and charter an independent gate-review panel (3–5 members) by Month 1.5 (2026-11-24); funding EUR 0.06M in Phase One.
  • Sign a Danish host institution MoU by Month 1 (2026-11-09).
  • Engage a HAZOP/LOPA safety consultant by Month 1 (2026-11-09).
  • Commission a patent search and strain-rights feasibility study by Month 2 (2026-12-09).
  • Lock the KPI framework by Month 1.5 (2026-11-24); deliver the HAZOP report by Month 2 (2026-12-09); issue the safety design basis and reactor decision rules by Month 2.5 (2026-12-24).
  • Deliver the Strain Feasibility Report by Month 4 (2027-02-09).
  • Identify the Kenyan partner and site by Month 3 (2027-01-09); sign prospective adopters by Month 7 (2027-05-09).
  • Lock deployment scenarios and time-stamp them at Month 9 (2027-07-09).
  • Hold Phase One evidence freeze by Month 9 (2027-07-09) and gate panel decision by Month 12 (2027-10-09).

Governance safeguards:

  • Unsigned partners and sites carry risk; we recommend a steering committee with authority to pause or redirect if adoption signals weaken.
  • Any funder deviation from the independent panel's recommendation must be published in writing and justified publicly.
  • Release of Phase Two and Phase Three budgets is conditional on the preceding gate decision.

Goal Statement: Establish The Open Protein Module, a non-profit open-source programme that delivers a safe, legally implementable, independently replicated process turning electricity, water, CO2 and a nitrogen source into protein with hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria, developed in Denmark and replicated in Kenya, with a full open source package, within 60 months and a provisional EUR 50 million ceiling (user constraint).

SMART Criteria

  • Specific: Produce and openly publish a complete, safety- and legally-reviewed engineering package for single-strain hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria protein production, validated by a Danish reference unit and an organizationally separate Kenyan replication under difficult infrastructure, with hypotheses A (local technician operation) and B (decentralized modules) reported separately.
  • Measurable: Go requires: on-spec biomass (protein >=60%, nucleic acid <=2% dry matter, moisture <=8%) (estimate) from documentation alone; 100% of safety-critical fault injections reach a safe state; >=90% of other fault tests recovered; six-month uptime >=90% (proposed threshold); operator safety pass >=90%; one locked scenario met; credible regulatory and scale-up routes.
  • Achievable: Builds on published open work (e.g. electroPioreactor, passive gas feeding) and commercial precedent. Staged gates with a EUR 6 million Phase One ceiling (user constraint) and planned spend of EUR 5.5M (estimate) limit exposure. Partners, funding, sites and permits are unsigned and uncontrolled; the deployment cost chain currently shows a gap (full cost EUR 19.93/kg vs EUR 12 cap) (estimate).
  • Relevant: Gives countries facing food-supply disruptions a route to local protein production without dependence on one company or exporter. Public-good value is measured by reproducibility, safety, cost and repairability, not revenue.
  • Time-bound: Project starts ASAP at Month 0 (2026-10-09).   • single-cell protein
  • open-source hardware
  • gas fermentation
  • food security

Risk Assessment and Mitigation Strategies

Key Risks

  • Hydrogen-oxygen explosion hazard from electrolyzer, gas lines and headspace
  • Strain rights, patent or Kenyan biosafety barriers blocking lawful replication
  • Scale-up failure: mass transfer, productivity and energy per kg do not hold; deployment cost chain gap (EUR 7.93/kg above cap) (estimate)
  • Product regulatory pathway or nucleic acid limits blocking the chosen category
  • Documentation gaps found only at replication, or compromised independence

Diverse Risks

  • Unsigned partners, host priorities or adopter withdrawal
  • Gate panel independence weakened, allowing continuation by momentum
  • Kenyan site chosen for convenience, or envelope drifting mid-project
  • Contamination or strain drift over long runs and power cycling
  • EUR/KES volatility; funding route for the EUR 274,820/yr deployment gap undecided (estimate)

Mitigation Plans

  • Engage independent HAZOP/ATEX consultant by Month 1 (2026-11-09); issue safety design basis and Adopter Change Boundary v0 by Month 3 (2027-01-09); independently review interlocks before any pressurized build
  • Front-load strain rights, patent search and informal Kenyan biosafety contact; deliver Strain Feasibility Report with primary and legally clean backup by Month 4 (2027-02-09)
  • Pre-register reactor selection rules and disproof thresholds; run triplicate matched comparisons with external audit; release reference-unit hardware (EUR 4.0M) only at the Phase Two gate
  • Run early independent paper-and-bench replication Months 14-24 (2027-12-09 to 2028-10-09) with defect tracker, auditor and reserved EUR 0.15M; use audited assistance log reviewed monthly
  • Charter funder-managed panel (EUR 0.30M) with published deviations; independent Kenyan site baseline by Month 4 (2027-02-09); hold EUR 4.0M programme reserve including EUR 0.5M currency fund; recommend reduced Phase Three or Research Only if cost chain still fails

Stakeholder Analysis

Primary Stakeholders

  • Danish university consortium project team (process engineers, microbiologist, safety engineer, regulatory expert)
  • Kenyan co-development partner and independent replication team
  • Independent gate-review panel (3-5 members)
  • Funder holding release authority
  • Prospective adopters (e.g. reserve agency, feed producer, humanitarian logistics organization)

Secondary Stakeholders

  • Strain holders and culture collections
  • Regulators: Danish/EU authorities, Kenya National Biosafety Authority
  • Independent ATEX/safety consultants, auditors and patent counsel
  • Existing open-hardware and gas fermentation researchers (e.g. AMYBO)
  • Equipment, nitrogen and mineral suppliers; local technicians

Engagement Strategies

  • Primary team and partners: quarterly steering committee, monthly progress and spend reports, prompt answers to information requests
  • Panel: written charter, briefing packs 4-6 weeks before each gate, published recommendations and any funder deviation
  • Adopters: structured interviews, scenario profiles by Month 6 (2027-04-09), signed commitments by Month 7 (2027-05-09), locked at Month 9 (2027-07-09), publish any withdrawal
  • Regulators and strain holders: early informal pre-submission dialogue, written feedback logged as design inputs
  • Researchers and suppliers: collaboration agreements, milestone updates, notice of scope or timeline changes

Regulatory and Compliance Requirements

Permits and Licenses

  • Contained-use authorization for the production organism in Denmark/EU
  • Kenyan biosafety approval and strain import permit
  • Site and ATEX-related operating permits for hydrogen systems in Denmark and Kenya
  • Feed or food product registration (category-dependent), not required for research success
  • Material transfer agreements and strain licences

Compliance Standards

  • ATEX and hydrogen process safety design, HAZOP/LOPA
  • Feed/food safety and novel protein composition requirements per category
  • Biosafety and contained-use rules
  • Electrical and pressure equipment codes
  • Open licence terms consistent with third-party patents and strain terms

Regulatory Bodies

  • Danish authorities and EU competent authorities (including EFSA for product safety)
  • Kenya National Biosafety Authority
  • Kenya Bureau of Standards and Ministry of Health
  • Patent offices in Denmark/EU, Kenya and Bangladesh (landscape)

Compliance Actions

  • Commission regulatory and patent landscape in Months 0-4 (2026-10-09 to 2027-02-09) and open informal authority dialogue
  • Complete HAZOP and independent interlock review before pressurized builds
  • Document strain rights and Kenyan import before design freeze
  • Publish per-jurisdiction patent restrictions; release operating instructions only after safety and legal review
  • Name provisional product category at Phase One gate; confirm at Phase Two gate on composition data

Primary Decisions

The vital few decisions that have the most impact.

The five Critical levers are the reactor concept, the safety design basis, the strain rights strategy, replication and gate governance, and deployment threshold locking. As a group they address productivity versus safety and repairability, openness versus lawful strain access, and evidence credibility versus cost and schedule. High levers cover outage handling, automation, downstream processing, the host site and scale-up. No major dimension is missing, though funding and partner agreements are only implicit.

Decision 1: Gas-Liquid Contacting and Reactor Concept

Lever ID: acd340f7-7592-4494-bfed-58a0c57225c8

The Core Decision: Determines how hydrogen is transferred into the culture and what that implies for hazardous-zone size, seals, energy per kilogram and repair skill. Scope covers pneumatic loop, pressurized stirred and passive-feed concepts, plus the measured productivity cost of simplification. Success metrics: volumetric productivity and mass-transfer coefficients with uncertainty ranges, kWh per kg dry biomass, and qualification level needed for repair.

Why It Matters: Reactor choice sets hydrogen transfer rate, energy per kilogram, explosion exposure and the skill needed to operate and repair the unit. Pneumatic loop designs have fewer moving parts but may cap productivity. Pressurized stirred designs raise productivity but add ATEX burden, seals and specialist maintenance. The productivity cost of simplification is itself a headline result, so both ends need measuring.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Develop a low-pressure pneumatic loop or bubble-column reactor with no mechanical agitation, and accept lower volumetric productivity in exchange for simpler repair and a smaller hazardous zone.
  2. Develop a pressurized stirred-tank reactor with high-productivity gas transfer, and accept ATEX certification, seal maintenance and specialist-qualified service as part of the design.
  3. Run matched pneumatic, stirred and passive-feed reactors on identical strain and media, then publish a measured productivity-versus-simplicity curve before choosing the Phase Three reference unit.

Trade-Off / Risk: Testing all three concepts gives the strongest evidence but consumes Phase One and Two budget and time, while committing early to one concept risks locking in a design whose scale-up assumptions fail late.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Supplies the measurements that Scale-Up Evidence Ladder and Disproof Experiments needs to test extrapolation, and informs Automation Depth and Operator Skill Boundary by defining how many moving parts, sensors and interlocks the unit requires.

Conflict: Pressurized stirred designs raise productivity but add ATEX burden, conflicting with Inherent Safety Design Basis and Adopter Change Boundary and with local repairability under Automation Depth and Operator Skill Boundary. Matched testing of all concepts also competes with Strain Portfolio and Rights Strategy for Phase One budget.

Justification: Critical, Central hub: sets mass transfer, energy per kilogram, hazardous-zone size and repair skill. It conflicts with safety, change boundary and automation, and supplies the data for scale-up. It controls the core productivity-versus-simplicity trade-off behind hypotheses A and B.

Decision 2: Strain Portfolio and Rights Strategy

Lever ID: a991eeee-72d9-4e6c-88fe-40bd04f3c9b3

The Core Decision: Selects the reference strain and a backup, and documents its rights for research, commercial production, redistribution, modification and derived strains. It also covers biosafety class, import permissibility into Kenya and nucleic acid content. Success metrics: written rights analysis per strain, confirmed lawful obtainability by independent implementers in target countries, and comparative productivity under identical conditions.

Why It Matters: The reference strain determines productivity, nucleic acid content, biosafety class and above all legal reproducibility. A public-collection strain such as C. necator H16 eases lawful access but may carry restrictions on commercial use or derived strains. Alternatives could perform better but weaken the requirement that independent implementers can lawfully obtain the strain in target countries.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Commit to a single public-collection reference strain, document its rights for research, commercial use, redistribution and modification, and confirm lawful import into Kenya before any design freeze.
  2. Screen several candidate strains in Phase One for productivity and rights, and carry a primary and a legally clean backup strain through Phase Two so a rights or performance failure does not stop the project.
  3. Isolate or evolve a project-owned strain from environmental samples or adaptive laboratory evolution, deposit it in a public collection under open terms, and compare it against the public reference strain.

Trade-Off / Risk: A project-owned strain could remove legal dependence on third parties, but it adds years of characterization, biosafety and regulatory work that may exceed the Phase One budget, and it may never match the reference's productivity.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Underpins Open Licence Stack and Stewardship Model, since publishable strain instructions depend on clear rights, and supports Replication Design and Gate Governance by letting the Kenyan team obtain the strain without developer help.

Conflict: Carrying a backup or project-owned strain adds characterization and biosafety work that competes with Gas-Liquid Contacting and Reactor Concept testing and with Regulatory Engagement Sequencing. A rights-clean strain may also be less productive than alternatives.

Justification: Critical, Foundational pillar: lawful strain access for independent implementers is a hard project requirement. It underpins the open licence stack, enables replication without developer help, and links to regulation and contamination control. A rights or performance failure could stop the whole project.

Decision 3: Replication Design and Gate Governance

Lever ID: 46bf5862-3ae2-48f5-bb1a-0f0a5fc459a4

The Core Decision: Defines how independence of the Kenyan replication is secured and who controls money at each gate. Scope covers team separation, the audited assistance log, documentation-defect tracking, reviewer funding independence, and written continue/modify/research-only/stop decisions. Success metrics: defects found per documentation release, share resolved before construction, reviewer independence verified, and no gate passed by default or momentum.

Why It Matters: This lever sets how independent the Kenyan replication is, how documentation gaps are discovered, and who can release or stop funding. A stricter separation yields more credible evidence of reproducibility, but it risks unsafe or wasted attempts if documentation is poor. Gate design determines whether the EUR 50 million ceiling is spent in stages or committed by momentum.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Run one full-scale Kenyan replication after the Danish reference unit is complete, using a separate team under an audited assistance log, and fund it only after the gate reviewers confirm documentation readiness.
  2. Add an early paper-and-bench replication in Phase Two, in which an independent group builds a small unit from draft documents, to find documentation defects before committing to full-scale construction.
  3. Fund an independent reviewer panel with its own budget and authority to release or withhold each phase's money, and require a written continue, modify, research-only or stop decision at every gate.

Trade-Off / Risk: An early documentation-only replication catches gaps cheaply, but it adds cost and schedule, and a small-scale success may give false confidence about full-scale builds, outage behavior and local sourcing.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Amplifies Scale-Up Evidence Ladder and Disproof Experiments, since pre-set gate criteria give disproof results binding force. Also strengthens Open Licence Stack and Stewardship Model, because logged ambiguities feed documentation fixes before publication.

Conflict: Strict separation and staged funding slow Kenyan Host Site and Partner Configuration, because a harsh site needs developer support that the assistance log restricts. It also competes with Inherent Safety Design Basis and Adopter Change Boundary where safe operation needs intervention.

Justification: Critical, Controls the independence of the replication and who releases funding at each gate. It gives disproof results and thresholds binding force and prevents continuation by momentum. It governs the trade-off between credible reproducibility evidence and cost, schedule and safe operation.

Decision 4: Deployment Scenario Anchoring and Threshold Locking

Lever ID: 69832a26-b5ef-4c64-b6e7-0e767bbe9057

The Core Decision: Defines the user scenarios the design must beat and fixes maximum production cost, minimum useful capacity and required reliability before any prototype evaluation. It gives the Phase Three Go decision its meaning. Key metrics are the number of locked scenarios, the quality of the benchmark data behind them, evidence of adopter input, and the absence of any post-hoc threshold change.

Why It Matters: Choosing which user scenarios the design must beat, and fixing maximum cost, minimum capacity and reliability before testing, determines whether the final Go decision means anything. Scenarios close to real adopters give the most credible evidence but depend on partners who are not yet signed. Hypothetical scenarios are easier to define but are easier to adjust to fit results.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Define two or three candidate scenarios with named prospective adopters, such as a national reserve agency or a regional feed producer, and lock their thresholds in a signed, time-stamped document before any prototype evaluation.
  2. Derive scenarios from published cost data on protein reserves, legumes and proprietary systems, and lock thresholds as the margin the open design needs over the best defensible alternative in each case.
  3. Appoint an independent adversarial review panel that sets and holds the scenario thresholds, and allow it to add a harsher scenario once Phase Two data are available but never to relax any existing one.

Trade-Off / Risk: Pre-set thresholds protect the Go decision from rationalization, but if they are set from weak cost data or without real adopter input, the project may pass or fail against a scenario no one would actually use.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Gives Replication Design and Gate Governance fixed pass/fail criteria for Go/Modify/Stop decisions, and gives Scale-Up Evidence Ladder and Disproof Experiments a concrete target capacity and cost to test against.

Conflict: Locking thresholds early restricts Gas-Liquid Contacting and Reactor Concept and Automation Depth and Operator Skill Boundary, which may later prove better with different trade-offs. Named adopters are also unsigned and may withdraw, forcing rework.

Justification: Critical, Gives the Phase Three Go decision its meaning by fixing cost, capacity and reliability thresholds before testing. It supplies pass/fail criteria to gates and targets to scale-up, and constrains reactor and automation choices. It governs the public-value case and prevents post-hoc rationalization.

Decision 5: Inherent Safety Design Basis and Adopter Change Boundary

Lever ID: 2aa84815-ce55-481c-b5f3-85b0e9261da3

The Core Decision: Determines how the hydrogen-oxygen ignition hazard is controlled: through inherent limits on gas composition and inventory, layered instrumented protection, or a machine-readable safety case. It also defines which parts and parameters adopters may change without reassessment. Metrics include hazard-analysis findings closed, independent interlock review results, safety incidents, and the productivity penalty measured against the safety margin.

Why It Matters: This lever sets how hydrogen-oxygen explosion risk is controlled: by gas-composition and inventory limits designed into the process, or by layered instrumented protection. It also fixes which components and parameters adopters may change without a full safety reassessment. A tighter boundary lowers the risk of unsafe local adaptation but reduces the repairability and substitution freedom that hypothesis B depends on.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Design the process around inherently safer limits, such as keeping gas mixtures outside flammable ranges and minimizing gas inventory, so most failures cannot reach an ignitable state without relying on instrumentation.
  2. Adopt layered instrumented protection with independently reviewed interlocks and emergency shutdown, and publish a short list of pre-assessed substitutable components and adjustable parameters for adopters.
  3. Publish a machine-readable safety case in which each parameter and component carries a computed safe-change envelope, so adopters can check a proposed modification against the hazard analysis before building it.

Trade-Off / Risk: Inherently safer limits may cut productivity because gas-liquid transfer often improves with richer, more reactive mixtures, so the safety margin and the productivity benchmark pull against each other and the cost must be measured, not assumed.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Supports Outage Survival and Hydrogen Buffering Strategy by bounding safe gas inventory during shutdown and restart, and underpins Open Licence Stack and Stewardship Model by letting operating instructions pass safety and legal review for release.

Conflict: Tighter limits can reduce gas-liquid transfer and productivity, conflicting with Gas-Liquid Contacting and Reactor Concept. A narrow adopter change boundary also limits the substitution freedom that Kenyan Host Site and Partner Configuration and hypothesis B depend on.

Justification: Critical, Hub controlling the hydrogen-oxygen explosion risk and what adopters may change. It trades safety margin against productivity and repairability, and conflicts with reactor, host site and licence choices. It supports outage handling and release of operating instructions, so it is a non-negotiable design constraint.

Secondary Decisions

These decisions are less significant, but still worth considering.

Decision 6: Reference Architecture Sourcing

Lever ID: 856adffe-4bbc-41ac-8941-72d93379b50c

The Core Decision: Sets the Phase One decision on whether published open work (for example the electroPioreactor or passive gas-feeding research) becomes the base design or is only a data source. Scope includes benchmark protocol, selection criteria and the licence status of inherited material. Success metrics: decision evidence recorded before blueprint v0.1, measured productivity and safety gaps versus requirements, and researcher collaboration agreements signed.

Why It Matters: This lever decides whether the project adopts an existing open design, such as the electroPioreactor or passive gas-feeding work, or defines its own architecture. Building on existing work shortens Phase One and builds researcher goodwill, but it inherits that work's scale and safety limits. A clean-sheet design gives control over safety and replicability but risks duplicating published effort and delaying measurements.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Adopt one published open design as the reference architecture, then extend it with safety engineering, product-quality control and documentation for independent builders.
  2. Run a short head-to-head benchmark of two or three published designs in Phase One, then select or hybridize on measured productivity, safety and buildability.
  3. Commission a clean-sheet process design from a safety-first specification, treating published designs only as data sources, to avoid inherited limits on scale and certification.

Trade-Off / Risk: Adopting an existing design saves time, but its assumptions about scale, gas safety and component availability may not hold in Kenya, so the Phase One decision needs measured evidence rather than familiarity or collaboration convenience.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Feeds Gas-Liquid Contacting and Reactor Concept by supplying candidate designs and baseline data, and strengthens Open Licence Stack and Stewardship Model when the inherited design carries compatible open licences that keep the core publishable.

Conflict: Adopting a published design early can pre-empt Gas-Liquid Contacting and Reactor Concept testing and bind Inherent Safety Design Basis and Adopter Change Boundary to another group's safety assumptions. Benchmarking several designs also consumes Phase One time and budget.

Justification: High, Decides in Phase One whether published open work becomes the base design. Feeds the reactor concept and licence stack, but can bind safety assumptions to another group. Important early and time-bound, though its influence is largely absorbed by the reactor and safety choices.

Decision 7: Outage Survival and Hydrogen Buffering Strategy

Lever ID: f132b399-c700-490e-bce8-ba01610786fe

The Core Decision: Defines how the unit behaves when grid or solar power fails without mandated hydrogen storage: safe shutdown, culture hold, documented restart and the maximum outage survived. It also drives electrolyzer sizing, battery needs and the energy-crisis resilience claim. Success metrics: outage duration survived, restart time, post-restart productivity recovery, and strain stability over repeated cycles.

Why It Matters: Because hydrogen storage is not mandated, the process must be designed for grid or solar interruptions through safe shutdown, culture hold and documented restart. This choice sets how much downtime the culture and product quality can tolerate and how much battery, storage or duplication is needed. It also changes the electrolyzer sizing and the energy-crisis resilience claim.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Design for on-demand electrolysis with no hydrogen storage, using automatic safe shutdown, a culture-hold protocol and a documented restart sequence, and measure the maximum outage the culture survives.
  2. Add a small, independently reviewed hydrogen buffer or battery bridge that rides through short outages, and keep the long-outage protocol identical to the no-storage design.
  3. Treat intermittent supply as the normal operating mode by coupling the electrolyzer directly to variable solar power and running the culture in deliberate on-off cycles, then test productivity loss against steady-state operation.

Trade-Off / Risk: Surviving outages without storage keeps hazards low, but repeated stress cycles may degrade strain stability and productivity, and intermittent operation could undercut the cost and uptime thresholds that make a deployment case credible.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Supports Kenyan Host Site and Partner Configuration, because a site with a measured outage pattern gives realistic test cases, and supports Deployment Scenario Anchoring and Threshold Locking by establishing the reliability that scenarios must meet.

Conflict: A hydrogen buffer or battery bridge adds hazard and cost, pulling against Inherent Safety Design Basis and Adopter Change Boundary. Repeated stress cycles can also undermine Contamination Control and Culture Continuity Regime and the strain's productivity stability.

Justification: High, Defines behaviour under power failure without mandated storage, driving electrolyzer sizing, safety exposure and the resilience claim. It links to the Kenyan site, scenario thresholds, safety and culture stability. Strong interactions, but narrower than the foundational design levers.

Decision 8: Automation Depth and Operator Skill Boundary

Lever ID: acc4906f-7eb6-4b83-985b-d48d6910d181

The Core Decision: Places the line between automated control and human judgement, determining which tasks locally trained technicians may do and which need defined qualifications. It governs controller choice, interlock architecture, software openness and training burden. Success metrics: operator competence after a short verified programme, mean time to repair with local parts, no interlock bypass, and fault-injection pass rates by operator level.

Why It Matters: Automation reduces the training needed for routine operation but increases the controller, sensor and software complexity that independent teams must source and repair. Too little automation raises operator error near hydrogen and oxygen. Choosing where the line sits between locally trained technicians and qualified specialists defines the evidence for hypothesis A and the repairability claim in hypothesis B.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Build a PLC-based system with interlocks and a documented parameter envelope on widely available commodity hardware, so routine runs need only short, competency-verified training.
  2. Use a deliberately minimal, mostly hardwired and mechanical safety layer with few software functions, and rely on stricter operator procedures and checklists for routine control.
  3. Split the system into a sealed, independently reviewed safety module that only qualified staff may service, and an open, modifiable process-control layer that local technicians may adapt within defined limits.

Trade-Off / Risk: Splitting safety from process control clarifies who may change what, but it creates a specialist dependency that conflicts with the goal of local repairability, especially where certified service is far away.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Provides the operational evidence for Inherent Safety Design Basis and Adopter Change Boundary by making change rights explicit, and helps Replication Design and Gate Governance by giving the Kenyan team a clear competence boundary to test.

Conflict: A sealed safety module creates specialist dependency that conflicts with Kenyan Host Site and Partner Configuration constraints on service access and spare parts. Deeper automation also adds software complexity that tension with open, independently repairable hardware.

Justification: High, Sets the line between automation and technician judgement, which is the direct evidence for hypothesis A and repairability in B. Connects to safety, reactor, downstream, contamination and the Kenyan site. It largely follows from the reactor and safety choices.

Decision 9: Nitrogen and Mineral Supply Localization

Lever ID: 432d7737-4969-4c79-9137-1a6fb38c81cf

The Core Decision: Decides which nitrogen compound and mineral medium the process uses, and how far each can be sourced locally or regionally. It governs hazard class, storage, purity tolerance and the days of production sustained without resupply. Success metrics: resupply-autonomy days per input, share of inputs sourced locally or regionally, and growth and biomass-quality variation across supplier purity ranges.

Why It Matters: The nitrogen source (ammonia, ammonium salts, urea or other forms) and the mineral medium determine hazard class, transport needs, and how many days production continues without resupply. Local or regional sourcing improves vendor independence but may bring variable purity that affects growth and biomass quality. Imported, standardized inputs make results reproducible but weaken the independence argument.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Standardize on a single commodity nitrogen compound with documented specifications and at least two alternative regional suppliers, and test growth across the purity range those suppliers deliver.
  2. Design the medium around locally producible nitrogen and minerals, such as fertilizer-grade salts or recovered streams, and measure the productivity and quality penalty relative to laboratory-grade inputs.
  3. Run a staged input-substitution programme in which each critical input is progressively replaced by a locally sourced equivalent, with the resupply-autonomy figure for each input recorded and published at each step.

Trade-Off / Risk: Substituting cheaper local inputs can quietly shift biomass composition and contaminant load, so savings in sourcing may reappear as extra downstream processing or regulatory burden if quality is not tracked alongside autonomy.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Supports Deployment Scenario Anchoring and Threshold Locking by supplying the local-sourcing and autonomy figures that scenario thresholds rely on. Also supports Kenyan Host Site and Partner Configuration, since the site tests real supply chains.

Conflict: Variable local input purity strains Contamination Control and Culture Continuity Regime and can burden the Downstream Protein Purification Train with extra contaminant or nucleic acid handling, offsetting sourcing savings.

Justification: Medium, Determines resupply autonomy and local sourcing share, which support scenario thresholds and the Kenyan site. Its effects are mostly input-level optimization, with side effects on contamination and downstream load. Less connected to the core strategic conflicts.

Decision 10: Downstream Protein Purification Train

Lever ID: 5e133b86-6e5d-455f-815e-2260b25c2aad

The Core Decision: Covers harvesting, cell disruption, nucleic acid reduction and drying, which turn raw biomass into usable, digestible protein. It sets the equipment, energy and labour burden beyond the fermenter and the range of eligible product categories. Success metrics: nucleic acid content, protein digestibility, energy and cost per kilogram of usable protein, and technician competence on each step, all measured on one fixed processing boundary.

Why It Matters: Harvesting, cell disruption, nucleic acid reduction and drying decide whether biomass is usable protein and how much equipment and energy sit beyond the fermenter. A heavier train raises protein quality and the range of eligible product categories but adds maintenance burden for local technicians. A lighter train protects simplicity but may restrict the product to uses with lower purity demands.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Build a minimal train of centrifugation or filtration and low-complexity drying, and accept a limited product range pending composition and digestibility data from Phase Two.
  2. Include a validated nucleic acid reduction step, such as thermal or enzymatic treatment, in the reference design and test whether technicians can run it within the defined competency envelope.
  3. Develop the downstream train as separable tiers, with a core tier for all adopters and optional upgrade modules, so that the fermenter design is not constrained by the most demanding product category.

Trade-Off / Risk: Downstream steps are often underestimated in techno-economic models, and the energy and labour they add can erase fermenter-level gains, so the same processing boundary must be used for every benchmark comparison.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Enables Regulatory Engagement Sequencing, since validated composition and purity data define the product-safety dossier. Also reinforces Deployment Scenario Anchoring and Threshold Locking by showing which product categories meet cost and quality thresholds.

Conflict: A heavier train conflicts with Automation Depth and Operator Skill Boundary by adding maintenance tasks beyond routine technician skills. It also competes with Scale-Up Evidence Ladder and Disproof Experiments for budget and test capacity.

Justification: High, Decides whether biomass becomes usable, digestible protein and how much energy, cost and maintenance sit beyond the fermenter. It shapes product category, regulatory dossier and operator burden. Often underestimated, so it needs a fixed processing boundary for benchmarks.

Decision 11: Kenyan Host Site and Partner Configuration

Lever ID: 7f1b38e0-d840-43ba-9493-cc044ad848c6

The Core Decision: Determines where and with whom the replication takes place, and so whether it truly tests unreliable power, water quality, climate, spares and local skills. It covers site selection, co-development partner roles, logistics and access to analytics and safety review. Success metrics: documented envelope measurements for the site, commissioning time, outage-survival results, and the share of failures attributable to logistics rather than design.

Why It Matters: The site and partner arrangement determines whether the replication really tests unreliable power, water, climate and supply chains, or becomes a showcase. A harsh site yields credible evidence but raises the risk of delays, failed tests and safety exposure. A better-supported site lowers risk but weakens the claim that the design works under difficult infrastructure.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Select a site in an area with documented frequent grid outages and limited spare-part access, and accept longer commissioning and higher logistics effort in return for stronger evidence on Hypothesis B.
  2. Select a mid-tier site with measurable but moderate infrastructure limits, and add controlled stressors such as induced outages and degraded water to reach the harsher envelope in a safer setting.
  3. Run a two-site design in which a harsh-infrastructure site does the unsupported build and fault-injection tests while a better-equipped partner site provides independent analytics and safety review.

Trade-Off / Risk: A site chosen for convenience will pass tests that a real adopter would fail, but a site chosen for hardship may fail for logistical reasons that obscure whether the documentation or the design was at fault.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Strengthens Outage Survival and Hydrogen Buffering Strategy by providing a real outage pattern against which to validate it. Also amplifies Nitrogen and Mineral Supply Localization, since real local supply chains expose true resupply autonomy.

Conflict: A harsh site raises safety exposure, which pushes against Inherent Safety Design Basis and Adopter Change Boundary. It also strains Replication Design and Gate Governance, since logistics failures can obscure whether documentation or design caused a test failure.

Justification: High, Determines whether the replication truly tests the harsh operating envelope or becomes a showcase. Links outage patterns, real supply chains, safety exposure and gate governance. Very important for the hypothesis B evidence, but depends on design choices and unsigned partners.

Decision 12: Open Licence Stack and Stewardship Model

Lever ID: 0c5f4dfa-77fa-47d3-999b-e0c3794c1c13

The Core Decision: Sets the licences for hardware, software, data and documentation, and the legal body that holds and enforces them. It governs whether the core stays open, whether adopters can build commercially without legal risk, and how conformity to the tested reference is shown. Success metrics: freedom-to-operate review completed per jurisdiction before release, adopter uptake, closed-fork incidents, and stewardship funding continuity.

Why It Matters: The licence mix for hardware, software, data and documentation, together with the legal body that holds them, decides whether the core stays open and whether adopters can build commercially without legal risk. Strong reciprocal terms protect openness but may deter industrial adopters. Permissive terms spread the design widely but allow closed forks, including by a single company, which the project aims to avoid.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Use reciprocal open licences across hardware, software and documentation so that improvements by adopters must be shared back, with a non-profit steward enforcing them.
  2. Use permissive licences for data and documentation and reciprocal licences only for safety-critical designs and control software, so that safety changes remain traceable.
  3. Place the design under a defensive-publication and patent-pledge structure managed by a neutral foundation, with a certification mark that lets adopters show conformity to the tested reference.

Trade-Off / Risk: Licence terms cannot override patents or strain restrictions held by third parties, so the governance model gives little protection unless the freedom-to-operate review is completed per jurisdiction before the release.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Amplifies Strain Portfolio and Rights Strategy, since clear strain rights allow the full package to be released under consistent terms. Also supports Replication Design and Gate Governance by giving the audited documentation a controlled, versioned home.

Conflict: Strong reciprocal terms may deter industrial adopters, working against Deployment Scenario Anchoring and Threshold Locking. Releasing operating instructions openly also pressures Inherent Safety Design Basis and Adopter Change Boundary, since uncontrolled forks may alter safety-critical parameters.

Justification: Medium, Keeps the core open and prevents closed forks, which fits the mission. However it depends on strain rights, freedom-to-operate review and safety review, and it cannot override third-party patents. Mostly an enabling layer rather than a driver of technical outcomes.

Decision 13: Regulatory Engagement Sequencing

Lever ID: 8fa32114-4c8e-4bfa-9ffe-b2f3e7cb0501

The Core Decision: Sets when and in what form the project approaches Danish, EU and Kenyan authorities, separating experimental operation (contained use, site permits), product safety validation and commercial distribution. Success is measured by the number of hard requirements identified before hardware is committed, written feedback logged as design inputs, and a documented regulatory pathway per jurisdiction by the Phase One gate.

Why It Matters: The timing and form of contact with Danish, EU and Kenyan authorities determines how early the project learns about hard requirements on strain classification, contained use, product safety and distribution. Early engagement can reshape the design before costs are sunk but exposes immature data. Late engagement protects focus but risks discovering a blocking requirement after hardware is built.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Open informal pre-submission dialogue with the competent authorities in Denmark/EU and Kenya during Phase One and use their written feedback as design inputs for the blueprint.
  2. Engage regulators only for experimental operation and contained-use permits until Phase Two data exist, then open product-safety discussions with a complete composition and digestibility dossier.
  3. Commission an independent regulatory firm to build a jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction requirements map, including routes in a third country such as Bangladesh, and rank the design options by regulatory friction before talking to any authority.

Trade-Off / Risk: Early regulator contact can surface a blocking requirement cheaply, but informal feedback is not binding, so a favourable signal could be mistaken for a pathway that formal review later closes.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Feeds Strain Portfolio and Rights Strategy with early strain-classification and contained-use rulings, and informs Deployment Scenario Anchoring and Threshold Locking by showing which product categories can realistically be distributed in each target jurisdiction.

Conflict: Early dialogue competes with Downstream Protein Purification Train and Scale-Up Evidence Ladder and Disproof Experiments for immature data and staff time. Regulators may demand dossiers before processing and composition data are stable, so design freedom can narrow prematurely.

Justification: Medium, Timing of authority contact affects how early blocking requirements surface, informing strain and scenario choices. Informal feedback is non-binding, and the lever mainly sequences effort. A credible pathway is required, but this lever is subordinate to product and strain decisions.

Decision 14: Scale-Up Evidence Ladder and Disproof Experiments

Lever ID: 6412e8f5-30eb-40c3-9617-77ae0e3d0968

The Core Decision: Connects the reference-unit capacity to the modeled deployment capacity through measured steps and experiments designed to disprove the main scale-up assumptions. Success means pre-registered failure thresholds, uncertainty ranges on every extrapolation, and consistent definitions of volumetric productivity and system energy use against published benchmarks. It guards against treating a working reference unit as proof of industrial viability.

Why It Matters: This lever defines how the reference-unit capacity and the modeled deployment capacity are connected, and which principal scale-up assumptions are tested to failure before Phase Two. A ladder of intermediate scales gives measured uncertainty ranges but consumes schedule and budget. Skipping rungs saves money but leaves extrapolation resting on models rather than measurements, which the plan rules out.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Build a stepwise ladder of bench, container-scale and reference-unit tests, with each rung required to reproduce the previous rung's mass-transfer and productivity numbers within stated uncertainty before proceeding.
  2. Run scale-down experiments that deliberately reproduce large-scale gradients in small reactors, so the scale-up assumptions are attacked cheaply in the laboratory before any larger hardware is committed.
  3. Commission an independent modeling group to build a competing scale-up model from the published data and to design the experiments most likely to falsify the project's own model.

Trade-Off / Risk: Disproof experiments only help if their failure thresholds are fixed before data arrive, and a competing model costs real money; without pre-registration, the ladder becomes a story told after the fact.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Supplies measured mass-transfer and productivity data to Gas-Liquid Contacting and Reactor Concept and Downstream Protein Purification Train, and gives Replication Design and Gate Governance evidence for the Phase Two kill gate.

Conflict: Extra rungs and competing models consume budget and schedule, constraining Replication Design and Gate Governance timelines and Kenyan Host Site and Partner Configuration. Pre-registered failure thresholds can also force early stops of promising reactor concepts.

Justification: High, Connects reference-unit data to modeled deployment capacity through pre-registered disproof experiments, guarding against treating a working unit as industrial proof. It strengthens the Phase Two gate and draws on reactor data. Important, but it largely operationalizes other choices.

Decision 15: Contamination Control and Culture Continuity Regime

Lever ID: dcbb34d4-efea-4c0e-863e-4840687b04c7

The Core Decision: Governs how the single pure strain is protected from contamination and kept viable, covering seed-train procedures, cryo-stock storage and revival, purity verification, and the limit on sterility requirements the operating envelope allows. Key metrics are batch loss rate, time to restore a lost line, purity-test pass rate, and whether product specification holds when sterility is relaxed.

Why It Matters: This lever governs how a single pure strain is kept uncontaminated and viable in settings with limited sterile infrastructure, including how seed cultures are stored, revived and verified. A strict aseptic regime protects product quality and safety but demands skills and consumables that may not exist locally. A relaxed regime fits the operating envelope but raises batch-loss and product-safety risk.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Specify a full aseptic protocol with sterilizable reactors, validated seed-train procedures and routine purity checks, with biological quality assurance reserved for explicitly qualified staff.
  2. Design for contamination tolerance by exploiting the selective growth conditions of autotrophic hydrogen-oxidizing growth, and test how far sterility requirements can be relaxed without failing product specification.
  3. Create a distributed seed-culture continuity scheme in which certified cryo-stocks are held at several independent sites, so a lost or contaminated line can be restored without the original developers.

Trade-Off / Risk: Relying on selective growth conditions to tolerate contamination is plausible but unproven for this configuration, and a single undetected contaminant in a food or feed product could outweigh any simplification gain.

Strategic Connections:
