Synergy: Strengthens Strain Portfolio and Rights Strategy through lawful cryo-stock distribution and traceable strain provenance, and supports Replication Design and Gate Governance by letting the Kenyan team recover lost lines without developer help.

Conflict: A strict aseptic regime conflicts with Automation Depth and Operator Skill Boundary and Kenyan Host Site and Partner Configuration, since it needs skills, consumables and sterilizable equipment that may be scarce locally. Tolerance-based approaches risk product safety.

Justification: Medium, Protects a single pure strain and enables recovery of lost lines without developers. It trades product safety against skills and consumables, touching automation and the Kenyan site. Mostly an operational optimization, reasonably contained within the strain and automation decisions.

Choosing our strategic path.

The Strategic Context

Understanding the core ambitions and constraints that guide our decision.

Ambition and Scale: Infrastructure-scale public-good R&D programme over about 5 years with a provisional ceiling of EUR 50 million (user constraint), of which Phase One is up to EUR 6 million (user constraint). It spans Denmark and Kenya, with Bangladesh in the patent and regulatory landscape. The aim is an open, independently replicable protein process for food-supply disruptions, not a commercial product.

Risk and Novelty: High novelty and high technical, safety and legal risk. No publicly documented, independently replicated, industrially relevant implementation is known (claim taken from the plan, not verified). Main risks are hydrogen-oxygen explosion hazard, gas-liquid mass transfer and scale-up, strain rights, nucleic acid content, product regulation, and documentation gaps found only at replication. The plan expects failure to be possible: it has kill gates and Go, Modify, Research Only and Stop outcomes.

Complexity and Constraints: Very high complexity. It has two separately tested hypotheses (A: operation by local technicians; B: decentralised modules) and a measured operating envelope. It needs outage survival, a full material and energy balance, ATEX-compliant design, and pre-locked deployment thresholds. The Kenyan replication team must be organisationally separate, with an audited assistance log. It also needs independent gate reviewers with no funding dependence, and funding, partners, sites and permits are treated as uncontrolled until signed. Prescribed comparisons (high-productivity vs simplified designs, the productivity cost of simplification) and a requirement for a lawfully obtainable reference strain constrain the design space.

Domain and Tone: Engineering and biotechnology (electrolysis, hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria gas fermentation) with public-good, open-source governance. The tone is rigorous and evidence-driven, sceptical of its own results, and explicit that examples are starting points and not decisions.

Holistic Profile: A high-ambition, high-uncertainty, gated open-engineering programme whose strategy is to let measurement decide. It explicitly asks for a landscape review, a measured comparison of reactor concepts, a reference strain with a rights-clean fallback, thresholds locked before testing, layered and independently reviewed safety with a defined adopter change boundary, and independent replication. It rewards staged evidence and early discovery of failure over bold early commitment or minimal-cost conservatism.

The Path Forward

This scenario aligns best with the project's characteristics and goals.

The Evidence-First Builder

Strategic Logic: Let measurements, not early commitment, decide the design. Run matched reactor comparisons and carry a primary and a legally clean backup strain, so that neither a performance failure nor a rights failure stops the project. Anchor the pass/fail thresholds in named prospective adopters, and use an early small-scale replication to catch documentation gaps cheaply. Layered, independently reviewed protection with a short pre-assessed change list keeps safety rigorous and adopter modification manageable, at moderate cost and schedule.

Fit Score: 9/10

Why This Path Was Chosen: Matched reactor comparisons deliver the plan's required productivity-cost-of-simplification result. A primary and a backup strain address rights risk, and named-adopter thresholds are locked before testing. An early small-scale replication finds documentation defects cheaply, and layered reviewed interlocks with a short change list match the plan's ATEX and adopter-boundary wording. The main weaknesses are moderate extra cost and unsigned adopters.

Key Strategic Decisions:

  • Gas-Liquid Contacting and Reactor Concept: Run matched pneumatic, stirred and passive-feed reactors on identical strain and media, then publish a measured productivity-versus-simplicity curve before choosing the Phase Three reference unit.
  • Strain Portfolio and Rights Strategy: Screen several candidate strains in Phase One for productivity and rights, and carry a primary and a legally clean backup strain through Phase Two so a rights or performance failure does not stop the project.
  • Replication Design and Gate Governance: Add an early paper-and-bench replication in Phase Two, in which an independent group builds a small unit from draft documents, to find documentation defects before committing to full-scale construction.
  • Deployment Scenario Anchoring and Threshold Locking: Define two or three candidate scenarios with named prospective adopters, such as a national reserve agency or a regional feed producer, and lock their thresholds in a signed, time-stamped document before any prototype evaluation.
  • Inherent Safety Design Basis and Adopter Change Boundary: Adopt layered instrumented protection with independently reviewed interlocks and emergency shutdown, and publish a short list of pre-assessed substitutable components and adjustable parameters for adopters.

The Decisive Factors:

  • Fits the plan's core logic: the plan wants measurement to decide. It requires a landscape review, a comparison of high-productivity and simplified designs, and a measured productivity cost of simplification. Only matched reactor testing delivers this.
  • Manages risk without over-spending: a primary and a rights-clean backup strain meet the requirement for a lawfully obtainable strain. Layered, independently reviewed interlocks plus a short pre-assessed change list match the ATEX and adopter-boundary requirements.
  • Gives gates meaning: thresholds locked with named adopters, and an early bench replication, expose failure before the large construction spend, which supports the kill gates.
  • Pioneer's Gambit: a pressurized reactor and a project-owned strain pre-commit and risk budget overrun.
  • Safe Foundation: a single pneumatic design cannot test hypothesis B or the simplification trade-off, and it finds documentation defects late.
  • Gate reviewers should still be independently funded (add-on from the plan).

Alternative Paths

The Pioneer's Gambit

Strategic Logic: Maximise technical and legal independence and productivity at once. Use a high-transfer pressurised reactor, a project-owned open strain, and a machine-readable safety case so that adopters can modify the design with checked safety. Replication starts early in Phase Two and thresholds are held by an adversarial panel, so documentation, safety-envelope and scenario weaknesses surface early. The cost is higher spend, specialist-qualified service, and a risk that strain development and ATEX work exceed the Phase One and Two budgets. This pathway also tests hypothesis A less directly than hypothesis B.

Fit Score: 3/10

Assessment of this Path: Commits early to a pressurized stirred reactor and a project-owned strain, which pre-empts the plan's required comparison of simplified and high-productivity designs. It also adds years of strain and biosafety work that conflicts with a lawfully obtainable public reference strain and the Phase One budget. It is weak on hypothesis A and on local repairability. Its early replication and adversarial thresholds do match the plan.

Key Strategic Decisions:

  • Gas-Liquid Contacting and Reactor Concept: Develop a pressurized stirred-tank reactor with high-productivity gas transfer, and accept ATEX certification, seal maintenance and specialist-qualified service as part of the design.
  • Strain Portfolio and Rights Strategy: Isolate or evolve a project-owned strain from environmental samples or adaptive laboratory evolution, deposit it in a public collection under open terms, and compare it against the public reference strain.
  • Replication Design and Gate Governance: Add an early paper-and-bench replication in Phase Two, in which an independent group builds a small unit from draft documents, to find documentation defects before committing to full-scale construction.
  • Deployment Scenario Anchoring and Threshold Locking: Appoint an independent adversarial review panel that sets and holds the scenario thresholds, and allow it to add a harsher scenario once Phase Two data are available but never to relax any existing one.
  • Inherent Safety Design Basis and Adopter Change Boundary: Publish a machine-readable safety case in which each parameter and component carries a computed safe-change envelope, so adopters can check a proposed modification against the hazard analysis before building it.

The Safe Foundation

Strategic Logic: Prioritise stability, low cost and reduced legal and safety risk. Commit to one public-collection strain and a simple low-pressure pneumatic reactor, and design for inherently safer limits so that most failures cannot ignite without relying on instrumentation. Fund a single full-scale Kenyan replication only after gate reviewers confirm documentation readiness, and set thresholds from published alternatives. This is the cheapest and most defensible route to hypothesis A. It accepts lower productivity and a risk of late-found documentation defects, and it may end in Research Only if no deployment case clears the margin.

Fit Score: 5/10

Assessment of this Path: It is cheap, legally simple and safe, and suits hypothesis A. It commits to one pneumatic design and one strain without measuring alternatives, so it cannot report the simplification cost or support hypothesis B. A late-only replication risks discovering documentation defects after construction, and thresholds taken only from published data lack adopter input.

Key Strategic Decisions:

  • Gas-Liquid Contacting and Reactor Concept: Develop a low-pressure pneumatic loop or bubble-column reactor with no mechanical agitation, and accept lower volumetric productivity in exchange for simpler repair and a smaller hazardous zone.
  • Strain Portfolio and Rights Strategy: Commit to a single public-collection reference strain, document its rights for research, commercial use, redistribution and modification, and confirm lawful import into Kenya before any design freeze.
  • Replication Design and Gate Governance: Run one full-scale Kenyan replication after the Danish reference unit is complete, using a separate team under an audited assistance log, and fund it only after the gate reviewers confirm documentation readiness.
  • Deployment Scenario Anchoring and Threshold Locking: Derive scenarios from published cost data on protein reserves, legumes and proprietary systems, and lock thresholds as the margin the open design needs over the best defensible alternative in each case.
  • Inherent Safety Design Basis and Adopter Change Boundary: Design the process around inherently safer limits, such as keeping gas mixtures outside flammable ranges and minimizing gas inventory, so most failures cannot reach an ignitable state without relying on instrumentation.

Purpose

Purpose: business

Purpose Detailed: Large-scale, public-good engineering and infrastructure initiative aimed at food-supply resilience and local protein production without dependence on a single company or exporter. It is a phased, gated R&D programme (provisional ceiling EUR 50 million) covering a landscape review, strain rights, safety design, techno-economic modelling, scale-up experiments, regulatory pathways in Denmark/EU and Kenya, open-licence publication of the full source package, and independent replication in Kenya. It is explicitly not profit-oriented, but it falls under societal, governmental and infrastructure-scale initiatives (public welfare, food security, large-scale resource management) with institutional hosting, funding accountability, kill gates and deployment scenarios. It is therefore classified as business under the societal-scale/infrastructure category.

Topic: The Open Protein Module: a non-profit, open-source engineering project to develop and independently replicate (Denmark development site, Kenya replication) a safe, reproducible, legally implementable hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria gas-fermentation process that converts electricity, water, CO2 and a nitrogen source into protein

Domain

Primary domain: Gas Fermentation Engineering

Secondary domains: Process Safety Engineering, Food Regulatory Affairs, Open Source Hardware

Rationale: Gas Fermentation Engineering is the only outcome-role candidate and owns the core success criterion: a working, scalable hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria process. Process Safety Engineering, Techno-Economic Analysis and the other candidates are constraints or methods subordinate to it.

Disciplines this project involves:

Domain Importance Specificity Role Reason
Gas Fermentation Engineering 5 5 outcome Hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria bioprocess, mass transfer and scale-up define the core success criterion.
Process Safety Engineering 5 4 constraint Hydrogen-oxygen explosion risk requires hazard analysis, ATEX design and independent interlock review.
Techno-Economic Analysis 4 5 method Cost model, scale-up uncertainty ranges, and deployment thresholds drive gate decisions and budget justification.
Downstream Bioprocessing 4 5 method Harvesting, nucleic acid reduction, drying and protein quality of single-cell biomass.
Water Electrolysis 4 5 method Electrolyzer selection, membranes, outage tolerance and hydrogen supply underpin the gas fermentation.
Food Regulatory Affairs 4 4 constraint Novel protein needs credible EU, Danish and Kenyan feed or food authorization pathways.
Open Source Hardware 4 4 method Complete open-licence source package with governance keeping the core open and replicable.
Industrial Microbiology 4 4 method Reference strain selection, rights, biological quality assurance, and nucleic acid reduction in downstream processing.
Intellectual Property Law 4 4 constraint Strain rights, patent restrictions per jurisdiction and open-licence governance must be cleared.

Plan Type

This plan requires one or more physical locations. It cannot be executed digitally.

Explanation: The plan is classified as physical. It sets up a non-profit engineering project that builds and operates real hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria gas-fermentation hardware. The work cannot be done online, and nearly every phase needs a physical site, equipment or materials.

  1. Laboratory and container-scale work (Phase One and Two). Initial experiments with candidate strains such as Cupriavidus necator need laboratory facilities, bioreactors, electrolyzers, gas supply, and physical measurement of mass transfer, productivity and energy use. Outage and robustness testing and scale-up experiments are physical tests on real equipment.

  2. Reference unit in Denmark (Phase Three). The plan builds a reference unit at the Danish development and test site. This involves construction, procurement, ATEX-compliant installation, commissioning, and six months of continuous operation to measure uptime.

  3. Independent replication in Kenya. A separate Kenyan team must obtain the strain, build the system from documentation alone, and produce biomass. The site must be a real-world one that tests the operating envelope: power outages, water quality, temperature and humidity, spare-part availability and local skills. The team also has to run physical fault-injection and component-substitution tests.

  4. Safety and the hydrogen-oxygen explosion risk. Process-hazard analysis, interlocks, emergency shutdown and ATEX design are all physical engineering. They must be verified on installed hardware.

  5. Physical inputs and logistics. The material and energy balance covers nitrogen sources, minerals, process chemicals, water treatment, cooling and replacement parts such as electrolyzer membranes. All of these must be sourced and shipped, and resupply autonomy has to be tested. Biomass must also be harvested, processed (including nucleic acid reduction) and dried, and then tested for composition and digestibility.

  6. In-person activities. The plan includes training and competency verification of local technicians, hosting by a university consortium with a Kenyan partner, regulatory sampling and product validation, and site visits for audits and gate reviews.

Some parts are digital. These are the landscape review, the techno-economic model, the patent and regulatory research, and the open-licence publication of the source package. They support the physical work and do not replace it. Nothing here comes close to being purely digital, so the classification is physical.

Physical Locations

This plan implies one or more physical locations.

Requirements for physical locations

  • Electrical supply with documented outage patterns for testing
  • Water supply with measurable quality constraints
  • Ambient temperature and humidity range suitable for fermentation
  • Space for laboratory, pilot-scale, and container-scale bioreactors
  • Hydrogen production, gas-handling and fermentation infrastructure (ATEX-compliant)
  • Spare-part availability and local technical skills for repairs and maintenance
  • Capacity to test power outages, restarts and culture continuity
  • Capacity for training and competency verification of local technicians
  • Access to analytical capability for biological quality assurance and composition testing
  • Safety review and process-hazard analysis infrastructure
  • Regulatory access (permitting, contained use, product validation)
  • Proximity to nitrogen sources and mineral inputs or supplier networks

Location 1

Denmark

University-based research and industrial site, such as Copenhagen or Aarhus region

Danish university consortium or research institute with bioreactor facilities, electrolysis capability, and ATEX-compliant laboratory and container-scale space

Rationale: The plan explicitly designates Denmark as the development and test site. Phase One and Two require laboratory experiments with candidate strains, gas-fermentation prototypes and scale-up testing. Phase Three requires a reference unit demonstrating six months of continuous operation, safety commissioning and ATEX design verification. A university consortium provides access to analytical capability, safety review, regulatory liaison and established infrastructure. The site must support matched reactor comparisons (pneumatic, pressurized stirred, passive-feed) on identical strain and media.

Location 2

Kenya

Real-world site with documented power outages, limited spare-part access and locally available technical skills, such as Nairobi region or agricultural zone

Kenyan co-development partner organization with capacity for on-site fermentation, commissioning, outage testing and fault-injection trials, separate from Danish developers

Rationale: The plan mandates Kenya as the independent replication site and specifies that the site must test the defined operating envelope: electricity availability and outage pattern, water quality, ambient temperature and humidity, spare-part availability and available technical skills. It must not be a well-equipped laboratory. The replication team must be organizationally separate, and the site must support outage-survival testing, documented restart procedures, locally trained technician operation, and a pre-defined audited fault-injection and component-substitution test programme. This is the primary evidence for hypothesis B (decentralized modules under difficult infrastructure).

Location 3

Global (regulatory and landscape review scope)

Patent, regulatory and market-research offices in Denmark, EU, Kenya and Bangladesh (optional third-country landscape)

Regulatory bodies: Danish Environmental Protection Agency or equivalent EU competent authorities for contained use; Kenya's National Biosafety Authority; Bangladesh regulatory agencies for patent and distribution landscape

Rationale: Phase One includes a landscape review of patent and regulatory requirements for experimental operation, product safety validation and commercial distribution in Denmark/EU, Kenya and Bangladesh. The plan requires early informal regulator engagement to surface hard requirements on strain classification, contained-use permits, product safety dossiers and distribution pathways before hardware is committed. This is a desk-based activity supported by site visits and pre-submission dialogue, but the physical locations are the regulatory bodies' offices where applications and consultations occur.

Location Summary

The Open Protein Module has three primary physical location requirements. Denmark hosts Phase One and Two laboratory and pilot work and the Phase Three reference unit, requiring a university consortium or research institute with bioreactor, electrolysis and ATEX-compliant facilities. Kenya hosts the independent replication team and site, which must test the defined harsh operating envelope (outages, limited supply chains, locally available skills) and is organizationally separate from Danish developers. A third dimension covers regulatory landscape review and early engagement with competent authorities in Denmark/EU and Kenya to identify hard requirements on strain classification, contained use, product safety and distribution before large hardware investment. The plan emphasizes that all funding, partners, sites and permits are treated as uncontrolled until signed, and that the Kenyan site must be chosen for realistic testing, not convenience or good laboratory conditions.

Currency Strategy

This plan involves money.

Currencies

  • EUR: Primary currency for budgeting, reporting and consolidated spending across the multi-country, multi-phase R&D programme. Denmark (eurozone) is the development and test site; EUR is used for international procurement, equipment costs and ceiling tracking (EUR 6 million Phase One, EUR 50 million total provisional ceiling).
  • KES: Secondary currency for local costs in Kenya (replication site salaries, local procurement, utilities, site establishment). Essential for measuring local sourcing share and supply-chain resilience, and for tracking the impact of local sourcing and resupply autonomy on the deployment case. Exchange-rate volatility should be monitored to ensure it does not obscure cost control or exceed budgets.

Primary currency: EUR

Currency strategy: EUR is the primary currency for consolidated budgeting, large procurement and budget-ceiling tracking. Kenyan costs are tracked separately in KES to measure local sourcing and supply-chain resilience impacts on the deployment case. For multi-currency contracts (equipment, staff, logistics spanning Denmark and Kenya), use forward rates or hedging to protect the budget against currency fluctuations and to ensure the EUR 50 million provisional ceiling is not exceeded by exchange-rate movement. All Phase One and Phase Three spending decisions and gate reviews should reference EUR equivalents to maintain budget discipline.

Identify Risks

Risk 1 - Safety & Hazard Control

Hydrogen-oxygen explosion hazard is the core technical safety risk. The process produces hydrogen and oxygen in proximity; ignition requires process containment, interlocks, emergency shutdown and ATEX compliance. If process-hazard analysis identifies a credible ignition path that cannot be closed by the proposed design (inherent limits, layered instrumentation, or both), the design must be reworked. Hydrogen gas inventory, control-system failure, seal rupture under pressure, electrolyzer malfunction or gas-feed backflow during power loss are plausible failure modes. An accident during Danish testing or Kenyan replication could cause serious injury or fatality, invalidate the site permit, or force design re-certification under stricter assumptions.

Impact: A serious safety incident during testing could delay the programme by 6–18 months for re-design, re-certification and permit recovery. Direct costs: re-design and safety re-analysis (EUR 200,000–500,000), extended independent safety review (EUR 100,000–300,000), potential site remediation and regulatory penalty. Indirect: reputational damage affecting partner engagement and funder confidence. If the hazard cannot be closed, the project may be forced to Stop or Research Only status, invalidating the entire infrastructure investment. Minor incidents (gas leaks, near-misses) discovered during commissioning could require design changes, adding 2–4 months and EUR 50,000–150,000 to schedule and cost.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Conduct a rigorous, formal Process Hazard Analysis (HAZOP or LOPA) during Phase One, before detailed design commitment. Specify the safety strategy explicitly: inherent limits (e.g., flammable-range composition or minimal gas inventory) or layered instrumented protection (interlocks, multiple sensors, independent emergency shutdown). Commission an independent third-party safety review of the interlock logic and emergency-shutdown design before any pressurized or high-gas-inventory configuration is built. Define which components and parameters adopters may change without re-certification (pre-assessed substitutes list) and which require a full safety re-analysis. Test the safety design on a small-scale mockup before committing to the Danish reference unit. Document all assumptions on seal integrity, electrolyzer reliability and control-system failure modes with uncertainty ranges, and validate them experimentally.

Risk 2 - Strain Rights & Regulatory Classification

The project requires a reference strain that is lawfully obtainable for research, commercial production, redistribution and modification in both Denmark and Kenya. If the primary strain (e.g., C. necator H16) is subject to third-party restrictions, material transfer agreements, or biosafety or import regulations that prevent lawful replication in Kenya, the entire open-replication pillar collapses. Patent claims on the strain, its derivatives or its use in hydrogen fermentation could also emerge during Phase One, blocking publication or commercial deployment. Strain rights are often opaque: public-collection strains may carry undisclosed restrictions, and biosafety classification can differ between jurisdictions (e.g., a strain classified as non-hazardous in the EU may require contained-use permits in Kenya). A rights or regulatory barrier discovered late (e.g., during Kenya import paperwork) could force a switch to a backup strain with unknown productivity, delaying Phase Two and Phase Three by 6–12 months.

Impact: If the primary strain cannot be lawfully imported into Kenya or used commercially, the project must switch to a backup strain, requiring 6–12 months of repeated rights verification, biosafety assessment and productivity benchmarking against the original. Cost impact: EUR 200,000–400,000 for rights analysis, import permits, and biosafety assessment in Kenya. If no legally clean strain can be found, the project may be forced to isolate or evolve a project-owned strain, adding 18–36 months and EUR 1–2 million to Phase One and Two (biosafety characterization, deposition in a public collection, regulatory approval). Regulatory rejection of the strain's biosafety classification in Kenya or the EU could block contained-use permitting, extending Phase One by 4–8 months and forcing design changes (e.g., higher containment levels, stricter aseptic protocols). Loss of a strain to contamination during replication, with no lawful backup, could halt Kenya testing indefinitely.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Begin Phase One with a detailed written rights analysis per candidate strain, covering research use, commercial production, redistribution, modification and derived strains. For each strain, confirm lawful obtainability by direct contact with the strain holder and the relevant regulatory body (e.g., Kenya's National Biosafety Authority). Commission a patent search covering hydrogen fermentation, protein production and the specific strain in Denmark, EU and Kenya to identify third-party claims blocking publication or deployment. Carry a primary and a legally clean backup strain through Phase One and Two so neither a rights nor a performance failure stops the project. Confirm strain import permits and biosafety classification in Kenya before any design freeze (by Month 3–4 = 2027-01-09 to 2027-02-09). If the primary strain is subject to restrictions, engage the strain holder early to negotiate freedom-to-operate or identify alternatives. Store cryo-stocks of the reference and backup strains at multiple independent sites (Denmark, Kenya and a third location) so a contamination event does not lose the strain.

Risk 3 - Regulatory & Permitting

The project must navigate permitting and product-safety pathways in Denmark (national + EU), Kenya and the global patent landscape. Regulatory risk covers: (1) Contained-use authorization for hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria fermentation in Denmark and Kenya; (2) product-safety dossier and classification (animal feed, fish feed, food ingredient, emergency nutrition) in EU and Kenya, which determines safety standards and approval timelines; (3) commercial distribution authorization, which may not be required for research success but must have a 'credible pathway'; (4) patent claims by third parties blocking use or publication; (5) nucleic acid content limits that may be stricter than expected, forcing downstream-processing redesign. Early informal engagement with regulators can identify hard requirements but gives no binding feedback. Late engagement (Phase Two or Three) risks discovering a blocking requirement after hardware is built. The product-category choice (Phase One end gate) is irreversible without re-doing regulatory work, so a wrong early choice could force a stop or costly pivot.

Impact: If the product category is rejected by EU or Kenyan regulators as unsafe or unclassifiable, the project must restart the regulatory process for a different category, adding 8–16 months and EUR 500,000–1,200,000 for new dossiers, testing and submission. If nucleic acid-content limits are stricter than designed, the downstream-processing train must be re-engineered, adding 4–8 months and EUR 300,000–600,000 to Phase Two. A blocking third-party patent claim (e.g., on hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria applied to food/feed) discovered after blueprint v0.1 could force re-design or mandate licensing fees, adding 3–6 months and EUR 100,000–300,000+ in legal and re-design work. Failure to obtain contained-use permits in Kenya by the start of Phase Three could delay replication by 6–12 months. A regulatory authority requiring a full safety and efficacy dossier before any in-country testing could push the entire Kenya replication into Phase Three (cost and schedule slip of EUR 2–5 million and 12–24 months).

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Commission a dedicated regulatory-landscape review in Phase One (Month 0–3 = 2026-10-09 to 2027-01-09) covering: (1) contained-use and permitted-organism rules in Denmark/EU and Kenya; (2) product-safety and classification pathways for animal feed, fish feed, food ingredient and emergency nutrition in target jurisdictions; (3) nucleic acid content limits and composition standards; (4) patent landscape on hydrogen fermentation, autotrophic protein and the reference strain. Open informal pre-submission dialogue with the Danish EPA (or EU equivalent) and Kenya's National Biosafety Authority during Phase One to identify hard requirements and gain written feedback on the proposed operating envelope and product category. Fix the product-category choice at the Phase One kill gate, and do not change it without a full regulatory re-assessment. Appoint an independent regulatory counsel to track changes in national or EU guidance and alert the project to new requirements. Obtain a written feasibility assessment from Kenya's regulatory body that confirms a pathway to contained-use authorization before committing to the Kenyan site or partner.

Risk 4 - Technical & Scale-Up

The project aims to connect bench-scale laboratory experiments to a deployment capacity with uncertain scale-up factors. Principal scale-up assumptions likely include: gas-liquid mass-transfer coefficients scale predictably with reactor geometry and power input; volumetric productivity does not decline with scale; energy per kilogram does not increase with size; downstream-processing yield and throughput are not constrained by large-scale equipment availability. If matched reactor testing in Phase One or Two shows that one or more assumptions fail (e.g., mass-transfer efficiency drops at larger volumes, or downstream bottlenecks emerge), the reference-unit design or the deployment-capacity model must be revised, consuming 3–8 months and EUR 200,000–500,000 in re-engineering and testing. The plan requires pre-registered disproof experiments with failure thresholds fixed before data arrive; if those thresholds are set too tight, a promising concept can be abandoned prematurely, while if too loose, weak evidence can pass. Hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria are not well-characterized at industrial scale: contamination, strain stability, nucleic acid accumulation and product quality over multi-month runs are not well-published, so empirical failures during Phase Two or Phase Three testing are plausible.

Impact: If critical scale-up assumptions collapse during Phase Two (e.g., gas transfer is limited by oxygen competition or downstream nucleic acid removal is far more energy-intensive than estimated), the reference-unit design must be reworked, adding 4–8 months and EUR 300,000–800,000 to Phase Two budget and delaying Phase Three by one year. If the model assumptions are discovered to be wrong during the Danish reference-unit build (Phase Three), the unit commissioning could be delayed by 6–12 months, and if the cost overrun is large, the project may be forced to select Modify or Research Only. Productivity or energy metrics that fall short of the locked deployment thresholds by more than 10–20% at Phase Three could invalidate the Go decision, forcing a Stop or Research Only conclusion even if the technology works. Strain instability over 6 months of continuous operation (Phase Three success criterion) could make the deployment scenario unrealistic, pushing the conclusion to Modify or Research Only.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: In Phase One, identify the principal scale-up assumptions (gas-liquid mass-transfer coefficients, volumetric productivity, energy per kilogram, downstream yield and throughput) and state them explicitly with uncertainty ranges derived from published data or conservative engineering estimates. Design matched bench-scale experiments (pneumatic, pressurized stirred, and passive-feed reactors on identical strain and media) to measure these assumptions directly and compare measured values against the model predictions. Pre-register the failure thresholds for each assumption (e.g., 'if volumetric productivity declines by more than 20% between bench and pilot scale, the reactor concept fails disproof') and lock them before Phase Two experiments begin. Run the disproof experiments in Phase Two using intermediate-scale reactors (0.5–10 L pilot-scale units) and document all deviations from model predictions, with uncertainty ranges. If an assumption fails, conduct a root-cause analysis and either re-design the system (e.g., change reactor type, optimize aeration) or explicitly state that the assumption must remain unproven. For scale-up from Phase Two to the Phase Three reference unit, use validated engineering models with stated uncertainty and experimental validation on the critical dimensions (mass transfer, mixing, downstream throughput, energy). Commission an independent technical review of the scale-up logic before the reference-unit procurement begins.

Risk 5 - Organizational & Partnership

The project requires an institutional host (university consortium or non-profit), a Kenyan co-development partner, prospective adopters for scenario anchoring, and independent gate reviewers. The plan states 'all funding, partners, sites and permits are treated as uncontrolled until signed', meaning none of these are committed yet. If a key partner withdraws or delays, the entire programme timeline could slip. University consortia often have competing priorities, slow decision-making and budget constraints; a Kenyan partner may face political or funding instability; prospective adopters may be reluctant to commit before seeing results; independent reviewers with true funding independence may be difficult to recruit in a small technical domain. A host institution's diversion of shared resources (laboratory space, analytical capability, staff time) to other programmes could delay milestones. A Kenyan partner's loss of local government support or visa restrictions on international staff could block replication access. Absence of a committed gate-review panel could allow continuation by momentum, invalidating the kill-gate mechanism.

Impact: If the host institution delays access to laboratory space or analytical equipment by 3–6 months, Phase One and Two timelines slip by the same duration, and costs escalate (extended staff contracts, delayed hiring). Cost impact: EUR 300,000–700,000 per 6-month delay. If the Kenyan partner withdraws mid-phase, recruiting and onboarding a replacement takes 4–8 months and costs EUR 200,000–400,000. Loss of committed gate reviewers could force the project to operate without independent checks, leading to continuation by momentum even if disproof experiments fail. Withdrawal of a prospective adopter after thresholds are locked could invalidate the deployment-scenario basis for the Go decision, requiring the threshold-setting process to restart (2–3 months delay and EUR 50,000–100,000). Delayed visa or work-permit approval for international staff in Kenya could push Phase Three replication back 3–6 months and increase local labour costs by 10–20% as contingency.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Before Phase One begins, secure written institutional commitments from the host university or non-profit, specifying: dedicated laboratory and analytical space, key staff roles and protected time, funding flow and contingency plans for resource conflicts. Ensure the host has explicit leadership buy-in from the rector or executive director, not just a department head. Similarly, secure a signed agreement with the Kenyan partner covering: organization, staffing, site access, logistics, and contingency plans for partner-staff loss. Commit prospective adopters to the threshold-locking exercise in writing before Phase One ends, with a clause stating they remain bound to the thresholds even if internal conditions change. Recruit the independent gate-review panel early (Month 0–1 = 2026-10-09 to 2026-11-09) and fund them from a separate budget line that does not depend on project continuation. Specify their independence criteria in writing: no employment or funding from the host institution, no direct involvement in design decisions, authority to recommend Stop or Modify without justification. Establish a quarterly steering committee with clear authority to escalate partner or resource conflicts and trigger contingency plans.

Risk 6 - Documentation & Replication Independence

A Kenyan team building the system from documentation alone is ambitious and will likely surface gaps and ambiguities in the source package. The plan requires every ambiguity to be logged and resolved, with all external assistance (safety, regulatory, specialist maintenance) recorded in an audited log. If documentation is incomplete or unclear (e.g., missing calibration procedures, unclear interlock logic, unlabeled wiring diagrams, unspecified spare-part sources), the replication team faces three choices: (1) infer from context and documentation, risking unsafe or non-functional builds; (2) seek undocumented help from the original developers, invalidating independence; or (3) halt replication and demand documentation fixes, causing schedule slip. Early small-scale replication (Phase Two) can catch gaps cheaply, but late discovery (during Phase Three full-scale build) forces expensive rework and schedule delay. The independence claim itself depends on rigorous logging and resolution tracking, which is labour-intensive and requires a neutral third party to audit.

Impact: If documentation gaps are discovered during the Phase II small-scale replication, fixes cost EUR 50,000–150,000 and take 1–2 months to release revised documentation. If gaps are discovered during Phase III full-scale Kenyan build, fixes cost EUR 200,000–500,000 and delay replication by 3–6 months. If the Kenyan team must seek substantial undocumented help from original developers to complete the build, independence is compromised, potentially invalidating the replication evidence and forcing the project to Stop or restart with stricter documentation standards. An unresolved ambiguity (e.g., a calibration procedure with no source document) could cause a fault to go undiagnosed during fault-injection testing, undermining confidence in test results. If the audited assistance log is incomplete or not properly maintained, the independent reviewer cannot certify independence, and the Go decision is vulnerable to challenge.

Likelihood: High

Severity: Medium

Action: Plan for systematic documentation-defect discovery from the Phase II small-scale replication onward. Establish a formal defect-tracking system in which every ambiguity found during build or operation is logged with: (1) location in documentation, (2) description of the ambiguity, (3) resolution (documentation update, design clarification, or work-around), (4) source of resolution (original developer, external expert, or Kenyan team inference), and (5) date resolved. Assign a neutral third-party auditor (external to the project and the host institution) to review the defect log quarterly and certify that resolutions are documented, changes are traceable, and no critical gaps remain. Conduct the Phase II small-scale replication with the understanding that its primary goal is to discover documentation defects before Phase III full-scale build. Allocate at least EUR 100,000 and 2–3 months in Phase II specifically for documentation review and revision after the small-scale build. Before Phase III begins, require the independent gate reviewer to sign off on documentation completeness, with a clause stating what constitutes an acceptable defect rate (e.g., no more than 5–10 unresolved ambiguities at the start of full-scale build). Establish a change-control process in which documentation updates during Phase III replication are released only after independent safety and legal review.

Risk 7 - Financial & Budget Control

The project has a provisional ceiling of EUR 50 million and a Phase One cap of EUR 6 million, neither of which is a spending target but rather a constraint. The plan emphasizes that spending must be justified from the cost model, and unspent money should not trigger extra spending just to avoid underrun. Large technical uncertainties (scale-up, strain rights, safety design) and unsigned partners mean the actual spend profile is unknown, and overruns in one phase could consume flexibility in later phases. Currency volatility between EUR and KES could silently erase budget if not managed, and distributed spending across Denmark and Kenya (with procurement, salaries and logistics in different currencies and markets) complicates cost control. If early phases significantly overrun, there is no contingency budget for Phase Three, and the project may be forced to select Modify or Stop. The plan requires killing the project if thresholds are not met, which signals that funding is conditional on evidence, but if gate reviewers lack authority or funding independence, they may approve continuation despite weak results.

Impact: A 10–20% overrun in Phase One (EUR 600,000–1,200,000) would reduce the available budget for Phase Two and Three proportionally, forcing descoping of planned experiments or raising the risk of a Stop decision due to incomplete evidence. Currency depreciation of KES against EUR by 10–15% during the 5-year programme could consume EUR 500,000–1,000,000 of the EUR 50 million ceiling if Kenyan costs are not hedged, squeezing later phases. Uncontrolled scope creep (additional reactor configurations, extra safety analyses, extended testing) could consume EUR 1–3 million in Phase One and Two without delivering the core evidence, leaving insufficient budget for Phase Three reference unit or Kenyan replication. If the independent gate reviewers are not separately funded and their budgets depend on project continuation, they may lack true independence to recommend Stop or Modify.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Establish a Phase-by-Phase spending plan tied to deliverables, with explicit decision criteria for each phase: define what evidence must be produced by the Phase One and Phase Two gates, and allocate budget to those deliverables, not to effort. Use zero-based budgeting in which every allocation must be justified from the cost model and the evidence roadmap, not from historical spending or organizational inertia. Set aside a 10–15% contingency budget within each phase for technical surprises, but do not spend it by default; use it only for disproof of a critical assumption or resolution of a discovery. Implement quarterly cost-control reviews comparing actual spending against planned burn-rate and deliverables achieved. For multi-currency spending, use forward-rate contracts or currency hedging to lock exchange rates for the major tranches of Kenyan spending and procurement, protecting the EUR 50 million ceiling from FX volatility. Separately fund the independent gate-review panel (budget at EUR 200,000–400,000 across the full 5-year programme) from a budget line outside the main project spend, ensuring their independence and their authority to stop or modify without facing financial pressure. Document all spending assumptions, cost drivers and uncertainty ranges in the cost model, and update the model quarterly as new data emerge. At each gate, require the project to re-estimate the cost to completion (Estimate at Completion, EAC) and report it transparently to the funder and reviewers.

Risk 8 - Supply Chain & Logistics

The project must source or produce hydrogen via electrolysis, gas-handling and fermentation equipment, nitrogen and mineral inputs, water treatment, cooling and spare parts (e.g., electrolyzer membranes). The Kenyan replication explicitly tests local sourcing and supply-chain resilience: how long production continues without resupply during an energy crisis coinciding with a food crisis. If critical components (electrolyzer membranes, fermentation-grade seals, analytical reagents) have long lead times or require specialist sourcing, the Kenyan site may face multi-month delays in procurement, forcing project suspension. Local sourcing of nitrogen and minerals in Kenya is not confirmed; if preferred sources dry up or purity is unpredictable, the design may face productivity penalties or product-quality failures. The material and energy balance is required to separate locally produced, regionally available and imported inputs, but the plan acknowledges this is unproven: supplier networks in Kenya may be weaker than assumed. A major supplier failure (e.g., electrolyzer-membrane supplier closure or extended backlog) could halt both the Danish reference unit and Kenyan replication for 6–12 months.

Impact: If a critical component (e.g., electrolyzer membranes, high-purity fermentation seals) cannot be sourced within Kenya or with reasonable lead times and cost, the replication team must either import the component (adding cost, complexity and donor dependence) or find a substitute, which requires re-validation. A 6–12 month sourcing delay for a critical component could hold up Phase III reference-unit commissioning or Kenyan replication build by the same duration, increasing costs by EUR 500,000–1,500,000 due to extended staff and facility costs. If local nitrogen or mineral sourcing fails, the design must pivot to imported inputs, underwriting the vendor-independence claim and adding recurring cost. A major supplier's business failure or production shutdown could strand the project without fallback supplies, especially if spare-part inventory is not maintained locally. Supply-chain disruptions (e.g., shipping delays, customs clearance issues) could delay the Kenyan replication start by 3–6 months. If the resupply-autonomy analysis (days of production without resupply) is overly optimistic, the Kenyan site may face unexpected downtime when supplies run out faster than forecast.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Commission a detailed supply-chain and sourcing assessment during Phase One, identifying: (1) all critical components and their suppliers (electrolyzer membranes, fermentation-grade equipment, seals, analytical reagents); (2) lead times, minimum order quantities and cost; (3) alternative sources for each critical item; (4) local nitrogen and mineral sources in Kenya (suppliers, purity, reliability, lead times). For each critical input, establish a supplier-diversification strategy: no single supplier for any critical component, and at least two alternative sources (one regional, one import-ready) for items with long lead times. Negotiate framework agreements with suppliers covering lead times, inventory availability and force-majeure conditions. Maintain a 3–6 month inventory of critical spare parts (electrolyzer membranes, seals, analytical consumables) at the Danish reference unit before Phase Three commissioning begins, and arrange for a similar stockpile to be built in Kenya before the replication start. In the resupply-autonomy analysis, use conservative assumptions: assume suppliers have only 2–4 weeks of inventory on hand, and set the 'maximum outage survived' metric assuming both Danish and Kenyan supplies are exhausted and shipping is delayed 4 weeks due to crisis conditions. Test the resupply-autonomy claim experimentally during Phase III by simulating a 2–3 month supply cutoff and monitoring how long production can continue and at what cost. Document all substitutions and workarounds in the Kenyan replication, and flag any that reduce the vendor-independence claim.

Risk 9 - Technical Feasibility & Contamination Control

The project requires maintaining a single pure strain of hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria in an aseptic or contamination-tolerant culture for months of continuous operation, across bench, pilot and full-scale reactors in two countries. Contamination by competing microorganisms would degrade product quality, reduce productivity or, in the worst case, outcompete the target strain entirely. The plan considers contamination tolerance (exploiting selective growth conditions of autotrophic hydrogen oxidation) but acknowledges it is unproven. Seed-train procedures, cryo-stock storage and revival, purity verification and the impact of variable local input purity on contamination risk are all unvalidated at the proposed scale. A lost or contaminated culture during replication could require revival from a frozen stock, which depends on lawful strain access and proper storage logistics; a failed revival would halt replication indefinitely. The plan requires culture continuity and outage survival: the strain must tolerate repeated power cycling, medium starvation during shutdown, and temperature and pH excursions that come with outages.

Impact: A single contamination event during Phase II or Phase III (loss of the culture line) would delay the project by 4–8 weeks while cryo-stocks are revived and the culture is re-grown to operational density. If a cryo-stock is lost or non-viable (e.g., due to cold-chain failure during shipping to Kenya), the project may be unable to recover without developer help, invalidating independence. If contamination tolerance is less effective than assumed (e.g., competing microbes can grow under the intended selective conditions), the aseptic burden increases, requiring stricter procedures, more frequent purity checks, more skilled technicians and higher operational costs. If repeated outage cycles degrade strain stability (e.g., mutation, plasmid loss, reduced fitness), productivity or safety properties could change unexpectedly during the 6-month Phase III uptime test, forcing re-validation and schedule delay. A product-quality failure attributed to contamination or strain drift (e.g., elevated nucleic acid content, off-flavor compounds) discovered late in Phase III could invalidate months of operation data and force re-design of the downstream-processing train.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Develop and validate strain-continuity procedures during Phase One and Two: establish seed-train protocols (size, frequency, storage conditions for intermediate stocks), cryo-stock preservation methods (cryoprotectant, freezing rate, long-term storage temperature and monitoring), and revival procedures with documented success rates. Deposit cryo-stocks at a minimum of three independent locations: Denmark (primary), Kenya (deployment), and a third neutral location (e.g., international culture collection or backup research institute) so that loss of one repository does not halt replication. Before shipping cryo-stocks to Kenya, validate the cold-chain logistics (transport time, temperature monitoring, contingency for failures) with a dry run using a non-hazardous surrogate strain. Implement routine purity verification using culture plating, microscopy or molecular methods (e.g., 16S rRNA PCR) at defined intervals (e.g., weekly during normal operation, after every restart). Document the strain's stability over repeated growth cycles and power/medium-starvation cycles by running a long-term continuous or fed-batch experiment (100+ generations) in Phase Two and measuring key productivity parameters (growth rate, biomass yield, oxygen consumption rate) for drift. If contamination tolerance is relied upon, validate it experimentally: run the reactor with intentionally introduced contaminants under the intended selective-growth conditions and confirm that the target strain outcompetes them without productivity loss. Maintain a detailed strain lineage and mutation history; if drift is detected, sequence the genome at regular intervals to track changes. Train the Kenyan team intensively on purity verification and contamination response, and assign a qualified staff member to oversee biological quality assurance, with remote support from an EU-based microbiologist (recorded in the assistance log).

Risk 10 - Regulatory Pathway for Product Distribution

The plan requires a 'credible regulatory pathway' in Denmark, EU and Kenya for product distribution, but full commercial authorization is not required for research success. The product category (animal feed, fish feed, food ingredient, emergency nutrition) is chosen at the Phase One gate based on provisional data and locked there; if the category is later deemed unsafe or unregulatable by authorities, the project cannot pivot without restarting regulatory work. Different product categories have different approval timelines and evidence requirements: emergency nutrition may require fewer safety studies than food ingredient, but it may have limited market uptake. If the Kenyan regulatory authority lacks established pathways for new protein products or takes a precautionary approach, a 'credible pathway' may not exist even if the product is safe. Nucleic acid content may be regulated differently in Denmark/EU vs Kenya, forcing different downstream-processing requirements or product specifications per jurisdiction, which complicates the single 'open design' claim.

Impact: If the product category chosen at the Phase One gate is later deemed unsaleable by regulators (e.g., Kenya prohibits direct human consumption of single-cell protein without years of safety testing), the project must pivot to a different category or accept that the deployment case does not exist, leading to a Research Only conclusion even if the technology works. Re-starting the regulatory process for a different category adds 8–16 months and EUR 500,000–1,200,000. If nucleic acid content limits differ unexpectedly between jurisdictions, the downstream-processing train must be configurable per region, adding complexity and cost. If Kenya's regulatory pathway involves mandatory in-country clinical or safety trials (not required in EU), the cost and timeline for product authorization in Kenya could exceed Phase Three budget and schedule, forcing a choice between commercialization in EU only (weakening the deployment case) or a separate, fully funded regulatory programme. A regulatory authority's request for historical safety data on the strain (e.g., acute toxicity, long-term feeding studies) not yet conducted could extend approval timelines to 2–3 years beyond Phase Three, pushing commercialization outside the project scope.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Conduct a detailed regulatory-requirements analysis per product category and jurisdiction during Phase One (Month 0–3 = 2026-10-09 to 2027-01-09), distinguishing experimental operation (contained use, site permits), product safety validation and commercial distribution. For each intended product category (animal feed, fish feed, food ingredient, emergency nutrition), document the approval pathway, timeline, required studies and cost in Denmark/EU and Kenya. Obtain written pre-submission feedback from the relevant authority (Danish EPA or EU equivalent, and Kenya's National Biosafety Authority) confirming a credible pathway before committing to a category. Fix the product category at the Phase One kill gate in a signed, time-stamped document, and do not change it without approval from all parties and a full regulatory re-assessment. By the Phase Two gate, produce Phase II compositional and digestibility data conforming to the selected category's regulatory dossier requirements, so Phase Three can proceed with minimal additional testing. If Kenya's regulatory pathway requires in-country trials or studies beyond the project scope, either fund them separately or explicitly scope them out of Phase Three and acknowledge the implication for the deployment case. For nucleic acid content and other composition specifications, work with regulators during Phase One to establish acceptable ranges, and design the downstream-processing train to achieve those ranges with documented margins (e.g., design for <2% nucleic acid if the limit is 3%, to account for analytical and operational variation).

Risk 11 - Downstream Processing & Product Quality

The project must turn raw hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria biomass into a usable, digestible, food-safe protein product through harvesting, cell disruption, nucleic acid reduction and drying. Downstream processing is often underestimated in techno-economic models: energy consumption, equipment complexity, maintenance burden and waste handling can erase fermenter-level gains in cost and energy efficiency. The plan requires a consistent processing boundary for all benchmark comparisons, but the actual processing train (minimal, moderate or comprehensive) is undecided. A comprehensive train (validated nucleic acid reduction, stringent purity) increases product-category options and regulatory acceptance but adds equipment, labour and specialist maintenance. A minimal train (basic centrifugation and drying) reduces burden but may restrict product use to less-demanding categories. If nucleic acid content is higher than expected, the downstream train may not achieve the product specification, forcing re-design or accepting a lower-value product category.

Impact: If the downstream-processing train is underestimated and actually requires more energy or equipment than the model predicted, the total energy per kilogram of usable protein could increase by 20–50%, potentially exceeding the deployment-scenario threshold and pushing the Go decision to Modify or Research Only. If a nucleic acid reduction step proves difficult to scale or requires unexpectedly expensive equipment or consumables (e.g., specialized membranes, enzymatic reagents), the cost per kilogram could increase by EUR 1–3, potentially invalidating the cost threshold. If downstream processing is not included in the fermentation cost model, the deployed system's true cost could be 20–40% higher than claimed, undermining the deployment case. A failure in downstream validation during Phase II (e.g., nucleic acid content remains >5% despite treatment) forces re-design of the processing train, adding 2–4 months and EUR 150,000–400,000 to Phase II. If the Kenyan team cannot operate the downstream train within the defined competency envelope (e.g., centrifuge maintenance is beyond local skills), the system must either be simplified (risking product quality) or require ongoing specialist support (weakening the independence claim).

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Define the downstream-processing scope and fixed processing boundary early in Phase One, specifying: harvesting method (centrifugation, filtration, settling), cell disruption (if any), nucleic acid reduction step (thermal, enzymatic or physical), drying method (spray, freeze, drum) and final product form (powder, paste, pellet). Use a consistent processing boundary for all benchmark calculations against published alternatives. Conduct a detailed cost and energy analysis of each processing step, with uncertainty ranges and identified bottlenecks. Allocate Phase II experiments specifically to validate the downstream train at pilot scale: test nucleic acid removal efficiency, product yield, energy consumption and equipment operability by trained technicians. If nucleic acid content cannot be consistently achieved below the regulatory limit using the proposed method, re-design the train or select a product category with a higher permissible limit. Document the sensitivity of the total system cost and energy to each downstream parameter (e.g., nucleic acid-removal method choice, drying energy, equipment scale); if any parameter has a >20% cost impact, allocate extra Phase II validation to reduce its uncertainty. For the Kenyan replication, match the downstream train to the available local skills and equipment; if the preferred train requires specialist expertise not available locally, design a simplified alternative and measure the product-quality and cost penalty. Validate that the simplified downstream train can be operated by trained technicians with documented procedures and contingency plans for failures.

Risk 12 - Hypothesis Testing & Threshold Setting

The project tests two hypotheses: (A) the process can be operated by locally trained technicians while keeping acceptable safety and productivity; (B) it can be decentralized into affordable, independently maintained modules under unreliable infrastructure. If either hypothesis fails (e.g., technicians cannot maintain the required safety envelope, or module costs are too high for decentralized deployment), the conclusion should be Modify or Research Only, not Go. However, hypothesis testing depends on pre-locked deployment thresholds (maximum cost, minimum capacity, required reliability) set before any prototype evaluation. If thresholds are set from weak data or without real adopter input, the project may pass or fail against a scenario no one would actually use, invalidating the hypothesis. If thresholds are tightened retrospectively to fit achieved performance, the Go decision is rationalized rather than evidence-based. The plan requires a kill gate at the end of Phase Two, with written continue/modify/research-only/stop decisions; if that gate lacks teeth (e.g., reviewers are not truly independent, or the project continues by momentum despite weak Phase II results), the expensive Phase III build and Kenyan replication consume EUR 20–30 million without clear justification.

Impact: If hypothesis (A) fails because technicians cannot safely operate the system without developer support, the project cannot claim local deployment viability, and the Go decision should be Modify (requiring simpler design, better training or more automation). If hypothesis (B) fails because module costs are 30–50% above the deployment threshold, the project cannot claim decentralized, vendor-independent deployment. A failed hypothesis should trigger a Modify or Research Only conclusion; if instead the project pivots to a different target scenario or loosens the threshold, the final Go decision loses credibility. If the Phase Two kill gate is not binding (e.g., weak Phase II data are approved to proceed to Phase III), EUR 20–30 million is committed without solid evidence. If the Go decision at Phase Three is made despite missing or failed tests, the project's scientific credibility is compromised, even if the technology works. A failed Kenyan replication (e.g., documentation gaps make independent build impossible) should trigger a Stop or Modify conclusion; if instead it is judged a 'success with documented help', the independence claim is weakened.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Before Phase One begins, establish a hypothesis-testing framework and a gate-review governance model: (1) Define hypothesis (A) and hypothesis (B) formally with measurable criteria for pass/fail; (2) Identify 2–3 named prospective adopters (e.g., national food reserve, regional feed producer, humanitarian logistics organization) and engage them in setting deployment thresholds: maximum acceptable cost per kilogram of usable protein, minimum useful production capacity, required uptime and outage-survival duration; (3) Lock these thresholds in a signed, time-stamped document before Phase One ends, with a clause stating thresholds are immutable unless all parties formally agree to change them (and the change is documented in the scientific record); (4) Recruit an independent gate-review panel with written charters: no employment or funding dependence on the host institution, authority to recommend stop/modify/continue without justification, and a separate budget line ensuring they can operate independently. At each gate (Phase One end, Phase Two end, Phase Three end), require the panel to produce a written decision document addressing: (a) Does the evidence support the hypotheses as stated? (b) Do the measured cost, capacity and reliability meet or exceed the locked thresholds? (c) If not, what specific evidence is missing or failed? (d) Is a continue, modify, research-only or stop decision justified? If the decision is modify or stop, require the project to produce a detailed analysis of why and a plan to address the shortfall (if modify) or conclusions (if stop). Publish all gate-review documents and decisions transparently to stakeholders and the funder.

Risk 13 - Kenyan Site Selection & Infrastructure

The Kenyan replication site must be chosen to test the defined operating envelope: documented grid-outage patterns, water-quality constraints, ambient temperature and humidity, spare-part availability and available technical skills. The plan emphasizes 'choose a Kenyan site that actually tests this envelope, not a well-equipped laboratory.' If a site is chosen for convenience or partner convenience rather than harsh-envelope realism, it may pass tests that a real adopter would fail, invalidating hypothesis B evidence. Conversely, a harshly chosen site faces greater risk of logistics-driven failures that obscure whether the design or documentation was at fault. A site's infrastructure can also change mid-project: local power supply reliability may improve, fuel costs may spike (affecting operating cost), political instability may disrupt access, or competing priorities may reduce partner capacity.

Impact: If the Kenyan site lacks the documented operating envelope conditions (e.g., it has reliable power, good water quality, nearby spare-part suppliers), it does not test hypothesis B, and the replication results do not validate the claim of deployment under difficult infrastructure. If a harshly chosen site experiences unexpected logistical failures (e.g., a parts delay due to shipping disruption, fuel shortage affecting operating cost), these can be misattributed to design flaws, leading to incorrect Modify or Stop conclusions. A site infrastructure change mid-project (e.g., grid power becomes more reliable, or political instability delays access) could force a site change or extension, costing EUR 200,000–500,000 and delaying replication by 6–12 months. If the Kenyan partner loses local-government support or faces visa restrictions on international staff, project access could be suspended indefinitely. A choice between a convenient, well-equipped site (which may not test the envelope but has reliable access) and a harsh-envelope site (which tests the design but is risky logistically) sets the trade-off between evidence quality and project safety.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: During Phase One, commission an independent site-selection study in Kenya documenting: (1) grid-outage frequency, duration and pattern (e.g., daily 2-hour rolling blackouts vs. weekly 12-hour unplanned outages); (2) water-supply reliability, seasonal quality variation and treatment constraints; (3) ambient temperature and humidity ranges; (4) local availability of key spare parts (electrical, mechanical, analytical consumables) and lead times for import; (5) available technical skills in the area (electricians, mechanics, laboratory technicians); (6) political stability, security and accessibility for international staff. Select a site that genuinely tests the envelope, not a showcase site. Document the envelope conditions in writing, and include them in the replication acceptance criteria: the site must remain within the defined envelope for the duration of Phase Three. Establish contingency plans for infrastructure changes: if grid power becomes more reliable mid-project, add controlled outage stressors to maintain the testing burden. Secure a site-use agreement in writing, specifying access rights, contingency for partner or staff changes, and a force-majeure clause. Assign a resident on-site project manager (hired locally, with international support) who can navigate local logistics and flag infrastructure or partner changes early. Monitor the site's operating envelope quarterly, and trigger contingency actions if envelope conditions shift by >20%.

Risk 14 - Open Licence & Intellectual Property

The project aims to publish the complete source package (hardware, software, data, documentation) under open licences so that independent organizations can build and operate the system. However, open-licence governance is complex: licence choice (reciprocal vs. permissive) affects whether improvements must be shared back and whether commercial forks are possible; third-party IP (patents, strain restrictions, material transfer agreements) can limit what the project can publish; and stewardship (who holds the licences and enforces terms long-term) is needed to prevent forking or closure by a single company. If the licence terms are too permissive, a commercial entity could build a closed, proprietary variant, undermining the open-source mission. If too restrictive, industrial adopters may avoid the design to reduce legal risk. If third-party IP blocks publication (e.g., a patent claim on hydrogen fermentation for protein production), the project may be forced to operate as Research Only, unable to publish or deploy at scale.

Impact: If a third-party patent claim blocks publication of key design elements, the project is forced to either work around the patent (adding cost and complexity), license the patent (adding recurring cost and dependence), or conclude Research Only. A licensing fee of even EUR 1,000–5,000 per deployed unit (if the patent is on the electrolyzer or fermentation design) could exceed the cost threshold for hypothesis B deployment. If the chosen licence terms deter industrial adopters or create legal uncertainty (e.g., ambiguous patent-pledge language), the adoption rate and deployment evidence may fall short of the threshold. If stewardship breaks down after Phase Three (e.g., the steward organization loses funding or closes), the design could be forked or claimed by a single entity, negating the open-source protection. If the freedom-to-operate review is incomplete before release (e.g., a patent claim emerges after publication), the project and adopters face legal liability or forced design changes.

Likelihood: Low

Severity: Medium

Action: Commission a comprehensive freedom-to-operate and patent landscape review during Phase One, covering: (1) published patents on hydrogen fermentation, autotrophic protein production, the reference strain and relevant processes in Denmark, EU, Kenya and Bangladesh; (2) third-party IP restrictions embedded in strain material transfer agreements, software licences or published data; (3) regulatory and trademark protection (e.g., certification mark for 'Open Protein Module' compliance). For each identified IP risk, document: the claim or restriction, the jurisdictions affected, the likelihood and cost of infringement, and mitigation options (design around, license, patent pledge, or publication barrier). Choose a licence stack (e.g., CERN Open Hardware Licence for hardware, GPL or Apache for software, CC-BY for data) that balances openness (requirement for derivative improvements to be shared back) with adoption ease (permissive enough for industrial use). For safety-critical designs (e.g., control software, interlocks), consider using reciprocal licences to ensure changes remain traceable. Publish a one-page legal summary per jurisdiction detailing: (1) what is licensed under what terms; (2) identified IP restrictions and their implications; (3) what adopters can and cannot do commercially without additional licensing. Establish an independent steward organization (e.g., a non-profit foundation) with sustainable funding to hold and enforce the licences, manage the source repository, and address patent disputes or forking attempts. Include in Phase Three budget at least EUR 100,000–200,000 for steward-entity setup and initial operations.

Risk 15 - Measurement & Benchmarking

The project requires consistent definitions of productivity, energy use and cost across all benchmark calculations, compared against published data using 'compatible definitions of volumetric productivity, system-level energy use, capacity utilization and processing boundaries.' The plan emphasizes the KPI framework but does not specify how published benchmarks will be sourced or how ambiguities in published definitions will be resolved. If different reactor concepts, published sources or product categories use different definitions (e.g., one includes electrolyzer efficiency losses and another does not), benchmark comparisons become meaningless. If the project's own measurements use different boundaries than published data (e.g., published data exclude downstream processing, but the project's model includes it), the comparison is invalid. A published benchmark of 'X kg protein per liter per day' may assume 100% capacity utilization and continuous operation, while the project's model assumes 70% utilization and regular maintenance downtime; failing to adjust for these differences leads to incorrect conclusion that the project is less productive than published work.

Impact: If the measurement framework is not pinned down before Phase II, conflicting definitions could delay publication by 2–4 months as data are re-analyzed to match published benchmarks. If the project's final productivity numbers are compared against published data using incompatible definitions, reviewers or adopters may challenge the results as non-comparable, undermining confidence in the Go decision. If the locked deployment thresholds were set using one definition (e.g., assuming 70% capacity utilization) but Phase III results are reported using another definition (e.g., nameplate productivity at 100% utilization), the system appears to exceed thresholds when it actually falls short, invalidating the Go decision.

Likelihood: Low

Severity: Medium

Action: Establish a measurement and KPI framework during Phase One before any bench-scale experiments begin. For each KPI (volumetric productivity, energy per kilogram dry biomass, energy per kilogram usable protein, installed cost per unit capacity, uptime, outage survived and restart time), document: (1) definition (formula and units); (2) system boundary (which components and processes are included); (3) capacity-utilization assumption (e.g., 70%, 100%); (4) operating mode (continuous, fed-batch, intermittent); (5) how it will be measured (instruments, sampling frequency, data processing). For each KPI, identify at least two published benchmarks (from different sources or studies) and document their definitions, boundaries and assumptions. For any KPI where definitions differ significantly, either harmonize the project's definition to match published work or clearly state the difference and justify the choice. Lock this measurement framework in a written document (e.g., a KPI Protocol) and require all bench-scale, pilot-scale and full-scale experiments to report data against these definitions. Before the Phase Two gate, conduct a sensitivity analysis on the locked deployment thresholds: if the thresholds are sensitive to the definition of a KPI (e.g., a 20% difference in the threshold if capacity utilization is 70% vs. 100%), publish the sensitivity and discuss the implication for adopters. Use the same KPI definitions consistently for all scale-up comparisons and published benchmarks.

Risk 16 - Training & Operator Competence

Hypothesis A claims the process can be operated by locally trained technicians after a 'short, competency-verified training programme.' Operator training content, duration, competency assessment methods and pass criteria are not yet defined. If training is too brief (e.g., 1–2 weeks), technicians may lack confidence or competence to handle safety-critical tasks or troubleshoot failures. If training is too long (e.g., 8–12 weeks), it may not be sustainable in practice for deploying sites. If competency assessment is subjective or inconsistently applied, replication teams may appear competent but fail during real operation. If the system requires frequent adjustments or specialist knowledge (e.g., electrolyzer membrane replacement, specialized diagnostics), the 'locally trained technician' assumption breaks down.
