Regulatory feedback log maintained in shared spreadsheet (updated weekly) with columns: authority, date, topic, feedback summary, binding or preliminary status, implications, project response. Decisions on strain-rights interpretation, patent-risk assessment or regulatory-pathway selection made by consensus of group + legal counsel; any disagreement documented with perspectives and escalated to Steering Committee for final judgment.

Meeting Cadence: Bi-weekly regulatory working group meetings (60 min) during Months 1-4 (2026-11-09 to 2027-02-09); monthly thereafter. Formal legal-counsel review meetings scheduled for Month 2 (2026-12-09) and Month 3 (2027-01-09). Strain Feasibility Report finalized and signed by Month 4 (2027-02-09). Thereafter, monthly monitoring of regulatory guidance changes and log updates (Months 5 onwards).

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Strain-holder responses: received confirmations, pending replies, any restrictions identified
  • Patent search progress: patents identified, relevant claims, jurisdiction coverage, freedom-to-operate assessment
  • Regulatory feedback: communications from Danish/EU/Kenyan authorities, preliminary guidance vs. binding requirements, timeline for formal applications
  • Strain-rights and IP-restriction summary for Strain Feasibility Report
  • Product-category recommendation: regulatory pathway, approval timeline, data requirements per category

Escalation Path: If strain-holder imposes restrictions blocking commercial production or Kenyan import, escalate to Steering Committee immediately: activate backup-strain pathway and adjust timeline. If patent search identifies a blocking patent in Kenya or Denmark, escalate to Steering Committee with legal counsel for options: design-around, license negotiation, or patent challenge. If Kenyan biosafety authority indicates contained-use authorization is unlikely, escalate to Steering Committee: assess whether to proceed with alternative site or product category. If regulatory feedback conflicts with other project assumptions (e.g., authority recommends a product category different from current plan), escalate to Steering Committee with full context and implications for scale-up and deployment thresholds. Any misrepresentation of regulatory status (e.g., preliminary feedback characterized as approval) is flagged immediately to Steering Committee and independent gate-review panel as a governance or integrity risk.

6. Technical Working Group: Deployment Scenarios, Thresholds and Adopter Engagement

Rationale for Inclusion: Deployment Scenario Anchoring and Threshold Locking is the fourth critical decision lever. The plan requires 2-3 named prospective adopters, locked cost/capacity/reliability thresholds fixed before prototype evaluation, and published decisions at each gate that clearly pass or fail against these locked thresholds. This working group identifies and engages prospective adopters during Phase One (Months 2-7 = 2026-12-09 to 2027-05-09), conducts structured interviews on deployment constraints and cost tolerance, consolidates scenarios and locks them in writing by Month 9 (2027-07-09). Without this group, scenarios remain hypothetical, thresholds are adjusted post-hoc to fit results, and the final Go/Modify/Stop decision loses credibility. The group also tracks any adopter withdrawal or renegotiation and escalates to Steering Committee and gate-review panel.

Responsibilities:

  • Identify 2-3 prospective adopters representing realistic deployment contexts (e.g., national food-security reserve agency, regional feed producer, humanitarian logistics organization); prioritize organizations with publicly stated mandates in food security or agriculture and decision-making authority over budget
  • Conduct structured engagement with each adopter: in-person meetings covering current supply chains and costs, production-capacity needs, acceptable cost premium for vendor-independent solution, operational constraints (power reliability, water quality, technical skills, space), timeline expectations
  • Validate adopter input by presenting scenario profiles and cost/capacity/reliability thresholds back to them; obtain feedback and refine scenarios iteratively
  • Consolidate adopter input into 2-3 formalized deployment scenarios with locked thresholds: maximum production cost per kg usable protein, minimum useful capacity, required uptime and outage-survival duration; document rationale and data sources
  • Obtain signed commitment from each adopter by Month 7 (2027-05-09), specifying: scenarios remain locked through Phase Three gate unless all parties formally agree to renegotiate; adopter withdrawal triggers public disclosure of reason; thresholds are used to evaluate Go/Modify/Stop decisions
  • Lock scenarios in time-stamped document at Phase One gate (Month 9 = 2027-07-09); publish to all stakeholders, Steering Committee, gate-review panel and funder
  • Monitor adopter status quarterly: flag any signals of withdrawal or renegotiation; report to Steering Committee and publish any formal withdrawals with stated reason
  • Track regulatory, market and competitive changes affecting adopter interest (e.g., new policy on alternative proteins, competitor technology progress); assess impact on scenario credibility and recommend Steering Committee action if needed
  • Prepare scenarios and thresholds chapters for Phase One gate report; include adopter interview summaries, scenario profiles, locked thresholds, and signed adopter commitments

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Month 1-2 (2026-11-09 to 2026-12-09): Conduct landscape research on prospective adopter profiles (national reserves, feed producers, humanitarian organizations, regional agricultural agencies); identify 5-8 candidates with stated mandates in food security or livestock
  • Month 2 (2026-12-09): Initiate outreach to 2-3 leading candidates; request in-person meetings or calls to explore project interest and data-gathering willingness
  • Month 2-3 (2026-12-09 to 2027-01-09): Develop structured interview guide covering: current protein supply chain and cost, capacity needs, cost tolerance for new/alternative sources, operational constraints, timeline and decision-making process
  • Month 3-4 (2027-01-09 to 2027-02-09): Conduct in-person or virtual interviews with each adopter; document responses in write-ups; develop preliminary scenario profiles

Membership:

  • Adopter Engagement Lead or Deployment Strategy Manager (overall engagement, adopter relationship management)
  • Techno-Economic Analyst or Cost-Model Lead (scenario cost and capacity assumptions, sensitivity analysis, threshold feasibility)
  • Adoption Specialist or Social Science Researcher (adopter motivation, constraint validation, market-landscape analysis)
  • Project Lead or Steering Committee Representative (governance liaison, escalation oversight)

Decision Rights: Group decides: selection and ranking of prospective adopters; scenario profiles (cost, capacity, uptime thresholds); threshold recommendations based on adopter input and cost-model sensitivity analysis. Steering Committee approves final locked scenarios and obtains adopter sign-off. Group cannot unilaterally adjust thresholds after Month 9 (2027-07-09); any renegotiation requires Steering Committee approval and all-party written agreement. Group recommends to Steering Committee how to handle adopter withdrawal or scenario-credibility threats.

Decision Mechanism: Monthly adoption working group meetings (60 min) during Phase One to coordinate interviews, discuss adopter feedback and refine scenarios. Adopter interviews conducted by 2-3 team members (interviewer + note-taker) to ensure accuracy and consistency. Interview summaries drafted and reviewed by group before next adopter meeting to identify convergent themes. Scenario profiles developed iteratively and validated with adopters via follow-up calls or meetings. Final locked scenarios approved by consensus of group + Steering Committee + all adopter signatories.

Meeting Cadence: Monthly adoption working group meetings (60 min) during Months 2-7 (2026-12-09 to 2027-05-09); increased frequency (biweekly) during final scenario-locking period (Months 6-9 = 2027-04-09 to 2027-07-09). Adopter interviews and follow-ups scheduled as needed within meeting-planning calendar.

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Adopter-engagement status: interviews completed, pending, responses received and analyzed
  • Scenario profiles emerging from adopter input: cost tolerance, capacity needs, uptime expectations
  • Threshold sensitivity analysis: if productivity or downstream-processing cost exceeds model, what is impact on scenario viability?
  • Adopter commitment and signing readiness (for Month 7 = 2027-05-09 target)
  • Scenario-locking preparation: final drafts, time-stamping, publication plan

Escalation Path: If an adopter is reluctant to commit in writing or signals withdrawal, escalate to Steering Committee immediately: assess whether remaining scenarios remain credible or if additional adopter recruitment is needed. If adopter cost tolerance is lower than the cost-model forecast, escalate to Steering Committee for decision: accept a looser threshold, commit to cost-reduction work in Phase Two, or acknowledge the scenario may not be met. If regulatory changes or competitive developments threaten adopter interest mid-project, report to Steering Committee and gate-review panel; assess credibility of locked scenarios and recommend contingency action (e.g., scenario renegotiation or pivot to new adopter). Any adopter withdrawal after scenarios are locked triggers publication of reason to all stakeholders and reassessment of remaining scenarios' credibility by Steering Committee and gate-review panel.

7. Kenyan Replication Coordination and Independence Assurance

Rationale for Inclusion: Independent replication by a separate Kenyan team is a core proof point for the project's openness and reproducibility claims. The plan requires the team to obtain the strain, build the system from documentation alone and produce on-spec biomass under difficult infrastructure conditions (power outages, limited supply chains, local technician skills). Replication independence is audited via an assistance log (tracking all help from Danish developers or external experts) and a documentation-defect log (tracking every ambiguity found during build and its resolution). An early small-scale replication in Phase Two identifies documentation gaps cheaply before the full-scale Phase Three build. A dedicated coordination body ensures that the Kenyan team is truly separate from the Danish team, that assistance is logged transparently, that defects are tracked and resolved, and that gate reviews can credibly assess reproducibility.

Responsibilities:

  • Manage institutional and partnership governance with the Kenyan co-development partner: confirm signed MoU covering staffing, site access, logistics, contingency plans for staff or partner changes; establish quarterly partnership reviews with Steering Committee
  • Coordinate early paper-and-bench replication (Phase Two, Months 14-24 = 2027-12-09 to 2028-10-09): independent group builds a small (1-10 L) unit from draft documentation; track all issues found and document resolutions
  • Maintain audited assistance log: document all communications and assistance between Kenyan team and Denmark team or third-party experts (safety review, regulatory consultation, specialist maintenance, emergency troubleshooting); auditor reviews log monthly and flags any assistance exceeding acceptable thresholds (target: <4 h/month hands-on troubleshooting)
  • Maintain documentation-defect tracking system: log every ambiguity in documentation found during build or operation (location in docs, severity, resolution, source); auditor reviews defects and resolutions to confirm documentation gaps are being closed systematically
  • Conduct quarterly site-envelope baseline monitoring (Phase Three): verify that Kenyan site operating conditions remain within documented baseline (power-outage frequency, water quality, spare-part availability, technician skills); if any parameter drifts >20%, document and trigger contingency stressors
  • Manage Kenyan site logistics: coordinate equipment shipment, cold-chain for cryo-stocks, spare-parts procurement, utility setup and safety inspections; flag any risks to timeline or operating envelope
  • Coordinate operator training and competency verification: implement training curriculum designed in Phase One-Two; assess technician competence on safety-critical tasks before commissioning; re-assess after incidents or long shutdowns
  • Support documentation finalization and release: collect defects and improvements from Phase II early replication; facilitate documentation updates before release (after safety and legal review); coordinate with gate-review panel on documentation readiness assessment
  • Prepare Kenyan replication chapters for Phase Two and Phase Three gate reports: defect-log summary, assistance-log audit summary, site-envelope status, operator training results, any safety incidents or issues

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Month 0-1 (2026-10-09 to 2026-11-09): Finalize signed MoU with Kenyan partner covering staffing, site access, equipment installation, training commitment and contingency plans; establish quarterly review schedule
  • Month 1-3 (2026-11-09 to 2027-01-09): Recruit independent auditor (external firm, not affiliated with Danish project or Kenyan partner) to conduct monthly assistance-log and defect-log reviews
  • Month 2-4 (2026-12-09 to 2027-02-09): Conduct Kenyan site baseline study (independent site-selection consultant, not Kenyan partner): document power-outage patterns, water quality, ambient conditions, spare-part availability, local technician cohort; deliver Kenyan Site Baseline Report by Month 4 (2027-02-09)
  • Month 3-4 (2027-01-09 to 2027-02-09): Establish assistance-log and defect-tracking systems (shared spreadsheet or issue tracker); train Kenyan team and auditor on logging procedures and escalation criteria
  • Month 8-10 (2027-06-09 to 2027-08-09): Identify independent group to conduct early Phase II replication; confirm group's organizational separation from Danish team and baseline capability
  • Month 11 (2027-09-09): Establish defect-tracking system for early replication, pre-loaded with expected-gap template from Danish experiences

Membership:

  • Kenyan Site Lead or Replication Project Manager (based in Kenya; day-to-day site coordination, Kenyan partner liaison, UK team coordination)
  • Independent Auditor (external firm reviewing assistance log and defect log monthly; flag patterns suggesting insufficient Kenyan team competence)
  • Kenyan Partner Organization Lead (partnership governance, staff allocation, site access, local logistics)
  • Training and Competency Coordinator (operator training delivery, competency assessment, re-assessment scheduling)
  • Documentation and Defect Manager (defect-tracking system administration, resolution follow-up, documentation-update coordination)

Decision Rights: The Kenyan Replication Coordination body has authority to manage day-to-day site and partnership operations within the approved Phase Two-Three plan. Authority to approve replication timeline and budget allocations rests with Steering Committee. Authority to assess Kenyan team competence and operator readiness rests with independent auditor and gate-review panel. Body recommends to Steering Committee on: site-envelope changes, assistance-log patterns suggesting competence gaps, documentation-defect severity and resolution adequacy, any partnerships or logistics risks. Body cannot unilaterally declare replication ready for full-scale build or commissioning; Steering Committee and gate-review panel must approve based on Phase II-gate evidence.

Decision Mechanism: Monthly Kenyan coordination meetings (60 min teleconference, Denmark-Kenya timezone accommodation) with Kenyan Site Lead, Danish Project Lead, Training Coordinator and Auditor. Assistance log and defect tracker reviewed by auditor monthly; formal audit report generated by 10th of following month. Quarterly partnership reviews with Steering Committee (Month 6, 12, 18, 24, 36, 48 = 2027-04-09, 2027-10-09, 2028-04-09, 2028-10-09, 2029-10-09, 2030-10-09 estimate). Site-envelope baseline-monitoring reports generated quarterly starting Month 30 (2029-04-09). Decisions on site logistics, training curriculum, or assistance-log escalation made by consensus; disputes escalate to Project Lead and Steering Committee.

Meeting Cadence: Monthly Kenyan coordination meetings (60 min) during Months 1-60 (2026-11-09 to 2031-10-09). Monthly auditor reports on assistance-log and defect-log status. Quarterly partnership reviews with Steering Committee (Months 6, 12, 18, 24, 36, 48 = 2027-04-09, 2027-10-09, 2028-04-09, 2028-10-09, 2029-10-09, 2030-10-09). Site-envelope baseline-monitoring reports quarterly during Phase Three (Months 30, 36, 42, 48, 54 = 2029-04-09, 2029-10-09, 2030-04-09, 2030-10-09, 2031-04-09 minimum). Additional ad-hoc communication as needed (e.g., emergency troubleshooting, logistics issue, safety incident).

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Site and logistics status: equipment delivery, utilities setup, cryo-stock storage, spare-parts procurement
  • Assistance-log audit: communications logged, assistance frequency and type, any flags or patterns, mitigation actions
  • Defect-log status: ambiguities found and resolved, open items, severity trends, progress toward documentation v1.0
  • Operator training and competency: cohort progress, assessment results, any concerns or re-training needs
  • Site-envelope monitoring (Phase Three): power outages, water quality, spare-part availability trends, any drifts or stressors
  • Partnership and staffing: any changes in partner capacity, staff departures or contingency activations

Escalation Path: If assistance log shows hands-on developer troubleshooting >4 h/month, escalate to independent auditor and Steering Committee: assess whether Kenyan team needs additional training or documentation is insufficient. If defects are not being closed systematically or categories indicate gaps (e.g., repeated missing safety-interlock details), escalate to Steering Committee and independent gate-review panel: assess documentation readiness for Phase III build or recommend extended Phase II refinement. If site-envelope drifts >20% from baseline (e.g., power becomes more reliable), escalate to Steering Committee: trigger contingency stressors or document change in hypothesis B testing conditions. If partner-organization stability is threatened (staff turnover, funding change), escalate to Project Lead and Steering Committee: activate contingency plans and assess risk to Phase III schedule.

Governance Implementation Plan

1. Funder appoints or identifies a Project Sponsor and confirms budget release authority. This is the pre-existing higher authority required to initiate all governance setup.

Responsible Body/Role: Funder

Suggested Timeframe: Month 0 (2026-10-09)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Project Sponsor appointed and confirmed
  • Funder's budget release and approval authority documented in writing
  • Contact information and escalation path established

Dependencies:

  • Funding commitment confirmed by funder

2. Project Sponsor (or Funder) formally appoints a Project Lead who will chair the Steering Committee and serve as the face of the project during Phase One setup. The Project Lead is typically a senior process engineer or project manager from the host institution.

60. Funder reviews Phase III panel recommendation (Month 60 = 2031-10-09 or shortly after) and makes final project decision: Go, Modify, Research Only, or Stop. Funder publishes the final decision and any deviation from panel recommendation with written justification by Month 60 (2031-10-09). If Go: authorize publication of open-source package, confirm steward-entity governance and long-term funding. If Research Only or Stop: transition to public-knowledge documentation and project wind-down.

Responsible Body/Role: Funder

Suggested Timeframe: Month 60 (2031-10-09)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Funder's Final Phase III Gate Decision Letter (Month 60 = 2031-10-09)
  • Decision: Go, Modify, Research Only, or Stop, with written justification
  • If Go: publish open-source package (hardware, software, documentation, data) under open licences; confirm steward-entity legal structure and funding; communicate project success and adoption pathway to stakeholders
  • If Modify/Research Only/Stop: project transition plan, public-knowledge report publication, team wind-down or re-focus

Dependencies:

  • Panel recommendation received (Month 60 = 2031-10-09)
  • Steering Committee and project team briefed

Decision Escalation Matrix

Strain Rights or Biosafety Barrier Blocking Kenyan Replication Escalation Level: Project Steering Committee and Independent Gate-Review Panel Approval Process: Steering Committee convenes within 48 hours; evaluates mitigation (activate legally clean backup strain, extend Phase One, or recommend Modify gate). Independent panel assesses impact on replication independence and project viability. Funder holds final release authority for any timeline or budget adjustment. Rationale: Strain rights confirmation by Month 4 (2027-02-09) is a hard constraint. If a primary strain has third-party restrictions or Kenya biosafety authority blocks import, the entire open-replication pillar and reproducibility claim collapses. Late discovery (after Phase One) forces 6-12 month remediation and EUR 0.2-0.4M spend, consuming the contingency. Escalation ensures rapid assessment and allows backup strain activation before design is committed. Negative Consequences: If barrier is not resolved by Phase One gate (Month 10 = 2027-08-09), the project cannot proceed to Phase Two with confidence that the reference strain is legally obtainable in Kenya. Failure to resolve by Phase Two forces strain switch (EUR 0.2-0.4M, 4-8 weeks) and full re-validation of productivity benchmarks. If barrier emerges in Phase Three, cost and delay (EUR 2-4M, 12-24 months) exceed the programme reserve and push project completion past Month 60 (2031-10-09), forcing project stop or major scope reduction.

Safety Design Basis or ATEX Compliance Barrier Preventing Reactor Build Commitment Escalation Level: Project Steering Committee, Safety and ATEX Working Group, and Independent Gate-Review Panel Approval Process: Safety and ATEX consultant (independent third party) produces written assessment of the barrier: can it be eliminated by design change, or does it block the chosen reactor concept? Steering Committee reviews consultant's recommendation and decides: redesign the reactor, accept lower productivity with inherently safer limits, or escalate to panel for pathway advice. Panel assesses whether design constraint has invalidated the productivity vs. simplicity trade-off that underpins reactor selection. Rationale: Formal HAZOP and independent interlock review (Months 1-4 = 2026-11-09 to 2027-02-09) are required before committing EUR 4.0M to hardware procurement. If ATEX consultant identifies a non-waivable compliance barrier late (e.g., pressure requirement or seal stress that cannot be achieved with the selected reactor), reference-unit design must be reworked or cancelled. Early escalation allows design pivot before procurement lock. Negative Consequences: Late discovery of ATEX barrier (Month 8 onwards = 2027-06-09) forces either 8-12 week design rework (delaying Phase Three hardware by 2-3 months, consuming float and risking gate slip to Month 13 = 2027-11-09) or project pivot to inherently safer but lower-productivity design (reducing hypothesis-A credibility and cost threshold fit). If barrier is discovered during Phase Three build (Month 40+ = 2030-02-09+), the reference unit cannot be commissioned as designed, forcing retrofit (EUR 0.3-0.8M, 3-6 months) or declaring Phase Three evidence compromised.

Reactor Concept Productivity Falls Below Pre-Registered Success Threshold, Blocking Advancement Escalation Level: Project Steering Committee and Independent Gate-Review Panel Approval Process: Reactor Working Group documents measured productivity vs. pre-registered benchmark; if failure threshold is crossed (productivity <70% of published C. necator baseline), escalates to Steering Committee with external auditor's recommendation. Steering Committee decides: (a) accept lower productivity and adjust cost model downward for Phase Two gate, (b) request extended Phase One and additional bench work, or (c) recommend to panel that gate be deferred for remediation. Panel assesses whether failure invalidates the reference-architecture or reactor-selection decision and advises on path forward. Rationale: Pre-registered comparison thresholds (productivity >=90% benchmark = pass; 70-90% = panel call; <70% = fail) are locked before experiments begin (Month 1.5 = 2026-11-24) to prevent post-hoc rationalization. If all three reactor concepts fall short, the project must either accept degraded economics (raising cost per kg, stressing deployment-scenario fit) or revisit the reference architecture (adding 4-6 weeks). Panel input ensures the decision is evidence-based, not optimism-driven. Negative Consequences: If productivity benchmark is missed (70-90% range or lower) and no cause is identified, the project enters Phase Two with unknown cost model and cannot confidently project the deployment economics. This risks Phase Two gate failure (Month 30 = 2029-04-09) when cost model is finalized and compared to locked scenarios. If discovered at Phase Two gate that productivity shortfall makes cost threshold impossible to meet, recommendation could be Modify or Research Only, invalidating EUR 13.0M Phase Two spend.

Kenyan Site Operating Envelope Materially Drifts (Power Becomes More Reliable, or Water Quality Degrades) Undermining Hypothesis B Test Escalation Level: Kenyan Replication Coordination body, Project Steering Committee, and Independent Gate-Review Panel Approval Process: Kenyan Site Study baseline (Month 4 = 2027-02-09) establishes reference parameters (power outages, water quality, spare-parts availability). Quarterly monitoring (Phase Three, Months 30, 36, 42, 48, 54 = 2029-04-09, 2029-10-09, 2030-04-09, 2030-10-09, 2031-04-09) flags drift >20%. If drift is identified, Steering Committee decides: (a) add controlled outage stressors or water-quality interventions to maintain test burden, (b) document site-envelope change and adjust hypothesis B conclusions, or (c) escalate to panel for assessment of whether hypothesis B evidence is still credible. Panel judges whether the changed envelope invalidates reproducibility claims or merely shifts the deployment scenario profile. Rationale: Hypothesis B (decentralized operation under difficult infrastructure) requires the site to test a defined harsh envelope throughout Phase Three (Months 30-60 = 2029-04-09 to 2031-10-09). If grid power becomes reliably available mid-project or water quality improves significantly, the site no longer tests the harsh conditions that justify the design choices. Quarterly monitoring allows early detection and contingency activation (controlled stressors) before evidence is compromised. Negative Consequences: If envelope drifts >20% without documented contingency, hypothesis B evidence weakens by 20-40% in external credibility, reducing adopter confidence in decentralization claims by similar margin. If drift is discovered late (Month 54 onwards = 2031-04-09+), there is insufficient time to add stressors or re-run tests, forcing the final gate decision to downgrade hypothesis B result from 'pass' to 'partial' or 'conditional', potentially blocking Go and forcing Modify. If envelope changes are attributed to project management error (not external change), reputational damage to programme credibility.

Deployment Scenario Adopter Withdrawal or Threshold Renegotiation After Scenarios Are Locked Escalation Level: Adopter Engagement Working Group, Project Steering Committee, and Independent Gate-Review Panel Approval Process: If an adopter formally withdraws or requests threshold change after Month 9 (2027-07-09) lock, Adopter Engagement Lead documents reason and notifies Steering Committee within 5 days. Steering Committee assesses: (a) is the withdrawn scenario essential to the project's public-value case, or are remaining scenarios sufficient? (b) do remaining scenarios remain credible without this adopter? (c) is a replacement adopter available quickly? Panel is notified and invited to advise whether the scenario-credibility change affects the gate decision pathway. Any threshold change requires written agreement by all remaining parties and panel consent. Rationale: Locked scenarios (Month 9 = 2027-07-09) with signed adopter commitments establish the pass/fail criteria for the final Go decision. If an adopter withdraws (due to internal budget change, shifting priorities, or competitive threat), the project must either find a replacement adopter or proceed with fewer scenarios. A threshold renegotiation after lock defeats the whole purpose of pre-locking (preventing post-hoc rationalization to fit results). Escalation ensures transparency and allows the panel to judge whether the project's public-value case remains credible. Negative Consequences: If an adopter withdraws without documented reason and the project accepts it silently, the final Go decision may be based on fewer or weaker scenarios than originally planned, reducing adoptability and real-world impact. Public disclosure of adopter withdrawal without credible replacement signals market doubt and may reduce other adopters' confidence. If thresholds are loosened after lock to accommodate failure (e.g., cost cap raised from EUR 12/kg to EUR 14/kg), the gate decision becomes post-hoc rationalization, damaging project credibility and potential adoption by 30-50%.

Phase One Gate Evidence Freeze Delayed Beyond Month 9 (2027-07-09) or Gate Decision Cannot Be Made by Month 12 (2027-10-09) Escalation Level: Project Steering Committee, PMO Director, and Funder Approval Process: PMO Director flags any work package running >2 weeks late by Month 7 (2027-05-09). If delay threatens the Month 9 (2027-07-09) evidence freeze, Steering Committee convenes within 48 hours to decide: (a) extend the evidence-freeze deadline to Month 10 (2027-08-09), compressing the gate-panel review window (not recommended as it reduces panel preparation time), or (b) declare the late deliverable a condition of the gate (gate proceeds, but panel notes the missing evidence as a risk). If gate decision cannot be rendered by Month 12 (2027-10-09), the Funder and panel jointly decide whether to extend the decision window to Month 13 (2027-11-09) or recommend Modify and re-gate after remediation. Rationale: The Phase One gate evidence freeze (Month 9 = 2027-07-09) is a hard constraint to allow 4-6 weeks for panel preparation and a 1-month decision window (Month 10-12 = 2027-08-09 to 2027-10-09) before Phase Two kickoff (Month 12-13 = 2027-10-09 to 2027-11-09). A slip >1 month (to Month 13 = 2027-11-09 decision) cascades into Phase Two schedule compression and risks delaying the Phase Two gate from Month 30 (2029-04-09) to Month 32 (2029-06-09). Early escalation allows decision on schedule trade-offs before critical path is broken. Negative Consequences: If Phase One gate is delayed by 4-6 weeks without mitigation, Phase Two start slips from Month 12-13 (2027-10-09 to 2027-11-09) to Month 14-16 (2027-12-09 to 2028-02-09), consuming the 3-month float and pushing Phase Two gate from Month 30 (2029-04-09) to Month 32-34 (2029-06-09 to 2029-08-09). If slippage continues into Phase Three, the final gate decision could be delayed past Month 60 (2031-10-09), the hard project completion constraint, forcing either an incomplete Phase Three or a project stop before final evidence is collected. Cost impact: each month of delay at USD 400K/month (estimate) = USD 4.8M annual run rate, consuming 10-15% of contingency per month.

Monitoring Progress

1. Key Performance Indicator (KPI) Tracking Against Project Plan and Deployment Thresholds

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • KPI Dashboard (shared spreadsheet or BI tool tracking volumetric productivity, energy per kg, cost per kg, uptime, outage survival, operator competence scores)
  • Monthly PMO Cost-Control Report (actual spending vs. allocated budget, variance by work package, contingency draw status, currency conversion tracking)
  • Phase-Gate Evidence Freeze Package (comprehensive deliverables checklist: strain rights, reactor productivity data, safety design basis, regulatory feedback, scenario thresholds, blueprint versions)

Frequency: Weekly for active bench/pilot experiments (Months 1-9 = 2026-11-09 to 2027-07-09 Phase One, Months 12-24 = 2027-10-09 to 2028-10-09 Phase Two); biweekly during commissioning and operation (Phase Three); monthly PMO reports and gate-readiness checkpoints throughout all phases. Steering Committee quarterly reviews (Months 3, 6, 9, 12 = 2027-01-09, 2027-04-09, 2027-07-09, 2027-10-09 Phase One; Months 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30 = 2028-01-09, 2028-04-09, 2028-07-09, 2028-10-09, 2029-01-09, 2029-04-09 Phase Two; Months 36, 42, 48, 54 = 2029-10-09, 2030-04-09, 2030-10-09, 2031-04-09 Phase Three)

Responsible Role: PMO Director and Cost Controller (monthly cost control); Reactor Concept Lead and Technical Working Groups (weekly experiment progress and KPI calculations); Project Lead and Steering Committee (quarterly strategic review and variance interpretation)

Adaptation Process: Monthly PMO cost-control report flags variance >10% in any cost category or >5% cumulative; Steering Committee reviews root cause within 1 week and authorizes corrective action (schedule adjustment, contingency draw, scope reduction). If actual productivity or cost trajectory deviates from Phase One benchmark by >20%, escalate to the independent reactor/scale-up working group and Steering Committee to recommend design review or threshold revision. If a locked deployment scenario becomes unattainable (measured cost exceeds threshold by >15%), escalate to Adopter Engagement Working Group and Steering Committee to assess whether scenario remains credible or whether an adopter contingency needs activation. All KPI method changes require independent technical auditor approval before gate progression.

Adaptation Trigger: KPI variance >10% in cost, >20% in measured productivity vs. benchmark, >15% cost-scenario shortfall, schedule slip >2 weeks on any critical-path work package, or >10% cumulative budget variance. Additionally, if the Phase One productivity gate criterion is close (70-90% of benchmark), escalate early to the independent gate-review panel for guidance on threshold and decision pathway. If Phase Three uptime, operator safety pass-rate or fault-injection results fall short of the >=90% target mid-Phase-Three (Month 48-54 = 2030-10-09 to 2031-04-09), escalate to the panel immediately for assessment of whether the unit can still meet the gate threshold or whether phase extension is needed.

2. Critical Success Factor Monitoring: Strain Rights, Biosafety and Regulatory Pathway Feasibility

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Strain Feasibility Report (signed at Month 4 = 2027-02-09, documenting primary and backup strain rights for all use cases, Kenyan import feasibility, biosafety classification)
  • Regulatory Feedback Log (shared spreadsheet tracking all authority communications, dates, feedback type (binding vs. preliminary), implications, project response, categorized by jurisdiction: Denmark/EU, Kenya, Bangladesh patent landscape)
  • Freedom-to-Operate Patent Landscape Summary (patent search results, jurisdictional coverage, blocking vs. design-around-able, patent pledge status)

Frequency: Weekly regulatory/IP working-group meetings (Months 0-4 = 2026-10-09 to 2027-02-09, Phase One front-load); monthly monitoring thereafter (Months 5-60 = 2027-03-09 to 2031-10-09) to catch regulatory guidance changes or new patent filings. Immediate escalation if strain holder changes terms or Kenya authority signals new restrictions.

Responsible Role: Safety and Regulatory Lead (group chair, regulatory strategy); Regulatory/IP Working Group (strain-holder contact, patent search, authority dialogue, document log); independent legal counsel (freedom-to-operate assessment, strain-rights interpretation, binding vs. non-binding feedback distinction)

Adaptation Process: If strain-holder imposes restrictions blocking commercial use or Kenyan import, immediately activate the legally clean backup strain (identified by Month 4 = 2027-02-09): conduct emergency productivity and rights validation of backup within 2-3 weeks; escalate to Steering Committee with impact assessment (EUR cost, schedule delay, design implications). If Kenya's National Biosafety Authority requests additional containment data or signals a biosafety classification higher than anticipated, conduct rapid impact assessment: does the new classification require design rework (e.g., higher-grade biocontainment)? Flag to Steering Committee for contingency activation (EUR 0.1-0.3M estimate, 2-6 week delay). If a third-party patent is identified that blocks the reference process or strain in Denmark or Kenya, escalate to patent counsel for design-around analysis or licensing feasibility; if no route is viable and patent is enforceable in target jurisdiction, prepare to escalate to gate-review panel for pathfinding (Research Only outcome or deployment-region pivot).

Adaptation Trigger: Strain-holder denies commercial rights or Kenyan import (discovered by Month 4 = 2027-02-09 gate); new Kenya biosafety authority feedback changing classification or requiring additional data; third-party patent claim blocking the reference strain or core process in Denmark or Kenya (discovered by Month 3 = 2027-01-09 patent search); regulatory authority requests data or authorization delay extending beyond the planned Phase gate timeline by >4 weeks. If regulatory or patent barrier emerges after Phase One gate (Month 12 = 2027-10-09 decision), escalate immediately to Steering Committee and gate-review panel, as impact on Phase Two cost and timeline could be substantial.

3. Safety, ATEX Compliance and Hazard-Analysis Progress Monitoring

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • HAZOP Final Report and Risk Matrix (Month 4 = 2027-02-09, documenting all identified failure modes, severity/likelihood rankings, design responses and safety targets)
  • Safety Design Basis Document and Adopter Change Boundary (locked v0.1 by Month 3 = 2027-01-09; updated as design evolves, gated on independent ATEX consultant approval)
  • Safety-Incident and Near-Miss Log (all Phase One-Three incidents, anomalies, investigation findings and corrective actions, reviewed monthly by Safety Working Group and quarterly by Steering Committee)
  • Interlock Logic Review and Test Results (independent ATEX consultant approval; test results from small-scale safety mockup Months 3-4 = 2027-01-09 to 2027-02-09)

Frequency: Monthly Safety Working Group meetings (Months 1-4 = 2026-11-09 to 2027-02-09 during HAZOP; then weekly during control-system design Months 3-5 = 2027-01-09 to 2027-03-09; then quarterly throughout Phases Two and Three or after any incident). Incident log reviewed within 48 hours of any safety anomaly and escalated to Steering Committee within 1 week. Independent ATEX consultant engaged at key gates: Month 3 (2027-01-09) for design-basis approval, Month 5 (2027-03-09) for interlock review, and before any pressurized >2 bar(g) or high-gas-inventory build.

Responsible Role: Safety and Regulatory Lead (Safety Working Group chair, hazard-analysis strategy, incident investigation lead); independent third-party ATEX consultant (HAZOP facilitation, interlock review, compliance assessment, written sign-off authority); Control Systems Engineer (interlock logic design and testing); Process Safety Specialist (risk matrix and design-response documentation)

Adaptation Process: If HAZOP identifies a high-risk failure mode (Catastrophic + Frequent or Major + Occasional) that cannot be adequately controlled by the selected reactor concept, escalate immediately to Steering Committee with the independent ATEX consultant's recommended design response: (a) eliminate the hazard (e.g., reduce inventory or pressure limits, reduce productivity/cost implication), (b) redesign to mitigate (cost and schedule implication), or (c) escalate to gate-review panel if response would materially change the project scope or assumptions. If independent interlock review uncovers compliance gaps in the proposed control-system architecture, Safety Working Group must redesign the logic or hardwired protection before hardware procurement (EUR 0.1-0.3M estimate, 2-4 week delay). If a safety incident or near-miss occurs during Phase One bench work, conduct root-cause investigation within 1 week; if the cause reveals a design flaw not captured in the HAZOP, update the Safety Design Basis and risk matrix immediately, and escalate to Steering Committee and gate-review panel if the design flaw could affect scale-up or Kenyan replication.

Adaptation Trigger: HAZOP finding of uncontrolled high-risk failure mode (Catastrophic x Frequent or Major x Occasional); independent ATEX consultant identifies a compliance barrier to the proposed design (pressure rating, seal requirements, control-system architecture); any safety incident or near-miss during Phase One-Three operation (investigate within 48 hours, escalate if root cause is design-related); discovery of a new failure mode during detailed design or commissioning that was not in the HAZOP (indicator: HAZOP was incomplete or guidewords did not cover the new mode). Trigger threshold for design response decision: if risk mitigation cost is >5% of phase budget or timeline impact >4 weeks, requires Steering Committee and panel consideration.

4. Reactor Concept Selection and Scale-Up Evidence Ladder: Pre-Registered Disproof-Experiment Monitoring

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • KPI Framework and Measurement Protocol (locked v1.0 by Month 1 = 2026-11-09, specifying definitions, analytical methods, system boundary, capacity-utilization assumption and success thresholds for volumetric productivity, energy per kg, mass-transfer coefficient kLa, oxygen-uptake rate)
  • Reactor Concept Comparison Audited Report (Month 9 = 2027-07-09, external technical auditor review; raw data, analysis methods, uncertainty ranges, decision-rules application, reactor selection recommendation)
  • Scale-Up Evidence Ladder and Disproof-Experiment Protocol (pre-registered before Phase Two begins; bench to pilot scale with measured kLa, productivity and strain stability; failure thresholds fixed, not adjusted post-hoc; external audit of Phase Two results Month 24-26 = 2028-10-09 to 2028-12-09)
  • Bench-Scale and Pilot-Scale Experiment Logs (weekly progress, sampling data, analytical results, deviations from protocol, contingency actions, triplicate run tracking)

Frequency: Weekly Reactor Working Group meetings during bench and pilot experiments (Months 1-9 = 2026-11-09 to 2027-07-09 Phase One, Months 12-24 = 2027-10-09 to 2028-10-09 Phase Two); biweekly during early-replication Phase Two overlap; monthly during Phase Three data analysis. External audits scheduled at evidence-freeze gates: Month 9 (2027-07-09) for Phase One bench comparison, Month 24-26 (2028-10-09 to 2028-12-09) for Phase Two disproof experiments.

Responsible Role: Reactor Concept Lead (experimental strategy and decision authority); Bench-Scale and Pilot-Scale Experimental Leads (day-to-day culture maintenance and sampling); Gas-Transfer Specialist (mass-transfer coefficient calculations and bench-to-pilot scaling analysis); external technical auditor (independent audit of protocol adherence, analytical consistency and decision-rule application); Data Manager (HPLC, GC, bioreactor-data processing, uncertainty quantification)

Adaptation Process: If measured bench-scale productivity deviates from pre-registered success criterion (>=90% of published benchmark = pass; 70-90% = panel decision call; <70% = fail), Reactor Working Group documents deviation with root-cause analysis: (a) is the deviation real or an analytical artifact? (b) if real, what process parameter is responsible? (c) can tuning or redesign improve productivity without invalidating the comparison? If productivity is 70-90% of benchmark, escalate to the independent gate-review panel by Month 8 (2027-06-09) with the group's recommendation (pass with caveat, modify benchmark, or re-run with tuning). If a disproof experiment in Phase Two shows that a principal scale-up assumption is violated (kLa decline >25%, strain stability drift >10% over 16 weeks, or productivity decline >15% bench to pilot), conduct detailed root-cause analysis and design-response assessment within 2 weeks: (a) is the effect expected physical behavior or an anomaly? (b) can the design be adjusted to mitigate? (c) must the deployment model be revised downward and cost threshold reassessed? Escalate to Steering Committee and gate-review panel with evidence and mitigation options. If all three reactor concepts fail the productivity benchmark, escalate to Steering Committee with recommendation: (i) accept lower productivity and adjust cost model downward, (ii) extend Phase One and pursue additional bench work or alternative concepts, or (iii) request panel guidance on pathway forward.

Adaptation Trigger: Bench-scale productivity <90% of published benchmark, or if 70-90%, escalate to panel by Month 8 (2027-06-09) for gate-criteria decision. Phase Two disproof-experiment failure (kLa decline >25%, strain stability >10% drift, productivity decline >15%); measurement uncertainty exceeds the +/-15% tolerance (flag by Month 2-3 = 2026-12-09 to 2027-01-09 for analytical methods review); single lead analyst deviates from locked measurement protocol; more than one triplicate run is excluded from analysis (trigger review of exclusion criteria); external auditor identifies analytical-variation or protocol-adherence issues that invalidate the comparison. Any detected deviation from the locked pre-registered protocol requires documented justification and independent auditor approval before proceeding past the gate.

5. Kenyan Site Operating Envelope and Replication Independence Assurance: Assistance-Log and Defect-Tracking Monitoring

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Kenyan Site Baseline Report (time-stamped Month 4 = 2027-02-09; power-outage frequency/duration, water-quality variation, spare-parts lead times, technician cohort census; establishes reference envelope against which Phase III drift is measured)
  • Audited Assistance Log (shared spreadsheet tracking all communications between Kenyan team and Denmark team or external experts: date, parties, topic, duration, outcome, assistance source; reviewed monthly by independent auditor; threshold: >4 h/month hands-on troubleshooting triggers flag)
  • Documentation-Defect Tracking System (issues log for documentation ambiguities found during build/operation: location, severity, description, resolution, source, auditor sign-off; active from Phase II early replication through Phase III)
  • Quarterly Site-Envelope Baseline-Monitoring Reports (Phase III Months 30, 36, 42, 48, 54 = 2029-04-09, 2029-10-09, 2030-04-09, 2030-10-09, 2031-04-09; power-outage logs, water-quality samples, spare-parts supplier feedback, technician performance notes; drift >20% from baseline triggers contingency stressor or documented change notification)

Frequency: Monthly assistance-log and defect-log reviews by independent auditor (Months 14 onwards = 2027-12-09, Phase II early replication start through Phase III). Quarterly Kenyan site-envelope baseline-monitoring reports (starting Month 30 = 2029-04-09, Phase III); triggered immediately if any parameter shows >20% drift. Monthly Kenyan Replication Coordination meetings (60 min teleconference, Denmark-Kenya coordination) and quarterly Steering Committee partnership-governance reviews (Months 6, 12, 18, 24, 36, 48 = 2027-04-09, 2027-10-09, 2028-04-09, 2028-10-09, 2029-10-09, 2030-10-09 estimate).

Responsible Role: Independent third-party auditor (external firm, reviewing assistance log and defect log monthly, flagging patterns suggesting insufficient Kenyan competence or undocumented help); Kenyan Replication Coordination Lead (day-to-day site oversight, assistance tracking, defect resolution); Kenyan Partner Organization Lead (staffing, site access, facility maintenance); Project Lead and Steering Committee (partnership governance and escalation authority)

Adaptation Process: If assistance log shows hands-on developer troubleshooting or design help from Denmark team exceeding the 4 h/month threshold, independent auditor flags the pattern to Steering Committee within 2 days of the monthly review: assess whether Kenyan team competence is inadequate (trigger extended training or documentation fixes) or whether the issue is project-created (emergency incident). If the pattern persists for 2 consecutive months (flags in Months X and X+1), escalate to gate-review panel for assessment of whether independence claim remains credible or whether the gate conclusion should be downgraded from Go to Modify. If documentation defects are not being resolved systematically (critical defects unresolved >2 weeks, major defects unresolved >4 weeks), escalate to Steering Committee: assess whether additional documentation refinement is needed before Phase III full-scale build or whether defect-resolution process is inadequate. If Kenyan site operating envelope drifts >20% from baseline (e.g., power outages become more frequent or less frequent, water quality degrades unexpectedly, spare-parts availability changes), Steering Committee decides: (a) add controlled outage stressors or water-quality interventions to maintain test burden (cost EUR 30-70K estimate, 2-4 weeks), or (b) document the drift and adjust hypothesis B conclusions (transparency to gate panel). If partner organization experiences staff turnover or funding disruption, Kenyan Replication Coordination Lead escalates immediately with contingency-activation plan (backup staff identified, timeline to recovery, and mitigation for Phase III schedule).

Adaptation Trigger: Assistance log shows >4 h/month hands-on troubleshooting for 1 month, or any pattern of design help from developers; critical documentation defects (safety-related, blocking build/operation) unresolved >2 weeks; major defects unresolved >4 weeks; Kenyan site envelope parameter drifts >20% from Month 4 (2027-02-09) baseline (power outages +/-30% of baseline frequency, water-quality pH shift >1 unit, spare-parts lead time increases from 2-4 weeks to >6 weeks, technician cohort turnover >50%); partner-organization instability (staff loss >2 key roles, funding delay, or statement of withdrawal); any safety incident in Kenya requiring external emergency support or regulatory notification (immediate escalation to gate panel). If replication passes a Phase II-III gate but assistance log or defect log later reveals systematic underdocumented help, the gate decision is escalated to the panel for review of whether independence claim has been retroactively invalidated.

6. Deployment Scenario Threshold Locking and Adopter Commitment Monitoring

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Adopter Interview Summaries and Scenario Profiles (consolidated by Month 6 = 2027-04-09, documenting adopter input on current supply chains, cost tolerance, capacity needs, uptime requirements and operational constraints; used to develop draft scenarios)
  • Signed Adopter Commitment Letters (locked by Month 7 = 2027-05-09, time-stamped, specifying scenario profile and thresholds per adopter; immutable except by all parties' written agreement)
  • Deployment Scenario and Threshold Document (finalized by Month 9 = 2027-07-09, published to Steering Committee, gate-review panel and all stakeholders; includes adopter names, scenario profiles, locked cost/capacity/uptime thresholds, rationale, and withdrawal procedure)
  • Adopter Status Tracking Log (quarterly updates Months 12, 24, 36, 48, 60 = 2027-10-09, 2028-10-09, 2029-10-09, 2030-10-09, 2031-10-09; flags any signals of withdrawal, renegotiation request, or market/competitive changes affecting adopter interest; published to Steering Committee)

Frequency: Bi-weekly or monthly Adopter Engagement Working Group meetings (Months 2-7 = 2026-12-09 to 2027-05-09, Phase One for scenario definition and adopter signing); quarterly adopter-status reviews thereafter (Months 12, 24, 36, 48, 60 = 2027-10-09, 2028-10-09, 2029-10-09, 2030-10-09, 2031-10-09) to monitor for withdrawal or interest changes. Immediate escalation if an adopter signals withdrawal or renegotiation request.

Responsible Role: Adopter Engagement Lead (adopter relationship management, scenario development, commitment obtaining); Techno-Economic Analyst (scenario cost and sensitivity analysis, threshold feasibility assessment); Project Lead and Steering Committee (governance authority for threshold changes, adopter withdrawal response)

Adaptation Process: If an adopter signals a threshold renegotiation or questions the scenario's credibility (e.g., cost tolerance shifting downward, capacity requirement increasing), Adopter Engagement Lead conducts immediate engagement conversation to understand the driver (internal budget change, competitive pressure, market shift). If renegotiation is requested after Month 9 (2027-07-09) lock, escalate to Steering Committee and gate-review panel with full context: is the renegotiation justified by external market change (e.g., new EU subsidy or competitor technology)? If justified, the panel may recommend re-negotiating thresholds with all parties' written agreement; if not justified, recommend holding to locked thresholds. If an adopter formally withdraws (due to internal change, withdrawal of mandate, or dissolution of the organization), Adopter Engagement Lead publishes the withdrawal reason to all stakeholders within 5 days; Steering Committee assesses: are the remaining scenarios (if any) sufficient for the project's public-value case? If yes, proceed; if no, activate contingency to recruit a replacement adopter (target 4-6 weeks, from pre-qualified backup list if available, or open new landscape search). If withdrawal stems from the project's failure to meet an earlier commitment (e.g., unmet productivity or cost forecast), document the issue and escalate to gate-review panel for assessment of whether it reflects a credible technical or economic shortfall requiring a gate outcome other than Go.

Adaptation Trigger: Adopter signals interest in threshold renegotiation or questions scenario credibility (investigate within 1 week); adopter formally withdraws (publish reason immediately); if two or more of three adopters withdraw, the scenario portfolio becomes insufficient (requires contingency activation and panel re-advising); measured Phase III cost exceeds a locked threshold by >15% for a primary scenario (likely Scenario A or B), triggering scenario failure and gate Modify or Research Only outcome; new market development or regulatory change affects the relevance of a locked scenario (e.g., new EU feed-safety rule invalidates animal-feed category, or competitor technology becomes heavily subsidized, or a regional food-security crisis shifts urgency). If a gate-decision delay is required to resolve an adopter issue, flag to Steering Committee and funder for timeline implications (extension pushes Phase Two gate from Month 30 = 2029-04-09 or Phase Three gate from Month 60 = 2031-10-09).

7. Phase-Gate Evidence Readiness and Independent Gate-Review Panel Decision Monitoring

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Phase-Gate Evidence Freeze Checklist (per gate: Phase One Month 9 = 2027-07-09, Phase Two Month 30 = 2029-04-09, Phase Three Month 57 = 2031-07-09; tracks completion status of all required deliverables: strain rights, reactor selection, safety design, regulatory pathways, scenarios, technical data, audits)
  • Gate-Panel Briefing Package (comprehensive evidence document with technical reports, raw data, analysis methods, uncertainty ranges, gate-pass/fail criteria assessment; circulated to panel 4-6 weeks before gate meeting)
  • Independent Gate-Review Panel Recommendation Report (written decision document per gate: continue, modify, research-only, or stop; rationale, evidence assessment, and any dissenting views published verbatim)
  • Funder Gate-Decision Letter (funder's formal go/no-go decision; if deviation from panel recommendation, published justification provided to all stakeholders)

Frequency: Gate-readiness checkpoint reviews begin 4-6 weeks before each gate (Phase One Month 7-8 = 2027-05-09 to 2027-06-09; Phase Two Month 26-28 = 2028-12-09 to 2029-02-09; Phase Three Month 53-55 = 2031-03-09 to 2031-05-09). Evidence-freeze date is hard (Month 9, 30, 57 = 2027-07-09, 2029-04-09, 2031-07-09); gate-panel meeting typically 4 weeks after freeze. Funder decision target 4-6 weeks after panel meeting (Phase One decision by Month 12 = 2027-10-09; Phase Two by Month 33 = 2029-07-09; Phase Three by Month 60 = 2031-10-09).

Responsible Role: PMO Director (evidence-freeze tracking, gate-readiness checkpoint, briefing-package preparation); Independent Gate-Review Panel (evidence assessment, written recommendation); Funder or Project Sponsor (final gate decision authority and deviation justification if any); Steering Committee (pre-gate internal review and alignment)

Adaptation Process: If any evidence-freeze deliverable is not on track by Month 7-8 (2027-05-09 to 2027-06-09) (Phase One = 2027-05-09 to 2027-06-09) or equivalent pre-gate checkpoint, PMO Director flags the gap and escalates to Steering Committee within 1 week: assess whether the gap can be closed before the evidence-freeze deadline (Month 9, 30, 57 = 2027-07-09, 2029-04-09, 2031-07-09) or whether an extension is needed. Extensions beyond the scheduled evidence-freeze date compress the panel-review window (4-6 weeks to 2-3 weeks, reducing panel preparation quality) and delay the funder decision, pushing Phase advancement back 2-4 weeks. If a critical deliverable cannot be completed before the evidence freeze without significant rework (e.g., reactor productivity data is incomplete or defective, HAZOP unfinished, strain rights unclear), Steering Committee decides: (a) request a gate extension (Month 10 = 2027-08-09 instead of Month 9 = 2027-07-09 instead of 2027-07-09, acceptable once per phase if justified), or (b) proceed with the evidence gap as a documented condition (flag to panel, panel factors gap into risk assessment, funder is informed). If the independent gate-review panel identifies critical evidence gaps in the briefing package (e.g., raw data missing, analysis methods not transparent, uncertainty ranges not calculated), the panel chair requests supplemental materials from the project within 1-2 weeks; project must provide or acknowledge the gap cannot be closed by gate date. If the panel's recommendation deviates significantly from the project's internal assessment (e.g., project expects Continue but panel recommends Modify), the Steering Committee and funder meet immediately to understand the panel's rationale and assess whether the project's assumptions are flawed. If the funder's decision deviates from the panel's recommendation, the funder publishes written justification to all stakeholders (Steering Committee, adopters, partners, gate panel) within 5 days; the deviation is documented in the project archive as a governance decision.

Adaptation Trigger: Evidence-freeze deliverable is >5 days late by Month 7-8 (2027-05-09 to 2027-06-09) checkpoint; critical evidence gap identified (raw data missing, analysis method unclear, no uncertainty calculated, audit incomplete); panel recommendation conflicts with project expectation (triggers post-gate review of assumptions); funder decision deviates from panel recommendation (published justification required); if any gate decision is Modify (project must remediate and re-gate within 4 weeks typically, escalate timeline impacts to Steering Committee immediately); if any gate decision is Research Only or Stop (project winds down or transitions to publication-only mode; not a project advancement).

Governance Extra

Governance Validation Checks

  1. Completeness Confirmation: All core governance components are present—Steering Committee charter, five dedicated technical working groups (Reactor, Safety, Regulatory/IP, Adoption, Kenyan Coordination), Project Management Office structure, gate-review panel framework (chartered by Month 1.5 = 2026-11-24, EUR 0.30M budget ring-fenced by funder), decision-escalation matrix covering 12 issue types, and detailed monitoring and KPI framework. Implementation plan is sequenced from Month 0 (2026-10-09) through Month 60 (2031-10-09) with 45+ initialization and transition steps. However, three components remain underspecified: (1) steward-entity governance and long-term IP stewardship (mentioned as 'designate steward' but no charter, legal structure or funding mechanism defined); (2) post-project governance (no succession plan if funder or host institution withdraws); (3) conflict-of-interest procedures (gate-panel charter specifies no employment ties, but no disclosure process, removal grounds or post-project restrictions documented).
  2. Internal Consistency Check: Logical alignment across governance components is strong. Implementation plan correctly references the decision-escalation matrix (escalations for strain-rights barriers, ATEX noncompliance, productivity shortfalls map to Steering Committee and gate-review panel authority per the matrix). Technical working groups feed evidence to gates on schedule (bench reactors → Phase One gate Month 10 = 2027-08-09; pilot disproof experiments → Phase Two gate Month 30 = 2029-04-09; Phase Three operation → final gate Month 60 = 2031-10-09). Kenyan Replication Coordination reports monthly to Steering Committee and quarterly to gate-review panel, enabling independence assurance at each gate. KPI framework is locked before experiments (Month 1.5 = 2026-11-24) and used consistently for reactor selection and deployment-threshold comparison. However, three alignment gaps are detected: (1) gate-panel charter (Month 0-1 = 2026-10-09 to 2026-11-09) specifies 3-5 members and published-decision authority, but implementation plan assigns panel only a 'recommend' role (Month 10 = 2027-08-09 onwards), creating ambiguity about whether panel decision is binding or advisory (escalation matrix states 'panel has override authority on safety' but does not clarify if panel can block a Continue decision); (2) assistance-log auditor is 'independent' but accountable directly to the Kenyan Replication Coordination body (which reports to Steering Committee), not to the gate-review panel, so audit independence may be compromised if the Steering Committee dislikes audit findings; (3) 'adopt pre-registered disproof thresholds' is specified (Month 1.5 = 2026-11-24) but no procedure is documented for what happens if post-hoc analysis shows that a threshold was unrealistic or that external context has shifted (e.g., a published benchmark becomes outdated).
  3. Potential Gaps and Areas for Enhancement—Adopter Engagement: Scenario locking (Month 9 = 2027-07-09) requires 'named prospective adopters' to be identified and signed by Month 7 (2027-05-09), but the implementation plan does not specify how adopters are pre-qualified or vetted for credibility. 'Prospective adopter' could mean a letter of interest or a formal mandate; the difference is material (a food-security agency's ministerial mandate is credible; a startup's stated interest is not). The signed commitment letters should specify a penalty or cost to the adopter for withdrawal, or alternatively, a process by which withdrawal triggers a re-gate assessment. Currently, the framework states 'adopter withdrawal triggers public disclosure and panel re-advising,' but this is weak governance if an adopter can withdraw cost-free, leading to a scenario-failure-at-gate that was foreseeable in Month 7 (2027-05-09) but not escalated to the Steering Committee. Recommend: (1) define 'named prospective adopter' as a signatory with organizational mandate or budget allocation, not a letter of interest; (2) include in the signed commitment a statement of material consequence (e.g., reputational cost of public withdrawal, or stake in a follow-on commercial opportunity); (3) establish a contingency-adopter recruitment tracker (e.g., three backup adopters pre-identified by Month 6 = 2027-04-09) so that a primary adopter's withdrawal does not require a full new landscape search.
  4. Potential Gaps and Areas for Enhancement—Gate-Panel Independence and Decision Authority: The gate-review panel charter (Month 0.5 = 2026-10-24) is drafted by the Project Lead and approved by the funder but is not yet negotiated with panel members or published. The charter specifies that 'panel's recommendation is binding in the sense that deviation requires published justification,' but this is vague—does 'binding' mean that the funder cannot override without public explanation, or does it mean the funder is legally required to follow the panel's recommendation? The escalation matrix states 'funder holds release authority' and 'any deviation [from panel recommendation] requires public written justification,' implying the funder can override. This is appropriate for a funder role, but the governance framework should explicitly state: (1) what constitutes a sufficient published justification (e.g., 'funder's justification must address each point in the panel's recommendation' vs. 'funder may cite proprietary business reasons'); (2) under what circumstances a funder override is acceptable (e.g., only for non-technical reasons such as funding availability or sponsor mandate change, not for technical judgment); (3) what recourse the panel has if it believes the funder's override is unjustified (does the panel publish a dissent letter? Can it request a second-opinion review?). Additionally, the gate-panel charter specifies that the panel is independent from the host institution and funded by the funder, but no conflict-of-interest disclosure process is documented. Recommend: (1) add a signed conflict-of-interest declaration to the gate-panel charter, covering employment, funding, intellectual property ownership and prior affiliations with project participants; (2) define 'sufficient justification' for a funder override in the gate-panel charter (e.g., justification must be non-technical or must explicitly acknowledge the panel's technical findings and state the reason for divergence); (3) establish a panel-dissent-publication procedure: if the funder overrides the panel, the panel may publish a brief statement explaining its recommendation and the specific grounds on which it disagrees with the funder's override; (4) schedule an annual gate-panel-funder alignment meeting (e.g., Month 6 = 2027-04-09, Month 18 = 2028-04-09, Month 42 = 2030-04-09) to review how well the panel-funder relationship is functioning and address any tensions.
  5. Potential Gaps and Areas for Enhancement—Assistance-Log Audit and Replication Independence Assurance: The framework specifies that an 'independent auditor' reviews the Kenyan assistance log monthly and flags hands-on troubleshooting >4 h/month, and that the auditor reports to the Kenyan Replication Coordination body. However, the auditor's independence is not defined: Can the Kenyan Replication Coordination body direct the auditor's findings or suppress unfavorable reports? Does the auditor have direct reporting access to the gate-review panel or the Steering Committee if the Kenyan team appears to be receiving undisclosed help? The assistance-log framework also does not specify what constitutes 'hands-on troubleshooting' vs. 'acceptable external assistance.' Examples: if a Danish safety specialist conducts a 2-hour remote interlock audit and writes a sign-off report, is that acceptable help (scheduled, safety-critical) or troubleshooting (undocumented design involvement)? If the Kenyan team emails the Danish team with a technical question and receives a 30-minute response with a diagnostic hypothesis, is that 8 instances of 30 minutes = 4 hours/month flagged? The framework should clarify: 'routine operation or design help from developers is not allowed; safe operation always overrides independence' is a principle, but in practice, the boundary is fuzzy. Recommend: (1) add to the auditor's charter a requirement that the auditor is contracted by the funder (not the host or Kenyan partner), operates on a separate budget line, and has a direct-escalation path to the Steering Committee and gate-review panel if it identifies patterns of undisclosed help; (2) define 'acceptable assistance' categories in the assistance-log charter (pre-scheduled safety reviews = yes; routine operation support = red flag; design changes initiated by developers = no; emergency troubleshooting during incident = yes if post-incident training documented); (3) establish a 'log audit readiness' checkpoint at the Phase II gate (Month 30 = 2029-04-09): the auditor produces a summary report assessing whether the Kenyan team's assistance pattern is consistent with 'independence for hypothesis B' or whether it suggests insufficient competence or documentation; the gate-review panel uses the auditor's assessment to advise on Phase III readiness.
  6. Potential Gaps and Areas for Enhancement—Contingency Reserve and Alternative Funding for Deployment Gap: The framework allocates EUR 4.0M programme reserve (EUR 3.5M technical + EUR 0.5M currency), but the deployment-cost model shows a gap of EUR 274,820/yr (or EUR 3.0M equivalent to cover the deployment-scenario cost target). The implementation plan notes 'gap funding route is an open decision' and recommends 'reduced Phase Three if cost chain fails.' However, the governance framework does not specify who makes the decision to reduce Phase Three scope, on what timeline, or how the reduction is authorized. If, for example, the Phase II gate evidence shows that the deployment cost cannot be brought below EUR 15/kg (vs. the EUR 12/kg cap), and the programme's free technical reserve is EUR 3.2M, the Steering Committee would need to decide by Month 30 (2029-04-09) whether to: (1) proceed with Phase III reference unit (consume EUR 4.0M of the EUR 4.0M reserve) and accept that the Kenyan replication is therefore zero-contingency, (2) reduce to Danish unit only (release EUR 1-2M to other work), or (3) escalate to the gate-review panel that the deployment case is not credible and recommend 'Research Only.' This decision should be anticipated and explicit in the governance framework. Recommend: (1) add a decision rule to the Steering Committee charter: 'At the Phase II gate, if the measured cost is >15% above the locked scenario threshold and the programme reserve is insufficient to fund all planned activities and contingencies, the Steering Committee shall escalate to the independent gate-review panel with three options: (a) proceed with full Phase Three and accept zero margin for unbudgeted technical risk, (b) reduce Phase III to Danish unit and documentation-based replication, or (c) recommend Modify or Research Only. The panel shall assess whether the deployment case remains credible under the reduced scenario.' (2) include in the Phase II gate briefing a reserve-burn forecast: 'remaining free technical contingency after Phase II completion: EUR X; forecasted Phase III cost: EUR Y; margin for risk >20% of Phase III cost: required EUR Z; deficit: EUR Y - Z + EUR X'.

Tough Questions

  1. By Month 4 (2027-02-09), will the independent patent-freedom-to-operate review and strain-holder legal confirmations unambiguously document that a primary and backup strain are both lawfully importable into Kenya for commercial production and redistributable to independent implementers, with no third-party IP blocking publication? What specific evidence (signed letters from strain holders, written Kenyan biosafety authority confirmation, patent search results with no blocking claims identified) will constitute 'documented' in the Strain Feasibility Report, and who will sign off that the evidence is sufficient?
  2. The matched bench-scale reactor comparison is pre-registered with a 70% productivity benchmark as a 'fail' threshold. If measured productivity across all three reactor concepts is 65-75% of the published C. necator baseline (within the ±15% analytical uncertainty), how will the gate-review panel distinguish between (1) the project's measurements being genuinely representative and the published benchmark being an outlier, and (2) the project's measurement framework or analytical method being flawed? What independent evidence or external validation will the panel require before judging the gate outcome?
  3. By Month 9 (2027-07-09) Phase One gate, are all three 'named prospective adopters' confirmed to be organizations with explicit decision-making authority and budget allocation for protein procurement (not merely letters of interest or research partnerships)? For each adopter, can you provide the organizational mandate, annual food-security or feed-supply budget, and a signed executive commitment that thresholds will hold through the Phase III gate (Month 60 = 2031-10-09) unless all parties renegotiate in writing?
  4. The Kenyan site baseline (Month 4 = 2027-02-09) is required to show >=4 unplanned grid outages per month with mean duration >=2 h and at least one >8 h per quarter. If the measured baseline shows fewer or shorter outages (e.g., 2-3 outages/month, <1.5 h mean), will the project (a) add controlled outage stressors to maintain the test burden (cost and complexity), (b) document that the actual site envelope does not test hypothesis B as planned and adjust the final conclusion accordingly, or (c) trigger a site replacement (6-12 month delay)? Specify the decision rule and the Steering Committee authority to invoke it.
  5. By Month 10 (2027-08-09) Phase One gate, the independent gate-review panel will receive the bench-scale reactor audited comparison, the HAZOP with safety design basis, and the Strain Feasibility Report. If the HAZOP identifies a safety issue (e.g., a control-system failure mode that cannot be adequately mitigated without reducing productivity by >30%), what is the panel's decision authority? Can the panel recommend that the project redesign the reactor concept and re-gate, even if this adds 8-12 weeks to the schedule and consumes EUR 0.2-0.3M of Phase One contingency? Or does the panel only 'recommend,' leaving the final design decision to the Steering Committee and funder?
  6. The deployment-scenario cost model shows a gap of EUR 7.93/kg (measured cost EUR 19.93/kg vs. locked threshold EUR 12/kg), corresponding to an annual funding need of EUR 274,820. By the Phase II gate (Month 30 = 2029-04-09), will the project have identified a funding route for this gap (subsidy, grant, operating cost reduction, or adopter market acceptance of higher cost), or will the gap remain unresolved? If unresolved and the measured cost trajectory in Phase II does not narrow the gap, what is the cascade of decisions: does the Phase II gate become a 'Modify' recommendation (reduce Phase III scope)? Does the final Phase Three Go decision require that at least one locked scenario is achievable without gap funding, or is gap funding assumed to exist outside the EUR 50M programme budget?

Summary

The Open Protein Module's governance framework combines stage gates with independent review, pre-locked deployment scenarios, measured evidence and kill-gate authority into a high-rigor structure suited to a EUR 50 million, 60-month R&D programme with two hypothesis tests and substantial technical, regulatory and organizational risk. Core strengths are the separation of gate-panel funding and authority from the host institution, early front-loading of strain rights and regulatory engagement (Month 4 = 2027-02-09), pre-registered measurement frameworks and disproof-experiment thresholds, and explicit defect tracking for Kenyan replication independence. The framework's effectiveness depends critically on five unresolved dependencies: (1) signed partnership agreements and host-institution commitment, (2) genuine prospective-adopter engagement with formal threshold lock-in, (3) independent gate-panel recruitment and sustained funding independence, (4) rigorous external auditing of measurement protocols and assistance logs, and (5) funder authority to enforce Modify or Stop decisions against project-team momentum. Governance documentation is detailed but several critical implementation details remain underdeveloped—particularly gate-panel charter enforcement mechanisms, assistance-log auditor independence standards, and contingency-activation decision rights under EUR 3.5M technical reserve conditions. The framework's credibility rests on transparent publication of all gate recommendations and any funder deviations, which is specified but not yet operationalized.

Suggestion 1 - Solar Foods – Solein (Factory 01 and Pilot 'Factory 01' in Vantaa, Finland)

Finnish company producing Solein, a protein from hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria grown on hydrogen, CO2 and minerals using electricity. Pilot operation since about 2019-2020; a larger Factory 01 in Vantaa was built to demonstrate commercial scale. Strain and process are proprietary. Scale and timelines are approximate and should be confirmed from company publications.

Success Metrics

Operating pilot and factory facilities (confirm current status from company reports). Regulatory approvals obtained in some jurisdictions (e.g. Singapore; EU status not verified). Published energy and productivity claims (approximate, not independently verified).

Risks and Challenges Faced

Novel-food authorization is slow; the company pursued EU and other national routes stepwise and used early regulator dialogue. Hydrogen-oxygen safety at scale; handled by industrial gas-safety practice and staged pilot-to-factory scaling. Electricity cost drives economics; addressed by siting and renewable power sourcing.

Where to Find More Information

https://solarfoods.com Company investor and annual reports (Nasdaq First North Helsinki) EFSA novel food register and opinions on Solein (search EFSA OpenEFSA)

Actionable Steps

Contact Solar Foods' regulatory affairs or science team via the contact form on their website to ask about publicly shareable benchmark definitions. Search LinkedIn for their process engineering and regulatory leads and send a brief public-good project inquiry. Review published scientific papers by company-affiliated authors (e.g. with LUT University) and contact corresponding authors.

Rationale for Suggestion

Same biological route and a Nordic regulatory and safety context close to Denmark. It is the main proprietary benchmark for productivity, energy per kg, nucleic acid handling and novel-food authorization. It also defines what the open design must differ from: vendor independence, repairability and openly published process data.
