This clarity enables Hypothesis A (local technician operation) and Hypothesis B (decentralized modules) to proceed with credible evidence of safety-aware design, reduces gate-review scrutiny on safety (freeing time for technical and regulatory assessment), and allows Phase Three to commission the reference unit without major safety re-work or regulatory delays.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Engage a qualified ATEX consultant immediately (by Month 0 = 2026-10-09 project start) via a simplified Request for Proposal (RFP) with fixed scope and deliverable date; if the primary consultant cannot commit by Month 1 (2026-11-09), have a second-choice consultant on standby to begin HAZOP by Month 1.5 (2026-11-24) rather than waiting for the preferred expert
  • If a full IEC 61882 HAZOP is deemed too time-consuming or costly, conduct an accelerated HAZOP focusing on the highest-risk subsystems (electrolyzer, gas-handling during power loss, ignition sources and interlocks) in Weeks 1–4 (by Month 1.5 = 2026-11-24), followed by a secondary HAZOP on lower-risk elements by Month 2.5 (2026-12-24); use pre-filled HAZOP templates for standard equipment (e.g., commercial electrolyzer specifications) to reduce analysis time
  • Commission a parallel LOPA (Layers of Protection Analysis, simpler and quicker than full HAZOP) as a check on HAZOP results; LOPA quantifies the number of independent protection layers needed to meet the residual-risk target, providing a complementary view of whether the Design Basis adequately controls risk
  • If the Design Basis for Safety cannot be locked by Month 2.5 (2026-12-24), deliver a 'Preliminary Design Basis' by that date with a 2–4 week window to finalize before the Month 3 (2027-01-09) Adopter Change Boundary publication; the preliminary version should identify the principal design limits and residual uncertainties, and commit to re-assessment if uncertainties are resolved
  • If Adopter Change Boundary definition is delayed beyond Month 3 (2027-01-09), publish a draft version (e.g., 'pre-assessed substitutes for pump type, tubing material; all pressure, composition and electrode changes require re-assessment') by that date with an explicit 2-month window for stakeholder feedback and finalization by Month 5 (2027-03-09); do not proceed to the Phase One gate without a completed Adopter Change Boundary
  • If ATEX sign-off cannot be secured from an internal or immediately available consultant, commission a second independent ATEX review from a regulatory consultant (e.g., a consultant with approval-process experience) by Month 3 (2027-01-09) to provide regulatory feasibility assessment even if full certification-readiness review is deferred to Phase Three
  • If the Design Basis cannot be applied uniformly to all three reactor concepts (e.g., pneumatic reactors cannot operate above a certain pressure, so pressurized concepts have different limits), document the concept-specific limits explicitly and publish justification for non-uniformity (e.g., 'pneumatic reactors operate at <0.5 bar and therefore ignition risk from overpressure rupture is eliminated; pressurized stirred reactors require independent relief at 2 bar to control equivalent risk'); use the documented justification to weight the reactor selection rule in favor of the simpler concept if safety differences are real but immaterial (e.g., <1% difference in residual ignition risk)

Create Document 4: Deployment Scenario Specification

ID: 90bac15f-8f87-4c5d-9a08-b631774b8fbf

Description: Time-stamped, signed document naming 2–3 prospective adopters and their locked deployment thresholds (maximum cost per kg usable protein, minimum capacity, required uptime, operating-envelope constraints). Each scenario includes: adopter name and mandate, cost basis (current supply chain cost, cost benchmark used to derive the threshold), capacity need and uptime requirement, any co-funding or subsidy commitment, and a withdrawal clause. Locked by Month 9 (2027-07-09). Intended audience: gate-review panel, funder, adopter organizations, project team. Provides the binding reference for the Phase Three Go decision: at least one scenario must be met for Go to be justified.

Responsible Role Type: Adoption Economist and Kenyan Co-Development Partner Lead

Primary Template: Stakeholder Engagement and Commitment Letter Template

Secondary Template: Scenario Development and Threshold-Locking Template

Steps to Create:

  • By Month 2 (2026-12-09), identify 2–3 named candidate adopters with published mandates in food security, emergency nutrition, or regional livestock feed (examples: national grain-reserve authority, humanitarian logistics organization, East African feed producer)
  • By Month 4 (2027-02-09), conduct structured in-person or virtual interviews with each adopter: current protein supply source and cost (with audited documentation if possible), required production capacity (kg/day), required uptime (%), power and water constraints, willingness to adopt an open design, cost premium for vendor independence, and any subsidy or co-funding availability
  • By Month 6 (2027-04-09), consolidate adopter input into 2–3 scenario profiles; for each scenario, present: (1) adopter name; (2) current supply chain baseline (cost EUR X/kg, source, capacity Y, uptime Z%); (3) proposed threshold (cost EUR A/kg, capacity B, uptime C%, operating envelope); (4) cost sensitivity ('would you adopt at EUR 12/kg? EUR 15/kg? What is your threshold?'); (5) co-funding availability or subsidy commitment
  • By Month 7 (2027-05-09), obtain signed written commitment from each adopter stating: 'We commit to these thresholds for Scenario [name]: cost ≤EUR X/kg, capacity ≥Y kg/day, uptime ≥Z%, provided that [any condition, e.g., government subsidy is available]. These thresholds are immutable unless [named parties] formally agree in writing to change them. We acknowledge that failure to meet these thresholds may result in a Modify or Research Only gate decision.'
  • Include a withdrawal clause: 'If circumstances change and this scenario is no longer feasible, we will provide 30 days' written notice to the project. The project will publish our withdrawal and request the independent gate-review panel to re-assess whether remaining scenarios remain viable for a credible Go decision.'
  • By Month 9 (2027-07-09), finalize the 'Deployment Scenario Specification' document consolidating all three scenarios with adopter signatures, locked thresholds, cost basis, and withdrawal clauses. Time-stamp and publish to all stakeholders.
  • Present to the independent gate-review panel by Month 9 (2027-07-09) for assessment: 'Are these scenarios credible? Do the adopters' thresholds align with their stated mandates and financial constraints? Are the scenarios realistic given the modeled costs?'

Approval Authorities: Named adopter organizations (signatures required); funder (acknowledgment); independent gate-review panel (credibility assessment)

Essential Information:

  • Identify the deployment-financing gap and funding sources: current model shows EUR 274,820/yr shortfall (full cost EUR 19.93/kg vs EUR 12 cap); specify whether gap will be closed by adopter grant, operating subsidy, cost reduction target, or left open for post-Phase-Three negotiation.
  • Define the steward entity structure and sustainable funding: specify the legal form (non-profit foundation, cooperative, or trust), governance (board composition, decision-making authority), IP management (licence enforcement, dispute resolution), and annual operating budget (estimate EUR 0.1–0.2M/yr); confirm funding source for Year 1–5 steward operations.
  • Document the open-licence stack and freedom-to-operate clearance: specify licences for hardware (CERN, Solderpad or equivalent), software (GPL, Apache or equivalent), data (CC-BY or equivalent), and documentation; confirm that all identified third-party patents and strain restrictions are either licensed, designed around, or subject to patent pledges; publish a one-page jurisdiction-specific legal summary (Denmark/EU, Kenya, Bangladesh) detailing what adopters can and cannot do commercially without additional licensing.
  • Establish the knowledge-steward and long-term maintenance protocol: specify who maintains the source repository, documentation versioning, and how defects and improvements are logged post-release; confirm funding and staffing for at least Year 5–10 post-Phase-Three stewardship (estimate EUR 0.05–0.10M/yr).
  • Specify the adopter support and certification pathway: define what post-release support (training, troubleshooting, design review) the steward provides vs. what adopters do independently; specify any certification mark or conformity claim process (e.g., 'Built to Open Protein Module Reference Design v1.0'); confirm cost and resource allocation for support.
  • Confirm the financial sustainability model for the Kenyan replication team: specify whether the Kenyan partner receives programme funding (if so, when and how much), or operates independently; if independently, confirm funding source for the two-year replication (Months 30–54 = 2029-04-09 to 2031-04-09) and post-replication team continuity; estimate cost of retaining Kenyan team as long-term steward partners (EUR 0.1–0.3M/yr estimate).
  • Define the deployment transition plan if Go is achieved: specify which organization(s) (steward, adopters, host institutions, or a new deployment entity) will lead deployment scaling; confirm funding route for first 1–3 deployer sites (estimated EUR 3–10M for three deployment-scale units and local training); clarify whether programme funding extends to deployment or transitions to adopter/government funding.
  • Lock the public-release package scope: specify what is published (hardware schematics, software code, data, standard operating procedures, safety case, troubleshooting guides, training materials, bill of materials); confirm that all releasing is conditional on independent safety and legal review; specify release timing (immediate upon Phase Three gate decision if Go, or staged if Modify).
  • Establish post-release governance and fork-protection strategy: specify how the steward monitors for closed forks or proprietary modifications; clarify enforcement mechanisms (licence-enforcement demand letters, reputational mechanisms, or community governance); confirm budget and authority for enforcement (estimate EUR 0.05–0.10M/yr).
  • Define the long-term research pathway for post-release improvements: specify whether the steward accepts and coordinates improvements from third parties; confirm process for validating improvements and updating reference designs; estimate cost of coordinating third-party research contributions (EUR 0.05–0.15M/yr estimate).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Deployment-financing gap remains undefined after Phase Three: adopters cannot finance replication without clarity on the EUR 274,820/yr subsidy or cost-reduction target; deployment stalls at 0–2 sites and public-value impact falls to <10% of potential.
  • Steward entity lacks sustainable funding or governance: if steward is poorly structured or underfunded, the open package decays post-release (documentation outdated, security vulnerabilities unfixed, licence enforcement abandoned); forks proliferate unchecked and the core becomes closed or abandoned within 5–10 years.
  • Freedom-to-operate not fully cleared: undisclosed third-party patents or strain restrictions emerge after release, forcing adopters to cease operation or infringe; reputational damage to the programme and potential litigation cost (estimate EUR 0.5–2.0M).
  • Open-licence stack incompatible with adopter commercial models: if licences are too restrictive (e.g., all-reciprocal terms), industrial deployers avoid replication and seek proprietary alternatives; if too permissive, closed forks proliferate and the open core is diluted by incompatible variants.
  • Adopter support undefined: post-release adopters encounter ambiguities or safety questions without a clear support pathway; unsafe modifications or incorrect operation cause failures, injuries, or regulatory violations; liability exposure for the programme and steward.
  • Kenyan team dissolved after Phase Three: if the Kenyan partner transitions off after the replication gate and no continuity entity is funded, Kenyan adopters lack a local knowledge source and the replication evidence cannot be maintained or transferred; hypothesis B (decentralized modules under difficult infrastructure) becomes a one-time demonstration, not a replicable model.
  • Deployment transition unfunded or unclear: if no organization is designated or funded to lead deployer-site scaling, deployment momentum is lost; adopters lack financial or technical access and the technology remains academic.
  • Public-release package incomplete or unsafe: if release is rushed without rigorous safety and legal review, the package may contain safety gaps or IP violations; adopters build unsafe systems or infringe patents, causing harm and forcing legal action.
  • Fork governance absent: without steward monitoring and enforcement, commercial and open-source forks diverge; incompatible variants cause confusion, regulatory issues and loss of coherence in the open ecosystem.
  • Post-release research pathway not established: improvements and adaptations proposed by adopters or researchers are not coordinated; parallel research efforts duplicate work or create incompatible modifications; the reference design is not improved and adopter-generated knowledge is not shared back.

Worst Case Scenario: The programme reaches the Phase Three gate with Go decision achieved (technology works, safety validated, hypotheses A and B proven, at least one deployment scenario met). However, the steward entity is established with insufficient funding (EUR 0.05M/yr instead of EUR 0.15–0.20M/yr estimate), and no post-release support structure, deployment-transition pathway or long-term financing model is specified. Adopters attempt replication but encounter ambiguous documentation, safety questions and licensing uncertainties without clear remedies. Within 12–24 months, adopter sites experience equipment failures and operator confusion; regulatory authorities in Kenya or Bangladesh become skeptical and impose additional approval hurdles. Commercial entities publish closed-source forks claiming compatibility with the open reference; the open ecosystem fragments. The steward lacks funds to maintain documentation, enforce licences or coordinate research improvements. By Year 5 post-release, the open core is outdated and abandoned; deployment sites have reverted to proprietary or non-functional systems. The programme's public-value impact is <5% of technical potential and the open design becomes a cautionary tale of failed technology transfer rather than a sustainable resource.

Best Case Scenario: The programme reaches Phase Three gate with Go decision, and a well-funded, independently governed steward entity (established by Month 50 = 2030-12-09 estimate) is operating with EUR 0.15–0.20M/yr core funding and a board of domain experts. A comprehensive, legally cleared open-licence package (hardware, software, data, documentation) is published with jurisdiction-specific legal summaries and a certification-mark pathway. Within 12 months post-release, five independent deployer sites are commissioned in Kenya, Ethiopia and Bangladesh, supported by the Kenyan team (retained and funded as steward partners) and a distributed training network. Adopters generate improvements (hardware variants, operational optimizations, downstream innovations) which flow back to the steward via a structured coordination process; the reference design is updated twice per year with cumulative improvements. By Year 5 post-release, 50+ deployer sites operate globally, with 200+ kg usable protein/day in aggregate, supporting local food security during climate and supply-chain stress. The steward enforces open-licence terms without litigation, preventing closed forks while enabling beneficial variations. Commercial entities contribute to the open core or license improved variants with royalties supporting the steward. Deployment financing is a mix of government food-security budgets, green development finance and adopter co-investment; the EUR 274,820/yr gap is closed by a combination of cost reduction (EUR 3–5/kg via scale and local sourcing) and subsidy (EUR 2–4/kg from food-security and development budgets estimate). The Open Protein Module becomes a credible, self-sustaining infrastructure for resilient local protein supply, with measurable impact on food security during crises.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If steward-entity governance cannot be finalized by Month 40 (2030-02-09), place the open package in temporary trusteeship with a neutral foundation (e.g., GOSH, Wikimedia, or academic consortium) with a mandate to hold and steward until a permanent steward is established; ensure trusteeship agreement specifies licence enforcement, documentation maintenance and transition procedures; allocate EUR 0.10–0.15M to the trustee for interim operations.
  • If deployment-financing gap cannot be closed through adopter or government budgets, explore performance-based (outcome) financing: structure an agreement with impact investors or development banks where the steward receives funding for each deployer site commissioned and operated for ≥12 months, meeting technical and social-impact criteria; negotiate a per-site fee (EUR 100,000–300,000 estimate) paid from impact-investment returns or blended finance pools.
  • If the Kenyan partner cannot transition to a long-term steward role, contract with a local NGO or social enterprise in Kenya and partner countries to serve as regional stewards; provide training, documentation and technical support (funded at EUR 0.05–0.10M/yr per region estimate) to enable regional entities to support local deployers and coordinate improvements.
  • If open-licence enforcement proves too resource-intensive (estimated >EUR 0.10M/yr in legal costs), adopt a defensive-publication and patent-pledge strategy instead: publish the design under a defensive-publication framework (which prevents others from patenting it) and add a patent-pledge statement ('We commit never to sue for infringement of our patents on this design'); rely on steward reputation and community norms rather than legal enforcement to prevent commercial closure.
  • If post-release technical support cannot be funded at programme cost, establish a community-support forum (GitHub Discussions, Discourse, or equivalent) where adopters and researchers answer questions; provide steward moderation and occasional paid support (EUR 0.02–0.05M/yr estimate) for safety-critical questions; supplement with pro-bono support from programme alumni and research collaborators.
  • If deployment transition remains unfunded after Phase Three, propose a Phase Four (Months 60–84 = 2031-10-09 to 2033-10-09 estimate) focused on deployer-site scaling, enabled by a separate funding stream (government food-security budgets, development finance, or climate-adaptation funding) rather than the initial programme; document the deployment model and cost structure (bill of materials, labour, supply-chain map) as a 'deployment kit' so that adopters or governments can fund scaling independently.
  • If Kenyan team expertise is at risk of loss, document all operational knowledge (standard operating procedures, troubleshooting guides, training videos, design rationale) by Month 48 (2030-10-09) so that knowledge transfer does not depend on key individuals; train a second cohort of Kenyan technicians by Month 54 (2031-04-09) to enable continuity even if primary team members depart.
  • If public-release package scope proves too large to validate (>1 year for safety and legal review), stage the release: publish documentation and Bill of Materials (low-risk) by Month 39 (2030-01-09), then hardware CAD files and software by Month 42 (2030-04-09) after independent safety review, then operating procedures and safety case by Month 45 (2030-07-09) after legal clearance; stagger publishing to reduce single-gate bottleneck risk.
  • If fork governance cannot be enforced due to resource or jurisdiction limits, establish an open-governance model in which the community (deployers, researchers, steward) collectively define and vote on design standards; forks that violate safety standards or claim false compatibility can be rejected by community consensus; use reputation (crowdsourced reviews, certification marks) rather than legal action to guide adopter choice.
  • If long-term research coordination is not resourced at the steward, establish a research consortium (multi-institutional partnership) that provides pro-bono coordination of improvements; members contribute staff time and the steward provides lightweight facilitation (EUR 0.02–0.05M/yr estimate); consortium meets semi-annually to review proposed improvements and recommend reference-design updates.

Create Document 5: Gate-Review Panel Charter and Authority Delegation

ID: b5c9a321-fd14-4c09-ad1f-82471d1f9b43

Description: Formal written charter establishing the independent gate-review panel's composition, recruitment, conflict-of-interest protocols, funding source and separation, decision authority, publication and override procedures, and escalation rules. Signed by the funder by Month 1.5 (2026-11-24) before any panel members are named. Intended audience: funder, host institution, panel members, stakeholders. Ensures panel independence, binding authority and transparency of gate decisions.

Responsible Role Type: Funder (with project director and legal counsel)

Primary Template: Independent Review Panel Charter and Authority Delegation Template

Secondary Template: Research Programme Governance and Conflict-of-Interest Protocol

Steps to Create:

  • Specify panel composition: 3–5 members with diverse expertise (process engineer, ATEX safety specialist, biotech regulatory consultant, adoption economist, optionally product expert). Each member must have: (a) no employment or funding ties to the host institution; (b) no prior involvement in the project design; (c) published expertise or track record in the relevant domain; (d) no financial stake in the project's outcome (honoraria only, capped)
  • Specify recruitment process: open call via established scientific networks, competitive selection, conflict-of-interest screening, and written vetting by the funder (not the host)
  • Define funding source and separation: EUR 0.30M total over 5 years (Phase One share EUR 0.06M) held in a separate funder-managed account, not flowing through the host institution or project budget; prevents implicit pressure on panel members to recommend continuation to protect their own employment
  • Define each panel member's term: fixed 5-year term (all phases), no renewal, no ongoing relationship after project end; provides independence and prevents 'renewal bias' toward continuation
  • Specify decision authority: 'The panel produces a joint written recommendation (continue, modify, research-only, or stop) at each gate [Phase One Month 10 = 2027-08-09, Phase Two Month 30 = 2029-04-09, Phase Three Month 60 = 2031-10-09]. The recommendation is based on evidence against pre-defined gate-pass criteria locked by Month 2 (2026-12-09) and not changeable retroactively. All panel members sign the recommendation.'
  • Specify funder's obligation: 'The funder's default action is to release funds if the panel recommends 'continue' and to withhold funds if the panel recommends 'stop' or 'modify.' Any deviation requires funder board decision and public written justification within 5 working days, published alongside the panel's recommendation.'
  • Specify panel's rebuttal right: 'The panel may issue a joint rebuttal to the funder's justification within 10 working days, also published, if the panel judges the funder's reasoning to be unsupported by evidence.'
  • Specify escalation for repeated overrides: 'If the funder overrides a 'stop' or 'modify' recommendation at any gate, a second independent panel review (separate panel, same charter) is required before funds are released at the next gate. This prevents systematic momentum-driven continuation.'
  • Specify publication requirements: 'All gate recommendations, funder decisions, and any deviations or rebuttals are published on the project website and in annual reports to all stakeholders within 10 working days of the decision.'
  • Include conflict-of-interest clause: 'Each panel member signs a written declaration stating: (a) no employment or ongoing funding dependence on the host, funder or project; (b) no financial interest in the project's outcome; (c) no prior involvement in design decisions. Panel members are required to recuse themselves from votes on any matter where a conflict exists and to notify the panel chair immediately if a conflict arises mid-project.'
  • Obtain funder's signature and board approval by Month 1.5 (2026-11-24) before any gate-panel recruitment begins

Approval Authorities: Funder (board or executive decision authority); host institution (acknowledgment of the funder's independent authority); panel members (signature on charter and conflict-of-interest declaration)

Essential Information:

  • Establish panel composition and expertise requirements: 3–5 members with no employment or funding ties to the host institution, no prior project involvement, and published expertise in process engineering, ATEX safety, biotech regulation, adoption economics, and/or food-safety product development.
  • Define recruitment process: open competitive call via established scientific networks, conflict-of-interest screening, and written vetting by the funder (not the host institution); recruitment to be completed by Month 1.5 (2026-11-24).
  • Specify funding source and separation mechanism: EUR 0.30M total programme funding (EUR 0.06M Phase One share) held in a separate funder-managed account, not flowing through host institution or project budget; prevents implicit pressure on panel members to approve continuation to protect their employment.
  • Document each panel member's term and independence: fixed 5-year term across all three phases with no renewal and no ongoing relationship after project completion; no financial stake in project outcome beyond capped honoraria; written conflict-of-interest declaration signed by each member.
  • Define decision authority and process: panel produces joint written recommendation (continue, modify, research-only, or stop) at three scheduled gates (Phase One Month 10 = 2027-08-09; Phase Two Month 30 = 2029-04-09; Phase Three Month 60 = 2031-10-09); recommendation is binding on the funder's default action (release funds if continue; withhold if stop/modify).
  • Specify gate-pass criteria and pre-registration requirement: gate-pass criteria are locked by Month 2 (2026-12-09) before any gate assessment work begins; criteria are not subject to retroactive change; panel assesses evidence against these pre-defined, immutable thresholds.
  • Establish funder's override procedure and transparency: funder may deviate from panel recommendation only via published written justification (within 5 working days); panel retains right to issue joint rebuttal within 10 working days if funder's reasoning is judged unsupported by evidence; all recommendations, decisions and deviations published on project website within 10 working days.
  • Define escalation rule for repeated overrides: if funder overrides a 'stop' or 'modify' recommendation at any gate, a second independent panel review (separate panel, same charter) is required before funds are released at the next gate; this prevents systematic momentum-driven continuation.
  • Establish recusal and conflict-of-interest governance: each panel member signs written declaration of no employment, funding dependence or financial interest in outcome; members recuse themselves from votes on matters with conflicts and notify panel chair immediately if conflicts arise mid-project.
  • Specify publication and stakeholder accountability: all gate recommendations, funder decisions, deviations, and rebuttals are published to all stakeholders (project website, annual reports) within 10 working days; creates public record and enables stakeholders to monitor independence.
  • Document charter approval pathway: charter requires funder board or executive signature by Month 1.5 (2026-11-24), before any panel recruitment begins; host institution acknowledgment of funder's independent authority; all panel members sign charter and conflict-of-interest declaration as condition of appointment.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Panel members remain financially dependent on host institution or project continuation, creating implicit pressure to recommend 'continue' even if evidence is weak; gate reviews become rubber-stamping mechanism rather than independent scrutiny.
  • Funder's override authority is unconstrained and not subject to transparency, allowing continuation by momentum despite panel's 'stop' recommendation; final Go/Modify/Research Only decision loses credibility with external stakeholders and adopters.
  • Gate-pass criteria are vague, subjective or not pre-registered, enabling post-hoc rationalization: panel members interpret criteria differently, or criteria are adjusted after data arrive to fit achieved performance; evidence-driven decision-making is compromised.
  • Conflict-of-interest protocols are weak or not enforced, allowing panel members with prior project involvement or financial stakes to vote on gate decisions; panel independence is illusory and judgments are biased.
  • Panel recommendations are not published or are published with long delays, reducing stakeholder transparency and accountability; adopters and regulators cannot verify whether gate decisions were evidence-based or momentum-driven.
  • Panel members lack sufficient technical depth in hydrogen fermentation, ATEX design, single-cell protein regulation, or scale-up uncertainty; technical gaps in design or safety are missed, allowing unsafe or unviable technology to advance through gates.
  • Panel recruitment and charter are controlled by the host institution rather than the funder, creating apparent or actual conflict of interest; host institution can influence panel selection to favor continuation.
  • Charter does not specify escalation procedures if funder systematically overrides panel recommendations; repeated overrides are normalized rather than flagged as a governance failure requiring intervention.
  • The EUR 0.30M panel budget is insufficient to recruit and retain qualified experts, or honoria structure creates pressure to complete reviews quickly without adequate technical scrutiny.

Worst Case Scenario: If the charter is weak or absent, the independent gate-review panel becomes a governance fiction. The funder or host institution controls the panel's composition and recommendations in practice; 'stop' or 'modify' recommendations are overridden without published justification; and momentum-driven continuation dominates despite weak evidence. By Phase Three, EUR 20–30M has been committed (construction, Kenyan replication) without credible evidence that hypotheses A or B are viable or that deployment scenarios are achievable. The final Gate decision is perceived as predetermined rationalization rather than evidence-based Go/Modify/Stop. Adopters, regulators and external researchers lose confidence in the programme's credibility, reducing adoption rates by 40–60% and project impact by similar magnitude. If a safety incident occurs during Phase III and investigation reveals that the independent panel flagged the hazard at Phase One or Two but the funder overrode the recommendation without published justification, reputational damage to the funder and host institution is severe, and regulatory bodies may restrict future hydrogen-fermentation research.

Best Case Scenario: A strong, transparent charter establishes a truly independent panel with recruited expertise in process engineering, ATEX safety, biotech regulation, and scale-up economics. Panel members are funded separately, free of employment dependence on the host, and bound by written conflict-of-interest protocols. Gate-pass criteria are pre-registered and published by Month 2 (2026-12-09); panel assesses evidence rigorously against these criteria at each gate (Phase One Month 10 = 2027-08-09, Phase Two Month 30 = 2029-04-09, Phase Three Month 60 = 2031-10-09). Panel recommendations are published transparently; any funder override is justified in writing and published alongside the panel's recommendation within 5 working days. If overrides are repeated, a second independent panel review is required before next-gate funding is released. This governance structure ensures the final Go/Modify/Research-Only decision reflects genuine evidence credibility rather than momentum. Adopters, regulators and external researchers trust the gate framework and adopt the technology based on demonstrated performance. If the technology proves viable (hypothesis A and B supported, cost thresholds met), the independent gate process strengthens adoption rates by 30–50% by providing external validation. If the technology proves non-viable (gates stop it at Phase Two), the transparent process protects stakeholder trust and prevents wasted Phase III spending of EUR 20–30M.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If independent recruitment and management are not feasible before Month 1.5 (2026-11-24), establish a 'minimum viable charter' with reduced scope: specify 3 core panel members (rather than 3–5) with clear expertise in one critical domain each (ATEX safety, biotech regulation, process scale-up); fund them via a funder-managed account separate from project and host institution; specify only the Phase One gate criteria (strain rights, productivity, Kenyan biosafety, reference architecture) with external audit, and defer full charter details to Month 2 (2026-12-09) for Phase Two refinement. This preserves independence for the most critical gate (Phase One) while allowing governance to mature.
  • If the funder lacks board-level authority to sign the charter by Month 1.5 (2026-11-24), establish a 'provisional charter' signed by the funder's executive director (or delegated authority) with explicit commitment to obtain full board ratification by Month 2 (2026-12-09); include a 30-day veto clause allowing board reversal only if it disputes the charter's governance structures (not individual composition or criteria).
  • If recruiting 3–5 independent experts with deep expertise in hydrogen fermentation, ATEX and single-cell protein proves difficult, expand the panel to include: 1 process engineer with fermentation/scale-up experience (primary domain), 1 ATEX/process-safety engineer, 1 regulatory/IP specialist, and 1 'generalist engineer' (with broader bioprocess or pharmaceutical expertise). Require the primary-domain expert to mentor the generalist during gate reviews; require all panel members to review written technical summaries 4–6 weeks before each gate meeting to equip generalists with domain context.
  • If the funder's governance structure does not allow separation of panel funding from project budget (because programme funds flow through a single institutional account), establish a 'ring-fenced sub-account' within the project budget marked 'independent panel—do not encumber or redirect.' Appoint an independent auditor (external to host and funder) to verify monthly that panel funds are not redirected to project expenses. Require the auditor to report quarterly to the funder and panel, and flag any encroachment as a governance breach requiring immediate correction.
  • If the funder prefers to retain override authority without publishing justification, offer a compromise: the funder may override a 'stop' recommendation only once per project (one override allowed across all three gates) without published justification; any subsequent override (second or later) requires published justification and automatic second-panel review. This preserves funder authority while preventing systemic momentum-driven continuation.
  • If scheduling gate meetings and producing recommendations within 30 days of the evidence freeze proves impractical, extend the gate decision window: evidence freeze at Month 9, 30, and 57 (2027-07-09, 2029-04-09, 2031-07-09); panel meets in Month 10, 31, and 58 (2027-08-09, 2029-05-09, 2031-08-09) (one-month delay); decision released by Month 11, 32, and 59 (2027-09-09, 2029-06-09, 2031-09-09) (another month); total decision window is 2 months. Communicate to stakeholders that gate decisions will be published by these dates, and use the two-month window to allow panel rebuttal if funder deviates.

Create Document 6: Techno-Economic Cost Model and Sensitivity Analysis Report

ID: 14bd70e5-98d3-4346-8463-fd5f9228e74c

Description: Comprehensive cost model connecting bench-scale productivity to deployment-scenario feasibility at 100 kg/day usable protein capacity (or alternative deployment units). Quantifies system-level cost per kg (electrolyzer + fermenter + downstream + capex + overhead + financing) under base-case assumptions and sensitivity scenarios (electricity price EUR 0.05–0.15/kWh, downstream energy reduction, module scaling). Identifies the EUR 7.93/kg cost gap versus EUR 12 scenario cap and assesses whether credible reduction paths exist. Deliverable by Month 9 (2027-07-09) with interim findings Month 6 (2027-04-09). Intended audience: funder, adopters, gate-review panel, project leadership.

Responsible Role Type: Techno-Economic Modeler and Cost Analyst

Primary Template: Techno-Economic Analysis and Sensitivity Model Template (NREL, IEA biotech cost-analysis frameworks)

Secondary Template: Monte Carlo Cost Uncertainty and Probability Distribution Template

Steps to Create:

  • By Month 3 (2027-01-09), consolidate baseline cost assumptions from bench productivity data, equipment specifications and published benchmarks: electrolyzer capex and efficiency, fermenter capex and operating cost, downstream processing (harvest, nucleic acid reduction, drying) capex and energy, staff cost, nitrogen source, minerals, water treatment, membrane replacement cycles, waste handling. Specify the system boundary (which components included: fermenter only, fermenter+downstream, full electrolyzer+fermenter+downstream?)
  • Model the base-case deployment unit: 100 kg usable protein/day (200 kg dry biomass/day nameplate), ~50% utilization = 34,675 kg usable protein/year. Calculate: annual electricity consumption (dry biomass 34,675 × 2 kg dry per kg usable × 40 kWh/kg dry = 2,774,000 kWh/year), annual electricity cost (2,774,000 kWh × EUR 0.08/kWh = EUR 221,920), non-electric opex (staff EUR 100k, inputs EUR 50k, maintenance EUR 30k), capex installed cost (EUR 3.0M estimated), debt service at 5% / 15 years (EUR 289k/year), total annual cost = EUR 601,920, unit cost = EUR 12.27/kg usable protein
  • Note: base-case model shows full cost EUR 19.93/kg per the canonical facts; reconcile difference (if any) by identifying which cost driver is underestimated (downstream energy, capex, or other). If reconciliation is impossible, flag the discrepancy and revise the model
  • Conduct sensitivity analysis on key cost drivers: (a) electricity price: from EUR 0.05/kWh (solar, best-case) to EUR 0.15/kWh (grid, worst-case); note the impact on total cost per kg (estimated sensitivity ~EUR 3–4/kg per EUR 0.01/kWh change); (b) downstream energy: from 40 kWh/kg current assumption to 20 kWh/kg (thermal nucleic acid reduction) or 60 kWh/kg (enzymatic); (c) scaling: model 50 kg/day and 200 kg/day units and assess how fixed capex leverage affects total cost; (d) capacity utilization: model 70%, 85%, and 95% annual utilization and assess impact on unit cost
  • Present interim sensitivity findings at Month 6 (2027-04-09): 'Under best-case assumptions (EUR 0.05/kWh electricity, downstream energy 20 kWh/kg, 95% utilization, scaled learning on capex), estimated cost is EUR 11–12/kg, meeting Scenario A threshold. Under conservative assumptions (EUR 0.12/kWh, downstream energy 60 kWh/kg, 70% utilization, no learning), estimated cost is EUR 18–24/kg, exceeding all scenario thresholds.' Identify which assumptions are controllable (solar coupling, downstream design) vs. uncontrollable (grid electricity price)
  • By Month 9 (2027-07-09), produce final report with: (a) base-case cost model and sensitivity matrix; (b) credible cost-reduction pathways: identify which levers (electricity price, downstream energy, scale) can close the EUR 7.93/kg gap and at what confidence; (c) residual gap after all identified reductions; (d) funding-route recommendation: if gap cannot be closed to EUR 12/kg, recommend either (i) a named adopter or government subsidy to cover the EUR 274,820/yr operational gap, (ii) redesign to a smaller-capacity unit (50 kg/day) that might fit the cap, or (iii) a reduced Phase Three (Danish unit only, Research Only outcome) if no funding route is credible
  • Document all assumptions, cost drivers and uncertainty ranges; specify which are from published sources vs. project estimates vs. contractor quotes. Include a scenario where the deployment cost remains EUR 19.93/kg (worst-case), showing the implications (no adopter without subsidy)

Approval Authorities: Funder (decision on gap-funding strategy); independent gate-review panel (assessment of cost-reduction credibility and deployment-scenario viability)

Essential Information:

  • Reconcile the canonical full-system deployment cost of EUR 19.93/kg against the EUR 12/kg scenario cap; identify which cost driver(s) explain the EUR 7.93/kg gap (electrolyzer, fermenter, downstream processing, capex amortization, or overhead).
  • Calculate base-case annual cost model for a 100 kg/day usable protein deployment unit (200 kg dry biomass/day nameplate at 95% utilization = 34,675 kg usable protein/year): itemize electricity cost (kWh × EUR/kWh), staff, nitrogen source, minerals, water treatment, membrane replacement, downstream energy (per kg dry biomass), capex amortization (installed cost, financing terms, debt service over 15 years).
  • Conduct sensitivity analysis on principal cost drivers with stated uncertainty ranges and measured impact: (a) electricity price (EUR 0.05–0.15/kWh, solar best-case to grid worst-case); (b) downstream energy (20–60 kWh/kg depending on nucleic acid reduction method); (c) installed capex (EUR 2.0–8.0M range); (d) capacity utilization (70%, 85%, 95% annual operation); (e) scale effects (50 kg/day, 100 kg/day, 200 kg/day units).
  • Identify credible cost-reduction levers with quantified impact: which changes (e.g., solar-coupled operation, passive nucleic acid reduction, modular scaling, shared overhead) close the gap to EUR 12/kg and at what confidence level (high, medium, low); distinguish controllable (design choices) from uncontrolled (market price) variables.
  • Report residual cost gap after all identified reductions; assess whether the gap can realistically be closed to EUR 12/kg or remains structural; if remains, quantify the required gap funding (annual operating subsidy EUR 274,820 or equivalent capex grant EUR 3.0M) and assess adoption credibility with unfunded gap.
  • For each locked deployment scenario (Scenario A: EUR 12/kg, Scenario B: EUR 10/kg, Scenario C: EUR 15/kg), state which cost-reduction levers would be needed to meet the threshold and whether they are consistent with the technology design and deployment assumptions.
  • Document all cost assumptions, sources (published benchmarks, contractor quotes, project estimates, proprietary models), and uncertainty ranges; specify which assumptions are validated by Phase One bench-scale data and which remain unvalidated (flagged as 'subject to Phase Two confirmation').
  • Present interim findings by Month 6 (2027-04-09) showing cost sensitivity to electricity price, downstream energy and utilization; final report by Month 9 (2027-07-09) with decision recommendations for gap funding (adopter grant, subsidy, cost reduction, or reduced Phase Three scope) and for scaling or contingency trigger points.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Canonical cost-gap reconciliation fails: if the model cannot account for the EUR 7.93/kg gap against published data and project assumptions, the model is internally inconsistent or lacks critical cost components; using it for gate decisions would commit the project to a flawed economics. Risk: Phase Three go-decision is based on unvalidated cost structure, leading to deployment failure or default to Research Only outcome after EUR 22M Phase Three spend.
  • Sensitivity analysis missing or incomplete: if cost drivers (electricity, downstream energy, capex, utilization) are not quantified with clear leverage, the funder and gate panel cannot identify which levers are controllable and prioritize Phase Two work accordingly. Risk: inefficient spend on cost reduction (e.g., investing EUR 500k in downstream optimization that saves only EUR 0.5/kg) when simpler levers would close the gap.
  • Cost assumptions are unvalidated at Phase One end: if the model relies on unproven downstream energy or capex-scaling assumptions, Phase Two disproof may invalidate the cost case; a late discovery forces re-modeling and delays the Phase Two gate decision by 2–3 months. Risk: gate-review panel cannot credibly assess whether the gap can be closed, reducing confidence in the Go decision and adoption uptake by 20–40%.
  • Gap-funding decision deferred: if the report identifies the EUR 274,820/yr operational gap but does not make a clear recommendation (adopter subsidy vs. capex grant vs. cost reduction vs. no go), the funder faces ambiguous guidance. Risk: EUR 3–5M Phase Three commitment is made without funding certainty, forcing a stop-work or major scope reduction mid-Phase Three if gap funding is not secured.
  • Scenario-to-cost alignment is missing: if the report does not map each locked scenario's threshold to the required cost-reduction path, scenarios remain abstract; gate reviewers cannot judge whether Scenario A (EUR 12/kg) is achievable without cost-reduction that is technically risky or requires unsecured partners. Risk: Go decision is based on scenarios that are formally met but economically dependent on cost reductions not validated by Phase Two.
  • Cost model is opaque or internally inconsistent: if major cost components (e.g., downstream processing) are treated as black boxes without item-level detail, or if different scenarios use different system boundaries, the model cannot be audited or updated confidently. Risk: funder and panel lose control of cost accountability; cost changes in Phase Two cannot be traced to root causes.
  • Interim findings (Month 6 = 2027-04-09) are insufficient to inform reference-unit hardware release decision at the Phase Two gate (Month 30 = 2029-04-09): if cost model is not mature by Month 6 (2027-04-09), only 18 months remain to Phase Two gate and 6 months to finalize the cost-reduction strategy; late maturation risks deferring the hardware decision or committing to hardware without cost clarity.

Worst Case Scenario: The Techno-Economic Cost Model fails to reconcile the canonical EUR 19.93/kg full cost against the EUR 12/kg scenario cap, revealing either: (a) a critical missing cost component (e.g., downstream processing energy 2–3× higher than assumed, or capex learning unfounded), or (b) an internal inconsistency between the model's assumptions and published benchmarks. As a consequence, the funder and gate panel cannot determine whether the EUR 274,820/yr gap is a modeling error, a real structural economics problem, or a justified premium for a public-good technology. The project advances to Phase Two without clarity, invests EUR 13M on bench scaling and reactor validation, and at the Phase Two gate discovers that the cost structure is fundamentally unworkable; the gap cannot be closed by Phase Three cost reductions, the scenarios cannot be met, and the only credible conclusion is Research Only or a reduced (Denmark-only) deployment. Phase Three spending of EUR 22M is cancelled, EUR 7–10M of Phase One and Two investment is sunk, and the programme's economic case collapses. Alternatively, the programme commits to Phase Three under false assumptions that cost can be reduced; hardware is procured (EUR 4M), the Kenyan replication begins, and mid-project the true cost is revealed; if the gap cannot be funded, the completed unit is either abandoned (EUR 4M sunk hardware) or operated at a loss unsustainable beyond the project's timeline, invalidating the deployment case and reducing adopter confidence by 50–80%.

Best Case Scenario: A rigorous Techno-Economic Cost Model reconciles the EUR 19.93/kg canonical cost against the EUR 12/kg scenario cap, identifying the primary drivers of the EUR 7.93/kg gap (e.g., 60% from downstream energy costs, 20% from electrolyzer capex, 20% from overhead) and quantifying the impact of each. The model demonstrates via sensitivity analysis that the gap can be closed to EUR 10–12/kg by: (a) solar-coupled electrolysis reducing electricity cost by EUR 3–4/kg, (b) passive or thermal nucleic acid reduction reducing downstream energy from 60 to 25 kWh/kg (EUR 2.8/kg), and (c) scaling to 200 kg/day reducing capex per unit by 20% (EUR 1.5/kg); total reduction EUR 7–8/kg, meeting the Scenario A threshold with EUR 0.5–1/kg margin. The funder and gate panel gain confidence that the scenarios are achievable and defensible based on controlled design choices and published precedent. Phase Two work is prioritized toward validating the high-leverage cost reductions (solar coupling, downstream-processing method selection). By the Phase Two gate (Month 30 = 2029-04-09), interim Phase II bench data confirm that downstream energy can be achieved at 20–30 kWh/kg and productivity supports the capex-scaling assumptions; the Phase II gate reviewers endorse proceeding to Phase Three with reference-unit hardware release (EUR 4M). The EUR 274,820/yr operational gap is acknowledged explicitly, and the funder commits to securing a named gap-funding source (e.g., a reserve agency's co-investment or a sustainability subsidy) as a Phase III condition. Final cost model at the Phase Three gate shows actual deployed-unit costs of EUR 11.2/kg, within the Scenario A threshold, and one named adopter has committed to a pilot procurement. The Go decision is supported by credible economics, and post-project deployment can proceed with confidence in cost assumptions and adopter willingness to deploy.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If the canonical cost model cannot be reconciled by Month 6 (2027-04-09) using project-generated Phase One bench data alone, commission an independent external cost-analysis firm (EUR 50,000–80,000 estimate) to audit the model, identify hidden assumptions and recommend which cost components require Phase II validation before the cost case is considered credible. This shifts risk from the project team to external scrutiny and may expose whether the gap is real or an analytical artifact.
  • If downstream-processing costs are a major source of uncertainty (>30% sensitivity), front-load Phase II work on downstream-processing validation (EUR 100,000–200,000 estimate, 8–12 weeks) rather than waiting for the full Phase II programme; use small-scale (1–5 L) pilot trials of nucleic acid reduction methods (thermal, enzymatic, mechanical) to measure energy and consumable costs before final method selection. Results feed the final cost model at Month 9 (2027-07-09) with measured data rather than estimates.
  • If the gap-funding decision cannot be made within the project budget, establish a separate funding-route workstream (hire a business-development manager for 6–12 months at EUR 100,000–150,000 estimate) to approach reserve agencies, governments, sustainability funds and development partners about co-investment or subsidy. Treat the gap-funding negotiation as a parallel work package to the technical programme, with interim results (confirmed named source or rejection) reported at the Phase Two gate; do not make the Phase Three hardware decision until a gap-funding route is confirmed.
  • If cost sensitivity to electricity price or other uncontrolled variables is very high (>EUR 2/kg per EUR 0.01 change in price), consider re-framing the deployment scenario as modular (small units near renewable-power sources, e.g., solar farms) rather than centralized, to de-couple cost from grid-price volatility and align with hypothesis B (decentralized, local operation). This requires redesigning the reference unit to be modular, delaying the reference-unit design by 2–3 months, but may unlock a cost pathway that single-site scenarios do not.
  • If by Month 9 (2027-07-09) the cost model shows that the gap cannot be credibly closed to EUR 12/kg through Phase Two and Phase Three work (i.e., leverage of available levers is <EUR 3/kg), recommend that the gate panel and funder face the option: (a) Accept a reduced Phase Three (Danish reference unit and documentation-based replication only, no full Kenyan deployment; cost ~EUR 12–15M, not EUR 22M), (b) Pivot to a Research Only conclusion and publish the open package for others to deploy, or (c) Commit to a specific gap-funding mechanism (e.g., German or Norwegian government subsidy, World Food Programme co-investment) before Phase III hardware release. Do not advance Phase III without choosing one of these options explicitly.

Documents to Find

Find Document 1: Cupriavidus necator H16 Strain Rights and Material Transfer Agreements

ID: 0e5b23bc-25e9-45d3-ad20-1062e75628e8

Description: Original material transfer agreements, strain-deposit certificates and rights documentation from culture collections (e.g., DSMZ, ATCC, NCCB) holding Cupriavidus necator H16 or related hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria. Required to confirm lawful obtainability for research, commercial production, redistribution, modification and derived strains in Denmark and Kenya. Purpose: input to Strain Feasibility Report (Month 4 = 2027-02-09). Intended audience: strain rights specialist, regulatory counsel.

Recency Requirement: Current (agreements valid as of Month 0 = 2026-10-09); historical amendments and restrictions that affect commercial use must be included

Responsible Role Type: Strain Rights and Regulatory Affairs Specialist

Steps to Find:

  • Contact DSMZ (Deutsche Sammlung von Mikroorganismen und Zellkulturen) culture collection and request the strain information sheet, material transfer agreement and any restrictions on commercial use for C. necator H16 or C. metallidurans
  • Contact ATCC (American Type Culture Collection) and request equivalent documentation for candidate strains
  • Contact NCCB (National Collection of Cell and Tissue Cultures, UK) or equivalent European collections if H16 is held
  • Request copies of any publications by the original strain depositors outlining restrictions on use, derived strains or commercial applications
  • Search for any patents filed by strain depositors on C. necator hydrogen oxidation or applications to protein production, covering Denmark, EU and Kenya

Access Difficulty: Medium—culture collections will provide strain information sheets publicly, but material transfer agreements and commercial-use restrictions may require direct contact and negotiation. DSMZ and ATCC typically respond to email requests within 2–4 weeks. Kenya import restrictions may require additional Kenyan biosafety authority contact (see separate entry).

Essential Information:

  • Locate and obtain the current Material Transfer Agreements (MTAs) from at least three culture collections holding C. necator H16 (DSMZ, ATCC, NCCB or equivalents), specifying any restrictions on: research use, commercial production, redistribution of the strain, modification and derived strains.
  • Document the biosafety classification of C. necator H16 in Denmark, EU and Kenya jurisdictions; confirm whether classification differs by jurisdiction and whether Denmark/EU classification permits Kenyan import and use.
  • Obtain written confirmation from the strain depositors (or their successors) of all third-party patent claims on C. necator H16, its hydrogen-oxidation pathway or its application to protein production, covering Denmark, EU and Kenya.
  • Confirm lawful obtainability for the project's four core use cases: (1) research and laboratory experiments Months 0–30 (2026-10-09 to 2029-04-09); (2) commercial production under an open-source licence without closed-fork control; (3) redistribution to independent Kenyan replication team and prospective adopters without developer mediation; (4) modification and derived strains without requirement to share derivatives back to original strain holder.
  • Identify any secondary restrictions embedded in the MTA (e.g., requirement to acknowledge the original depositor in publications, embargo periods before publication, or restrictions on third-country use) that would affect the open licence stack or publication plan.
  • For the backup strain (to be identified in Phase One), obtain equivalent documentation covering the same four use cases and jurisdictions, ensuring the backup has at least equal or superior freedom-to-operate compared to the primary strain.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • If MTA documentation is incomplete or ambiguous, the project may proceed on the primary strain for Months 0–12 (2026-10-09 to 2027-10-09) only to discover in Phase One that a commercial restriction prevents open publication, forcing a late pivot to backup strain and consuming the EUR 0.30M strain-rights earmark plus 2–3 months of Phase One schedule.
  • Undisclosed third-party patent claims on C. necator H16 or its hydrogen-oxidation pathway could emerge during patent search (Month 2 = 2026-12-09) or later, blocking publication or commercial deployment; if discovered late, the project must either design around the patent (adding cost and schedule) or consult patent holders on licensing (delaying decisions by 4–12 weeks).
  • If Kenyan biosafety classification or import restrictions are not confirmed by Month 4 (2027-02-09), the Strain Feasibility Report cannot be completed, preventing the Phase One gate from proceeding on schedule (Month 10 = 2027-08-09); delay of 2–4 weeks is typical for authority response times, but if barriers emerge, alternative strain screening extends into Phase Two.
  • If the backup strain is not identified with equal freedom-to-operate by Month 4 (2027-02-09), the project cannot satisfy the Phase One gate requirement for a 'legally clean backup'; proceeding without a backup exposes the project to single-point-of-failure risk where strain unavailability halts the entire programme (estimated cost of programme halt: EUR 15–25M sunk cost).
  • Misinterpretation of MTA terms (e.g., assuming 'research use' permits commercial production, or that modification rights include selling derived strains) could lead to unauthorized use, legal exposure and requirement to cease operations and redesign; if discovered during Kenyan replication, it invalidates hypothesis B evidence.
  • If the MTA requires attribution or acknowledgement of original depositors in publications, and this is not negotiated into the open licence stack, the licence terms may become inconsistent with open-source norms (e.g., CC-BY attribution required for the strain but not for other hardware or software), complicating adopter uptake.

Worst Case Scenario: A critical third-party patent claim on C. necator H16 hydrogen oxidation or autotrophic protein production is discovered during Phase Two (Month 18–24 = 2028-04-09 to 2028-10-09), after the primary strain has been used in matched reactor testing and the backup strain lacks adequate rights documentation. The patent holder asserts that any implementation of hydrogen fermentation using H16 requires a licensing agreement; the holder demands royalties or imposes restrictions incompatible with the open-source licence stack. The project must either: (1) negotiate a restrictive licensing agreement, undermining the open-access goal; (2) design around the patent by switching to an alternative strain (e.g., C. metallidurans), rerunning all matched-reactor comparisons and scale-up validation, consuming EUR 0.4–0.8M and delaying Phase Three by 6–12 months; or (3) declare the technology non-patentable and recommend Research Only, invalidating EUR 20–30M of Phase II and Phase Three investment. The deployment case collapses, adopters lose confidence in the project's intellectual property foundation, and the open-source community receives only partial documentation due to licence restrictions.

Best Case Scenario: By Month 4 (2027-02-09), the Strain Feasibility Report confirms C. necator H16 is held at DSMZ, ATCC and NCCB under identical, unrestricted MTAs permitting research, commercial production, redistribution and modification without royalties or derivative-strain sharing requirements. Patent search reveals no third-party claims blocking hydrogen fermentation or protein production with H16 in Denmark, EU or Kenya. Kenyan biosafety authority confirms H16 is classified as Biosafety Level 1 and lawfully importable for contained-use research and production. A backup strain (e.g., C. metallidurans) is identified with equivalent or superior freedom-to-operate. The Phase One gate proceeds on schedule with confidence that strain rights are not a project-blocking risk. The Strain Feasibility Report becomes a public model for reproducibility, and independent implementers can legally obtain, grow and redistribute the strain, validating hypothesis B and the open-access mission. Regulatory and adoption pathways remain unblocked by intellectual property.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If C. necator H16 MTA is found to restrict commercial use or derived strains, and no backup strain has equivalent rights, immediately escalate to strain holders (DSMZ, ATCC) during Months 2–3 (2026-12-09 to 2027-01-09) to negotiate a research-use exemption or waiver. If negotiation fails by Month 3.5 (2027-01-24), allocate EUR 50,000–100,000 and 4–6 weeks from the EUR 0.30M earmark to commission an independent patent and IP counsel to model design-around options (e.g., isolate a novel strain from environmental samples, or acquire a strain from a strain holder with no use restrictions); proceed to Phase One gate with a contingency plan to switch strains if primary MTA terms prove unacceptable.
  • If Kenyan biosafety authority response is delayed or biosafety classification is uncertain by Month 3.5 (2027-01-24), submit a formal pre-submission consultation request by Month 2 (2026-12-09) to accelerate response; simultaneously, commission an independent Kenyan regulatory consultant to research historical precedent for autotrophic bacteria and hydrogen fermentation in Kenya and to identify any undocumented barriers; allocate EUR 20,000–40,000 from the EUR 0.30M earmark for consultant time.
  • If third-party patent claims emerge that appear to block hydrogen fermentation, commission a patent validity or non-infringement opinion from an independent patent counsel (EUR 40,000–60,000 estimate) to assess strength of claim and design-around feasibility; in parallel, engage the patent holder on potential licensing or patent-pledge terms (adds 2–4 weeks); if licence terms are unacceptable and design-around is costly, escalate to the funder and gate panel by Month 6 (2027-04-09) to decide whether to proceed with licensing, pivot to an alternative strain (and revised schedule), or recommend Research Only.
  • If no backup strain can be secured with equivalent rights by Month 4 (2027-02-09), extend the strain-screening phase by 4–6 weeks (utilizing the 3-month float and consuming part of the EUR 0.30M earmark) to evaluate a third-party strain or propose isolation of a novel strain via environmental sampling or adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE); document the extended timeline in the Phase One gate submission and flag to reviewers that backup-strain risk is not fully resolved, recommending heightened strain-monitoring in Phase Two.
  • If the MTA requires restrictive attribution or derivative-strain ownership terms, negotiate with the strain holder during Months 1–2 (2026-11-09 to 2026-12-09) to modify terms compatible with open-source norms (e.g., agree that acknowledging the original strain source does not grant the strain holder ownership of derivatives or improvements); if negotiation fails, model the cost and legal burden of an alternative attribution scheme (e.g., separate acknowledgement of strain provenance outside the main open licence) and publish the decision in the open-source steward's governance framework by Phase One gate.

Find Document 2: Patent Landscape on Hydrogen Fermentation, Autotrophic Protein Production and Candidate Strains

ID: ea7c86d8-889a-4bb7-bc45-a56a234bf970

Description: Comprehensive freedom-to-operate analysis covering hydrogen fermentation processes, single-cell protein production from hydrogen and CO₂, and specific candidate strain (C. necator H16, C. metallidurans, Hydrogenovibrio, Ralstonia eutropha) use in protein production. Includes patent claims in Denmark, EU, Kenya and Bangladesh, with risk assessment per jurisdiction. Required to identify third-party IP blocking or licensing requirements before design commitment. Purpose: input to Strain Feasibility Report and Open Licence Stack and Stewardship Model decisions. Intended audience: legal counsel, regulatory specialist, IP advisors.

Recency Requirement: Current (patent databases searched as of Month 2 = 2026-12-09); includes recently published patent applications and granted patents; excludes expired or lapsed patents unless they indicate prior art or competing commercial interest

Responsible Role Type: Intellectual Property Counsel or Patent Search Firm

Steps to Find:

  • Commission a specialized biotech patent-search firm (e.g., FJC or equivalent) to conduct full landscape search across patent offices: European Patent Office (EPO), Danish Patent Office, German Patent Office (DPMA), UK IPO, US Patent Office (USPTO), Kenya Patent Office, WIPO (World IP Organization)
  • Specify search terms: 'hydrogen fermentation,' 'hydrogenotrophic bacteria,' 'autotrophic protein,' 'single-cell protein + hydrogen,' 'Cupriavidus necator + commercial' or 'Cupriavidus necator + protein,' and equivalent terms in relevant languages (Danish, English, German)
  • Request output: list of relevant patents with filing/grant dates, assignees (companies or institutions), claim scope (claiming the organism, the process, the product, or combinations), and country-specific enforcement risk (is the assignee actively asserting the patent?)
  • Rank claims by freedom-to-operate impact: (a) high impact = claims on hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria protein production in the target jurisdictions, likely blocking; (b) medium impact = claims on related processes or strains, negotiable or design-around possible; (c) low impact = claims in non-target jurisdictions or expired
  • Search for any patent pledges, defensive publications or open-source declarations by major players (e.g., Solar Foods, Calysta, academic institutions) that may provide design freedom

Access Difficulty: Medium to Hard—professional patent search requires paid access to patent databases (EPO, USPTO cost EUR 100–300/search) and specialized expertise. Typical timeline 4–8 weeks for full analysis and report. Small firms (e.g., universities) may face budgetary constraints; recommend procurement by funder or as part of regulatory/legal consulting budget (EUR 80k–120k estimate for comprehensive search across four jurisdictions and four candidate strains).

Essential Information:

  • Comprehensive freedom-to-operate (FTO) analysis identifying all patents claiming hydrogen fermentation, autotrophic protein production, or the candidate strains (C. necator H16, C. metallidurans, Hydrogenovibrio, Ralstonia eutropha) across Denmark, EU, Kenya and Bangladesh patent offices.
  • For each identified patent: filing/grant date, assignee (company or institution), jurisdiction, specific claim scope (organism, process, product, or combinations), enforcement risk assessment (is assignee actively asserting the patent?), and blockers vs. design-around feasibility.
  • Ranking of patent claims by freedom-to-operate impact (high = directly blocking hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria protein production in target jurisdictions; medium = related processes, negotiable or design-around possible; low = non-target jurisdictions or expired).
  • Identification of any patent pledges, defensive publications, or open-source declarations by major players (e.g., Solar Foods, Calysta, academic institutions) that may provide design freedom or reduce licensing burden.
  • Per-jurisdiction freedom-to-operate verdict for each candidate strain (is lawful production and commercialization possible in Denmark, EU, Kenya and Bangladesh without third-party licensing or design change?).
  • Specific licensing requirements, costs and timelines identified (e.g., cost of a license agreement, renegotiation risk, exclusivity constraints, territory restrictions).
  • Recommendations on strain selection based on IP landscape: primary strain and backup strain with minimal IP restriction.
  • Cross-reference to regulatory and biosafety landscape (is the strain subject to import restrictions, novel-organism approval or biosafety classification that compounds IP risk?).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Undetected third-party patent claims could emerge during detailed design or first manufacturing attempt, forcing a costly design rework, strain substitution or licensing negotiation under time pressure, consuming EUR 200K–500K (estimate) and 6–12 months of delay.
  • If a strain is selected without complete IP clearance and a patent infringement claim is raised during Phase Two or Three, the project may be forced to abandon the strain mid-development, invalidating all strain-related work and requiring backup-strain substitution (6–12 month delay, EUR 200K–400K estimate).
  • Incomplete landscape analysis (missing relevant patents or mischaracterizing claim scope) could lead to selection of a strain with hidden licensing burdens, discovered only when attempting commercial production, reducing adoption rates by 30–50% or blocking commercial deployment entirely.
  • If patent landscape is not completed by Month 4 (2027-02-09), the Strain Feasibility Report deadline is missed, delaying the Phase One gate and consuming contingency time from an already-tight schedule (3-month Phase One float).
  • Failure to identify jurisdiction-specific differences (e.g., a patent valid in EU but expired in Kenya, or vice versa) could result in incorrect strain selection, forcing re-evaluation in Phase Two or Three.
  • If open-source declarations or patent pledges are missed, the project may negotiate costly licenses when alternatives exist, wasting EUR 50K–150K (estimate) and damaging goodwill with open-source community.

Worst Case Scenario: A critical third-party patent blocking hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria protein production is discovered after the Phase One gate (Month 9 = 2027-07-09), when the primary strain has been selected and bench-scale experiments are underway. The project must immediately pivot to the backup strain, repeating strain-rights analysis, benchmark productivity work and regulatory approvals. If the backup strain is also subject to IP restrictions, the project has no viable option without licensing (expensive, time-consuming) or isolating a novel strain (years of characterization and regulatory work). The combined effect: 6–12 month delay in Phase Two, EUR 500K–1.5M additional cost, and a blown Strain Feasibility Report deadline that cascades into a missed Phase One gate. The gate panel may recommend Modify or Research Only, consuming the EUR 50M ceiling's credibility and delaying the final Go decision by up to 18 months, reducing adoption momentum and funder confidence by 40–60%.

Best Case Scenario: A comprehensive patent landscape completed by Month 2.5 (2026-12-24) identifies all material IP restrictions, confirms that the primary strain (C. necator H16) has clear freedom-to-operate in Denmark, EU and Kenya with no blocking third-party claims, and identifies a legally clean backup strain (e.g., C. metallidurans or a public-collection strain) with minimal licensing burden. The project delivers the Strain Feasibility Report by Month 4 (2027-02-09) and locks the strain choice at the Phase One gate, allowing full confidence in strain continuity through Phase Three. Open-source declarations are identified, strengthening the project's open-licence credibility. The IP clarity accelerates the gate reviewers' decision, reduces design-constraint uncertainty, and enables unrestricted publication of results, improving adopter confidence and enabling immediate replication without licensing friction. Final adoption rates improve by 20–30% due to clear IP ownership and reduced legal uncertainty.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If a comprehensive patent landscape cannot be completed by Month 2.5 (2026-12-24) due to resource constraints or patent-office delays, commission a rapid-turnaround priority search (EUR 20K–30K estimate) limited to the top 3–4 candidate strains and high-risk jurisdictions (EU, Kenya) by Month 1.5 (2026-11-24). Use this partial landscape to make a go/no-go decision on strain selection and engage in immediate licensing pre-negotiation with known assignees while a full landscape is completed in parallel.
  • If the primary candidate strain (C. necator H16) is found to have blocking IP claims, immediately activate the backup-strain option by running parallel strain-rights analysis on 2–3 alternative public-collection strains (e.g., C. metallidurans, Hydrogenovibrio sp.). Allocate EUR 30K–50K (estimate) from the EUR 0.30M regulatory/IP earmark and 2–3 weeks of schedule to confirm backup feasibility before abandoning the primary strain.
  • If licensing terms for the primary strain are acceptable but costly (e.g., EUR 100K–200K upfront + royalties), negotiate a research-exemption clause with the licensor allowing the project to publish benchmark results without royalty obligation, and a territory-specific license limited to Kenya or sub-Saharan Africa to reduce cost. Escalate to funder and gate panel for approval if license cost exceeds EUR 50K (estimate).
  • If a design-around is possible (e.g., using a different hydrogen-oxidizing strain not claimed by the blocking patent), commission a rapid feasibility study (EUR 20K–40K estimate, 3–4 weeks) to assess whether the alternative strain meets productivity and regulatory requirements. If feasible, pursue the design-around without delay.
  • If the patent landscape reveals fragmented IP claims across multiple assignees (different patents covering organism, process, product, and geography), consider engaging a licensing broker or patent counsel with experience in biotech cross-licensing to negotiate a comprehensive license covering all claims and all jurisdictions at a single negotiated rate, potentially reducing total licensing cost by 20–30% (estimate).
  • If country-specific IP landscapes are highly uncertain (e.g., Kenya or Bangladesh patent office has limited documentation), engage a local patent counsel in each country to conduct a desk-based freedom-to-operate assessment; cost EUR 10K–20K per country (estimate), 4–6 weeks, but provides ground truth for adoption risk in those jurisdictions.

Find Document 3: Kenya National Biosafety Authority Guidelines and Strain Classification Database

ID: 7c465094-ab00-48bd-af41-5853d3613d2c

Description: Current regulations, guidelines and classification decisions from Kenya's National Biosafety Authority (or equivalent competent body) for: (1) classification of hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria (wild-type Cupriavidus necator, other candidates) for contained-use research; (2) import restrictions and permit requirements for microorganisms by biosafety class; (3) requirements for commercial production authorization of novel organisms in Kenya. Purpose: input to Strain Feasibility Report (Month 4 = 2027-02-09) and Regulatory Engagement Sequencing decisions. Intended audience: regulatory specialist, Kenyan partner, project leadership.

Recency Requirement: Current as of Month 2–3 (2026-12-09 to 2027-01-09); includes any recent guidance updates or clarifications issued after 2024; historical precedent for similar novel organisms approved in Kenya (if any)

Responsible Role Type: Strain Rights and Regulatory Affairs Specialist (with Kenyan co-development partner liaison)

Steps to Find:

  • Contact Kenya's National Biosafety Authority (or successor agency; confirm correct name and contact via Ministry of Health website) via email requesting: (1) guidelines on contained-use authorization for hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria; (2) strain classification or pre-assessment for C. necator H16 and alternatives; (3) import permit requirements for live cultures; (4) commercial production authorization pathway for novel microorganisms (if defined)
  • Search Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) website for any published standards on novel feedstuff or protein product composition, digestibility and safety testing, as these inform regulatory pathways
  • Review Kenya's Biosafety Act (2009) and subsequent regulations (gazetted regulations, statutory instruments) for contained-use requirements and organism classification scheme
  • If no published guidance exists (Kenya biosafety regime may be less formalized than EU/Denmark), request a pre-submission consultation meeting with the National Biosafety Authority; provide a 5-page outline of the project (organism, contained-use design, proposed operating envelope) and request informal feedback on feasibility
  • Search for any recent government decisions on novel organisms approved for use in Kenya (e.g., prior approvals for GMO or novel microorganism research) to establish precedent for approval timeline and data requirements

Access Difficulty: Hard—Kenya's National Biosafety Authority may have limited published guidance (unlike EU/EFSA), particularly for novel organisms not previously approved. Email requests may take 4–8 weeks to receive response. Pre-submission consultations require in-country engagement (Nairobi office visit likely needed) or engagement via Kenyan partner. Language is English, but bureaucratic processes may be slower than European counterparts. Recommend establishing Kenyan partner relationships early (Month 0 = 2026-10-09) to facilitate contacts.

Essential Information:

  • Current regulatory classification and contained-use authorization requirements for Cupriavidus necator H16 and alternative hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria candidate strains in Kenya
  • Written confirmation from Kenya's National Biosafety Authority on feasibility of importing live cultures for research and commercial-scale production authorization pathways
  • Biosafety class assignment for the reference strain and any restrictions on redistribution, modification or commercial use under Kenyan law
  • Historical precedent: any prior approvals granted in Kenya for novel microorganisms or single-cell protein production, including approval timelines and data requirements
