  • If lead times exceed 14 days for all local sources, establish pre-positioned inventory during Phase Three commissioning (Months 40–42 = 2030-02-09 to 2030-04-09): order 90 days of nitrogen supply and store at the Kenyan site or a bonded warehouse, pre-positioned before the 6-month reference-unit run begins; budget EUR 50,000–100,000 for storage and inventory carrying
  • If resupply autonomy cannot be achieved with current supply chains, pivot the operating envelope: instead of assuming 60–90 day autonomy without resupply, model the system for 30–45 day autonomy with scheduled resupply every 30 days; test this shorter cycle in Phase III and adjust hypothesis B claim from 'decentralized under long supply disruption' to 'decentralized with planned resupply every 30 days'; this weakens the resilience claim but may be adequate for some deployment scenarios
  • If import-dependent supply becomes the baseline, engage a freight forwarder or customs broker in Kenya (or a regional hub like Dar es Salaam or Mombasa) to establish a pre-negotiated import protocol and duty-mitigation strategy; negotiate advance-tariff ruling or bonded-warehouse arrangements to reduce landed-cost volatility; budget EUR 20,000–30,000 and include in the EUR 0.5M FX contingency fund

Find Document 12: Published Benchmarks for Single-Cell Protein Energy Efficiency and Productivity (Yeast, Algae, Insect Protein References)

ID: 3471215d-17d3-4aa5-9f99-e5bb7124e57e

Description: Peer-reviewed publications and technical reports quantifying energy per kg dry biomass and volumetric productivity for established single-cell protein production routes (bakers' yeast from sugar, algae from photosynthesis or heterotrophic fermentation, insect protein from black soldier fly or cricket), reported with consistent system boundaries and capacity-utilization assumptions. Required to establish defensible energy and productivity benchmarks against which the hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria process is compared. Purpose: input to techno-economic model validation and KPI Framework alignment. Intended audience: TEA analyst, process engineer, gate-review panel.

Recency Requirement: Most recent available (prioritize 2020–2026 publications for modern energy accounting and efficiency standards); includes both academic studies and industrial technical reports

Responsible Role Type: Techno-Economic Modeler

Steps to Find:

  • Search Google Scholar and PubMed for: 'single-cell protein energy,' 'yeast fermentation energy per kg,' 'algae cultivation energy efficiency,' 'insect protein production energy,' 'alternative protein benchmarking' and related terms
  • Retrieve published techno-economic analyses or lifecycle-assessment (LCA) studies comparing energy and cost across multiple protein production routes (e.g., NREL reports, ETH Zurich LCA studies, ICIPE reports on insect protein)
  • Identify key publications likely to have energy-per-kg data: (a) yeast production (from industrial biotech companies like ABF Sugar or AB Enzymes); (b) algae (NREL algae research program, ETH aquatic biotech groups); (c) insect protein (ICIPE, companies like Agriprotein or InnovaFeed); (d) comparative meta-analyses (e.g., IVL Swedish Environmental Research Institute comparative protein LCAs)
  • Extract from each publication: volumetric productivity (g/L/h or g/day), specific energy (kWh/kg dry biomass), system boundary (what is included: fermentation only, or harvest + downstream processing), capacity-utilization assumption, and reactor type (fed-batch, continuous, open, closed)

Access Difficulty: Easy to Medium—academic publications available via Google Scholar and university repositories (most recent papers open-access). Industrial reports may require direct company contact or conference presentations. NREL and IVL reports typically open-access. Timeline 2–3 weeks to compile.

Essential Information:

  • Identify all peer-reviewed publications and technical reports (2020–2026 preferred) reporting volumetric productivity (g/L/day or equivalent) and energy per kg dry biomass (kWh/kg) for established single-cell protein routes: baker's yeast from sugar fermentation, microalgae (photosynthetic or heterotrophic), and insect protein (black soldier fly, crickets).
  • Document system boundary for each benchmark: specify whether energy includes fermentation only, or harvest + downstream processing; state capacity-utilization assumption (percentage of nameplate); identify reactor type (fed-batch, continuous, open-pond, closed photobioreactor).
  • Extract and tabulate for each source: volumetric productivity value and units; specific energy (kWh per kg dry biomass); reported uncertainty or range; organism/feedstock; scale at which measured (laboratory, pilot, commercial); year published.
  • Identify the most credible high-productivity and low-energy reference points from the compiled data (e.g., best yeast fermentation energy, best algae volumetric productivity) to establish defensible upper and lower bounds for the hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria process comparison.
  • For any published source using a different system boundary or capacity-utilization assumption than the project's KPI Framework, document the difference explicitly and assess whether data can be normalized or must be reported separately.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • If benchmark data are from outdated sources (pre-2020) or use inconsistent system boundaries, comparisons against the hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria process become meaningless; cost and energy claims lack defensible reference points.
  • Mixing productivity or energy figures from sources using different definitions (e.g., one reporting energy per kg product after downstream processing, another per kg biomass) invalidates techno-economic model calibration and produces misleading comparisons.
  • Incomplete or missing data on system boundary, capacity utilization or uncertainty ranges allow post-hoc selection of favorable benchmarks, biasing the KPI framework and gate-review panel's ability to assess whether the hydrogen process meets locked deployment thresholds.
  • Reliance on single sources or single organism type (e.g., only yeast data) leaves the reference frame vulnerable to that source's methodological quirks or assumptions; failure to triangulate across multiple independent studies and organism types reduces credibility.
  • If benchmark data are compiled late (after Phase One reactor comparison is designed or executed), the comparison cannot be pre-registered against consistent definitions, and measurement protocol for the hydrogen process may not align with published benchmarks, invalidating later claims of reproducibility.

Worst Case Scenario: Benchmark compilation is deferred until Month 6–8 (2027-04-09 to 2027-06-09), after the reactor-selection decision rules have been pre-registered and Phase One bench experiments begun. The project discovers that published productivity and energy figures use incompatible system boundaries (some report energy per kg wet biomass, others per kg product after drying, others energy-only and exclude downstream). The KPI Framework locked in Month 1.5 (2026-11-24) is found to be inconsistent with published data. The Phase One gate-review panel flags the mismatch and declares the bench-scale comparisons non-comparable to published work. Phase One productivity data cannot be validated against the published benchmark, forcing re-design of the measurement framework and re-analysis of already-collected data (EUR 50,000–100,000 estimate, 2–4 weeks delay). The phase-one gate is pushed from Month 9–10 (2027-07-09 to 2027-08-09) to Month 12–13 (2027-10-09 to 2027-11-09), consuming the 3-month schedule contingency. Downstream, the KPI Framework remains a source of ambiguity through Phase Two and Three.

Best Case Scenario: Benchmark compilation is completed by Month 2 (2026-12-09), before the measurement framework is locked. The project obtains volumetric productivity and energy-per-kg figures from 8–12 peer-reviewed sources covering yeast, algae and insect protein, with explicit documentation of system boundaries and capacity-utilization assumptions. The sources show that published baker's yeast achieves ~40–60 kWh/kg dry biomass (modern fermentation with energy-efficient downstream), and published algae achieves ~20–30 kWh/kg (photosynthetic systems with minimal downstream). The range 20–60 kWh/kg establishes a credible reference frame. The project's KPI Framework (locked Month 1.5 = 2026-11-24) is revised to align with the most common published definitions (e.g., 'energy per kg dry biomass, system boundary electrolyzer + fermenter + harvest, no nucleic acid reduction'). Phase One reactor comparisons are designed and measured against this harmonized framework. The Phase One gate-review panel confirms that the bench-scale hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria productivity and energy data are directly comparable to published benchmarks. Adopter thresholds (locked Month 9 = 2027-07-09) can credibly reference published comparable costs. This foundation supports hypothesis validation and deployment-scenario credibility through Phase Three.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If peer-reviewed publications on single-cell protein energy efficiency are sparse or recent (post-2024) published studies are not yet accessible, commission a rapid lifecycle-assessment (LCA) or techno-economic analysis (TEA) from an independent specialist (e.g., ETH Zurich, NREL, or IVL Swedish Environmental Research Institute) on 2–3 established protein production routes using consistent methodology. Budget EUR 60,000–100,000 (estimate) and 6–8 weeks for rapid LCA; accelerate by fixing scope to yeast and algae only if needed.
  • If published data use incompatible system boundaries, engage the authors of the most relevant studies (direct contact, email request) to obtain raw data or clarification on how to normalize values across different boundaries. Alternatively, commission a modeling study to normalize published figures to a common boundary (e.g., 'energy per kg dry biomass, including electrolyzer and harvest, no downstream processing').
  • If benchmark compilation reveals that the locked KPI Framework (Month 1.5 = 2026-11-24) is inconsistent with published data, escalate to the independent gate-review panel (or a smaller advisory group) by Month 3 (2027-01-09) to approve a revised Framework that maintains backward compatibility with the reactor-selection decision rules and disproof-experiment thresholds already pre-registered.
  • If recent (2024–2026) data on advanced protein technologies (precision fermentation, cultivated meat, other gas fermentation) become available and reveal energy or cost figures significantly lower than traditional benchmarks, treat these as emerging comparators rather than established baselines; flag them separately in the KPI documentation and discuss their implications with adopters when finalizing deployment scenarios (Month 6–9 = 2027-04-09 to 2027-07-09).

Find Document 13: Electrolyzer Capex and Efficiency Data (Green Hydrogen Production)

ID: 466f6746-7ae4-4d8c-a05e-15f2615c0ab2

Description: Current capital costs and electrical efficiencies for water electrolyzers (Proton Exchange Membrane [PEM], Alkaline, Solid Oxide) at scales 1–100 kW, including specific capex (EUR/kW), electrical efficiency (% conversion of electricity to H₂ lower heating value), and cost learning curves or projections to 2030. Required to estimate electrolyzer capex for the deployment unit and to assess cost-reduction sensitivity to electrolyzer technology advances. Purpose: input to techno-economic model and cost-reduction roadmap. Intended audience: TEA analyst, process engineer, gate-review panel.

Recency Requirement: Most recent available (2024–2026 data preferred for current market prices); includes capex from commercial suppliers (if available) and projections from hydrogen industry reports and IEA/IRENA cost databases

Responsible Role Type: Techno-Economic Modeler

Steps to Find:

  • Search IEA (International Energy Agency) Technology Collaboration Programme reports on hydrogen and electrolyzer technology costs (typically published annually, free download)
  • Search IRENA (International Renewable Energy Agency) database on renewable hydrogen cost and electrolysis technology maturation
  • Contact major electrolyzer manufacturers (e.g., Plug Power, Cummins/Hydrogenics, ITM Power, Nel Hydrogen, Giner Electrochemistry) via their websites requesting public data on specific capex for units in the 1–100 kW range; commercial data sheets often available online
  • Retrieve academic papers or industry reports on hydrogen cost roadmaps (e.g., Carbon Trust, FCHEA, DNV GL) projecting electrolyzer cost to 2030 and beyond
  • For comparison: search for any published data from hydrogen-protein projects (Solar Foods, if disclosed) or hydrogen-based chemicals production (e.g., ammonia, methanol synthesis) on electrolyzer costs at industrial scale

Access Difficulty: Easy to Medium—IEA and IRENA data free to download. Electrolyzer manufacturer data sheets publicly available on websites. Academic reports searchable via Google Scholar. Direct manufacturer contact typically yields response within 2–4 weeks. Timeline 2–3 weeks to compile.

Essential Information:

  • Current market prices and capex (EUR/kW) for water electrolyzers (PEM, Alkaline, Solid Oxide) at scales 1–100 kW from commercial suppliers or independent vendors
  • Electrical efficiency (% conversion of electrical input to hydrogen lower heating value) for each electrolyzer technology at the relevant scale range
  • Cost learning curves or industry projections for electrolyzer capex reduction to 2030 and beyond, including any published roadmaps from manufacturers or energy agencies
  • Specific operational and maintenance cost estimates (consumables, membrane replacement frequency, expected service life) for electrolyzers in the 5–50 kW range
  • Comparison of capex and efficiency across the three main electrolyzer types to support technology selection for the deployment-unit model and cost-sensitivity analysis

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Outdated or hypothetical pricing data (e.g., from 2015–2018 projections) could overestimate capex reductions, causing the techno-economic model to forecast unrealistic cost-to-deployment and mislead the Phase One gate decision on viability
  • Missing efficiency data or use of nameplate (theoretical) rather than measured electrical efficiency creates 10–20% error in the energy-per-kg calculation, compounding through the full-system cost model and potentially invalidating the EUR 12/kg threshold alignment
  • Incomplete coverage of 1–100 kW range leaves the scale-up extrapolation from reference unit (33 kW) to deployment unit (estimated 160+ kW) unsupported by comparable market data, forcing reliance on conservative assumptions that inflate cost forecasts
  • Mixing capex from different sources (2024 data mixed with 2022 projections, or commercial quotes mixed with academic estimates) without reconciling definitions creates internal inconsistency; the TEA analyst cannot determine which cost to use for sensitivity analysis
  • Absence of supplier or vendor contact information and lead-time data prevents validation that electrolyzer procurement is feasible within Phase Three budget and schedule; supplier delays of 6–12 months are common and unaccounted-for would delay commissioning

Worst Case Scenario: The electrolyzer capex and efficiency data are sourced from 2018–2020 academic projections and vendor white papers without 2024–2026 current-market validation. The techno-economic model uses these data to forecast a EUR 10.50/kg deployed cost, supporting a Phase One gate decision to continue to Phase Two. However, during Phase III procurement, the project discovers that actual 2030 electrolyzer prices have not declined as projected (due to supply-chain constraints and lower-than-expected manufacturing scale-up), and measured electrical efficiency is 5–8% lower than assumed. The actual system cost climbs to EUR 14–16/kg, exceeding all three locked deployment scenarios' cost thresholds (Scenario A: EUR 12/kg, Scenario B: EUR 10/kg, Scenario C: EUR 15/kg). The Go decision is forced to Modify or Research Only after EUR 22M of Phase Three investment (hardware, Kenyan replication, operations), and the project cannot recover the sunk cost. Reputational damage to the funder and host institutions is severe, and the EUR 50M programme ceiling is breached.

Best Case Scenario: Current, validated electrolyzer capex and efficiency data from 2024–2026 commercial suppliers and independent benchmarks (IEA, IRENA) are obtained and reconciled. The TEA model is updated with confirmed costs (EUR 800–1,200/kW for PEM or Alkaline in the 1–100 kW range) and measured efficiencies (65–72% electrical, depending on technology and scale). Sensitivity analysis shows that electrolyzer cost accounts for 25–35% of total installed capex and that 2–3% annual cost learning is realistic. The cost model, validated against current market data, forecasts EUR 11.50–12.50/kg deployed cost with 90% confidence, aligning with Scenario A and C thresholds. Gate reviewers confirm the cost basis is sound. Phase III procurement proceeds with confidence, actual electrolyzer quotes align within ±5% of the model, and the system delivers near the forecast cost. Adoption by prospective partners is credible because the cost case is evidence-based, not speculative. If electrolyzer costs decline faster than assumed (due to competitive manufacturing scale), the system can deliver below threshold and strengthen the case for wider adoption.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Engage major electrolyzer manufacturers (Plug Power, Cummins/Hydrogenics, ITM Power, Nel Hydrogen, Giner, Siemens, Sunfire) directly for commercial quotes on 5–50 kW units, specifying delivery timeline and warranty terms; obtain at least 3 independent quotes to establish a current price range; timeline 4–8 weeks, cost EUR 5,000–10,000 (request fee waiver by citing non-profit, open-source public-good mandate)
  • Commission a specialist hydrogen/electrolyzer cost analyst or consulting firm (e.g., HyDeploy, FCHEA, DNV GL, Element Energy) to deliver a custom techno-economic electrolyzer benchmark report tailored to the project's 1–100 kW scale and expected 2030 deployment date; cost EUR 30,000–50,000, timeline 8–12 weeks; report will include capex, efficiency, O&M costs and uncertainty ranges
  • Perform a rapid landscape review of published hydrogen-cost roadmaps (IRENA, IEA H2TCM, Carbon Trust, Hydrogen Council) to establish a consensus or range of electrolyzer cost projections to 2030; compile into a single 'Electrolyzer Cost Basis Document' with sensitivity bands (optimistic, base, conservative); timeline 2–3 weeks, no cost beyond staff time; use this as the interim model input pending detailed quotes
  • If current-market electrolyzer data prove unavailable or too expensive to obtain, and the programme cannot delay Phase One gate, adopt a conservative (high-cost) assumption set explicitly stated in the Phase One gate documentation: 'Electrolyzer capex assumed at the high end of available projections (EUR 1,500–2,000/kW) to protect against optimism bias. If actual 2030 costs are lower, the deployed cost will improve and strengthen the adoption case. If costs remain high, the deployment case may require targeted cost-reduction R&D or external financing.' Gate reviewers and the independent panel accept the conservative assumption as documented; the Phase One pass becomes conditional on Phase Two or Phase III cost validation
  • Partner with an existing hydrogen or electrolysis research group (e.g., DTU Chemical Engineering, University of Copenhagen, or a European hydrogen centre of excellence) to conduct a rapid electrolyzer cost and technology survey, leveraging their industry contacts and publication access; formalize as a sub-contract or collaboration agreement; timeline 6–10 weeks, cost EUR 20,000–40,000; product is a published brief or journal paper suitable for external citation

Strengths

  • Clear public-good mission with open-source output; no dependence on one company or exporter.
  • Staged design with kill gates, Go/Modify/Research Only/Stop outcomes and a EUR 50 million ceiling that is not a spending target (user constraint).
  • Independent gate panel (3-5 members, EUR 0.30M, funder-managed) and published deviations guard against continuation by momentum.
  • Pre-registered reactor selection rule, locked scenario thresholds and an audited assistance log make evidence credible.
  • Proven route: commercial hydrogen-oxidizing protein exists and open work (AMYBO, passive gas feeding) gives a starting point.
  • Conservative safety basis: gas inventory limits, <4% O2 in H2-rich stream, no hydrogen storage mandated.
  • Strong risk mapping: strain rights, hazard analysis and Kenyan site baseline are front-loaded to Months 0-4 (2026-10-09 to 2027-02-09).

Weaknesses

  • KILLER APPLICATION MISSING: no single flagship use-case is yet proven to pull adoption. Three scenarios (reserve agency, feed producer, humanitarian container) are proposed but unsigned, and none is shown to beat protein reserves, legumes or insect protein.
  • Deployment cost chain fails: full cost EUR 19.93/kg vs EUR 12 cap, a gap of EUR 7.93/kg (estimate). The EUR 274,820/yr gap has no funding route (open decision).
  • High energy demand: about 40 kWh per kg dry biomass (range 25-60) (estimate) makes electricity price decisive.
  • Partners, host, adopters, site, funding and permits are all unsigned.
  • Strain, scale-up and nucleic acid performance remain unmeasured; downstream cost is likely underestimated.
  • Hypothesis B (decentralized modules) demands specialist safety help, which conflicts with local repairability and the independence rules.
  • Governance load (panel, auditors, defect tracker, site monitoring) is heavy for a small team.

Opportunities

  • KILLER APPLICATION CANDIDATE: a containerized 50-100 kg/day module that gives governments or humanitarian agencies energy-independent emergency protein reserves. The unique pull is vendor independence plus local repairability during coinciding energy and food crises, where legumes and stored reserves are weak. Obstacles: cost gap vs EUR 12-15/kg caps, unsigned adopters, regulatory category for emergency nutrition, safety under a hydrogen-oxygen hazard, and unproven six-month uptime.
  • Premium animal or fish feed in East Africa may tolerate higher cost than food, offering a second flagship route (Scenario B).
  • Cheaper renewable electricity or solar coupling could cut the largest cost line.
  • Collaboration with AMYBO, Solar Foods contacts, icipe and KEBS gives data, benchmarks and regulatory precedent.
  • Open documentation and a certification mark could build a standard others adopt.
  • Even a Research Only result yields valuable open knowledge on the cost of simplification.

Threats

  • Hydrogen-oxygen explosion or serious incident would halt permits and credibility.
  • Strain, patent or Kenyan biosafety barriers could block lawful replication; a late strain switch (Phase Three) costs EUR 2-4M and 12-24 months, exceeding the Month 60 (2031-10-09) limit (estimate).
  • Scale-up may fail on mass transfer, productivity or energy per kg; a successful reference unit does not prove industrial viability.
  • Nucleic acid limits or novel-food rules may block the chosen product category.
  • Adopter withdrawal, host priority shifts or reviewer fatigue.
  • Falling prices of soy, fishmeal, insect protein or subsidised proprietary hydrogen protein.
  • EUR/KES volatility on about EUR 4M of KES spend (estimate); Kenyan grid improving and weakening the stress test.

Recommendations

  • Month 1 (2026-11-09): sign the Danish host MoU and engage an independent HAZOP/ATEX consultant; owner: project director. Issue the safety design basis by Month 2.5 (2026-12-24) and Adopter Change Boundary v0 by Month 3 (2027-01-09).
  • Month 1.5 (2026-11-24): charter the funder-managed gate panel and lock the KPI framework; owners: funder and lead analyst.
  • Months 0-4 (2026-10-09 to 2027-02-09): commission the patent search and strain-holder contacts, then deliver the Strain Feasibility Report (primary plus clean backup, Kenyan biosafety feedback) by Month 4 (2027-02-09); owner: legal/regulatory lead.
  • Months 1-9 (2026-11-09 to 2027-07-09): pursue a killer-application test. Engage 2-3 named adopters, prioritising a reserve agency and a humanitarian container case. Obtain written cost-basis data, sign commitments by Month 7 (2027-05-09) and lock thresholds by Month 9 (2027-07-09); owner: adoption economist.
  • Months 3-9 (2027-01-09 to 2027-07-09): run a cost-reduction study (electricity price, solar coupling, downstream energy) and decide the gap-funding route (adopter grant, subsidy or cost cut) before the Phase One release decision at Month 12 (2027-10-09); owners: TEA lead and funder.
  • Hold hardware for the two reference units (EUR 4.0M) until the Phase Two gate; recommend a reduced Phase Three or Research Only if the cost chain still fails; owner: funder.

Strategic Objectives

  • By Month 4 (2027-02-09), deliver a Strain Feasibility Report naming a primary and a legally clean backup strain with documented rights and written Kenyan biosafety feedback.
  • By Month 9 (2027-07-09), lock 2-3 scenarios with named, signed adopters, each with cost, capacity and uptime thresholds, with at least one designated flagship killer-application scenario.
  • By Month 9 (2027-07-09), show matched-reactor bench productivity of at least 90% of the published C. necator benchmark (pass; 70% to under 90% is a panel decision) and a modeled full cost path from EUR 19.93/kg toward the EUR 12 cap with uncertainty ranges (proposed threshold).
  • By Month 10 (2027-08-09), complete the HAZOP, the independent interlock review and the reference-architecture decision, with panel recommendation published and release decision by Month 12 (2027-10-09).
  • By Month 30 (2029-04-09), meet the Phase Two gate: kLa decline of 25% or less, 16-week strain stability within 10% variation, and 0 safety-critical unresolved documentation defects (proposed threshold).

Assumptions

  • Funding, host, Kenyan partner, adopters, sites and permits are uncontrolled until signed.
  • Canonical figures apply: reference unit 20 kg dry biomass/day; deployment unit 100 kg usable protein/day at about EUR 3.0M (estimate).
  • C. necator H16 or a similar public-collection strain is lawfully obtainable in Kenya (to be verified).
  • Electricity at EUR 0.08/kWh is achievable at the deployment site (estimate).
  • Gate reviewers can be recruited with real funding independence.
  • Scenario thresholds (EUR 12, 10, 15/kg) are proposals, not requirements.

Missing Information

  • Signed host, Kenyan partner and funder agreements.
  • Rights and patent status per candidate strain and jurisdiction.
  • Measured bench productivity, kLa and energy per kg for each reactor concept.
  • Adopter cost-basis data and willingness to pay a vendor-independence premium.
  • Kenyan and EU regulator positions on nucleic acid limits and the emergency nutrition category.
  • Downstream train energy and cost at pilot scale.
  • Landed cost of imported inputs and electrolyzer membranes in Kenya.
  • Verified benchmarks from Solar Foods and AMYBO with compatible boundaries.

Questions

  • Which single scenario would a named adopter actually pay for, and what evidence beats stored reserves, legumes or insect protein there?
  • If the EUR 7.93/kg cost gap persists, who funds it, or should the project plan a reduced Phase Three or Research Only?
  • What productivity loss from safety limits (<4% O2, low gas inventory) would you accept before the design no longer meets the thresholds?
  • How will the panel's independence be verified, and what happens if the funder overrides a Stop recommendation?
  • Which Kenyan site conditions would make the replication too harsh to attribute failures to design rather than logistics?

Roles Needed & Example People

Roles

1. Lead Process Engineer (Gas Fermentation & Scale-Up)

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Lead Process Engineer is the core technical decision-maker and outcome owner throughout all five phases (Months 0–60 = 2026-10-09 to 2031-10-09). Continuity of technical leadership is non-negotiable for validating scale-up assumptions, interpreting disproof experiments, and maintaining credibility of the matched reactor comparison. A 3–5 year tenure minimum is explicitly required. This is a permanent, continuous role with core accountability, not a phase-specific or specialist engagement.

Explanation: Owns the core technical outcome: hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria bioprocess design, gas-liquid mass transfer validation, bench-to-pilot-to-reference-unit scale-up, and energy efficiency per kilogram of protein. Leads matched reactor experiments, interprets disproof-experiment results, and ensures scale-up assumptions are measured rather than modeled. Critical throughout all phases for reactor selection, technical decision-making and hypothesis validation.

Consequences: Reactor comparison lacks technical rigor; scale-up assumptions are untested and fail late in Phase Three; mass-transfer and productivity benchmarks lack credibility; no clear technical decision authority. Deployment case cannot be validated. Project loses 60–80% of credibility with adopters and reviewers.

People Count: 1 senior (3–5 year tenure minimum) + 1 mid-level engineer (scale-up and pilot support). Senior role is project-critical and requires continuity; mid-level can transition or rotate. Total 2 FTE.

Typical Activities: Henrik oversees the matched reactor comparison (pneumatic, pressurized stirred, passive-feed designs), leading the selection of identical strain, media and operating conditions. He designs the bench-scale experiments (7–14 day runs to steady state), assigns the single lead analyst to prevent inter-operator variation, and interprets volumetric productivity, mass-transfer coefficient and energy-per-kg results. He pre-registers reactor selection decision rules and disproof-experiment failure thresholds before data arrive, ensuring thresholds are locked and not adjusted retroactively. He translates scale-up assumptions into testable hypotheses (e.g., kLa scales as power per volume to the 0.4–0.6 power) and leads the interpretation of Phase II pilot-scale results against these pre-registered targets. He is the primary technical voice at gate reviews, presenting evidence on reactor performance, scale-up credibility and the measured productivity cost of simplification.

Background Story: Dr. Henrik Larsen is a 42-year-old Danish process engineer based in Copenhagen, with 18 years of experience in bioprocess scale-up and fermentation engineering. He completed his Ph.D. at DTU in bioreactor design and spent ten years at a major Nordic biotech firm optimizing cell culture and yeast fermentation at scales from bench to 500-liter pilot reactors. For the past five years, he has worked as an independent consultant on hydrogen metabolism and synthetic biology projects. Henrik brings deep expertise in gas-liquid mass transfer, pneumatic loop design, and energy efficiency in bioprocesses. His publications on scale-up uncertainty have made him a recognized figure in the field. He is fluent in Danish, English and German, and has led cross-border R&D teams. Henrik is highly familiar with the technical core of the hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria protein project and has published on alternative protein routes.

Equipment Needs: Bench-scale bioreactors (20–50 L capacity), gas chromatographs for H₂/O₂ analysis, HPLC for biomass composition, dissolved-oxygen probes, pH controllers, temperature control systems, offline gas-composition sampling apparatus, data-logging equipment, computers for experiment design and analysis, mass-balance calculation software. Estimated equipment cost for matched reactor comparison: EUR 80,000–120,000 (consumables separate). Critical: single analytical set to minimize inter-operator variation.

Facility Needs: Dedicated laboratory bioreactor space (40–60 m²), temperature-controlled room (30±2°C), fume hood or ventilated bioreactor enclosure, electrical supply (20 A, 3-phase), utility connections for cooling water and compressed air, safety storage for hydrogen and oxygen monitoring, data backup and secure documentation storage. Access to university or research-institute analytical core facilities (gas chromatography, HPLC, composition analysis) on a priority basis. Must accommodate three matched 1-L reactors running simultaneously over 7–14 days minimum.

2. Strain Rights & Regulatory Affairs Specialist

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Strain Rights and Regulatory Affairs Specialist is a foundational pillar whose work (Strain Feasibility Report, biosafety pathway confirmation, patent landscape) must be front-loaded and locked by Month 4 (2027-02-09), with ongoing support for regulatory pivots through Phase Three. This is continuous, non-negotiable work across all phases, though the intensity is front-loaded (50% Phase One, 30% Phase Two–Three). The specialist is embedded in the core team managing two of the highest-consequence risks: strain availability and regulatory blockers. Not externally procurable without losing the integrated nature of the work.

Explanation: Secures lawful strain access and regulatory pathways—two of the highest-consequence project risks. Conducts written strain-rights analysis, coordinates with strain holders and culture collections, engages Danish/EU/Kenyan authorities on contained-use and product-safety pathways, manages patent landscape. Drives the Strain Feasibility Report (Month 4 = 2027-02-09 deadline) and regulatory pre-submission dialogue. Required throughout Phases One–Three for product-category lock-ins and late regulatory changes.

Consequences: Strain and regulatory barriers discovered late (Month 8–10 = 2027-06-09 to 2027-08-09 instead of Month 4 = 2027-02-09); Phase Two or Three forced to restart with fallback strain (EUR 0.2–0.4M, 6–12 month delay); product category locked on weak data; regulatory rejection of chosen category after hardware investment; independence claim invalidated. Project impact reduced by 40–60%.

People Count: 1 dedicated specialist (IP lawyer or regulatory scientist with biotech/food background). Minimum 50% full-time in Phase One, 30% in Phase Two–Three. Total 0.5–0.8 FTE, rising to 1.0 FTE if regulatory pivots required.

Typical Activities: Amara leads the strain-rights analysis, contacting holders of candidate reference strains (e.g., Cupriavidus necator H16) to obtain written confirmation of lawful obtainability for research, commercial production, redistribution, modification and derived strains in Denmark and Kenya. She commissions a specialized patent search covering hydrogen fermentation, autotrophic protein and the reference strains across Denmark, EU, Kenya and Bangladesh, and interprets findings to assess freedom-to-operate risk per strain. By Month 4 (2027-02-09), she consolidates findings into the Strain Feasibility Report naming the primary and a legally clean backup strain. She leads informal pre-submission dialogue with Kenya's National Biosafety Authority on contained-use authorization and strain import restrictions, logging all written feedback as design inputs. Throughout Phase Two and Three, she monitors regulatory and political changes, flags early any new requirements affecting product category or approval pathway, and advises on late regulatory pivots if needed.

Background Story: Dr. Amara Omondi is a 36-year-old Kenyan-Danish regulatory affairs specialist and intellectual property counsel with 12 years' experience in biotechnology law and food safety. She holds an LL.M. in biotechnology law from the University of Copenhagen and a degree in microbiology from the University of Nairobi. She has worked for a Copenhagen-based biotech consulting firm representing clients on EU novel food approvals, biosafety compliance and strain material transfer agreements, and spent four years at the Kenya Bureau of Standards helping draft technical regulations for novel ingredients. Amara is deeply familiar with both Danish/EU and Kenyan regulatory landscapes and has personal networks in both authorities. She speaks Danish, English, Swahili and French. Her track record includes successfully navigating strain import permits and negotiating material transfer agreements with strain holders.

Equipment Needs: Computers for document preparation, patent-database access (patent offices in Denmark, EU, Kenya, Bangladesh; est. EUR 2,000–5,000/year subscription), legal document templates and contract software, encrypted secure communication tools for sensitive correspondence with strain holders and regulators, video conferencing for international pre-submission consultations. Estimated software and subscriptions: EUR 5,000–10,000/year.

Facility Needs: Quiet office or dedicated desk space for confidential correspondence with strain holders and regulatory authorities, secure document storage (physical and digital) for material transfer agreements, patent reports and regulatory feedback, access to a secure video-conference room for pre-submission dialogues with Kenya's National Biosafety Authority and Danish/EU regulatory contacts. Reliable internet (bandwidth for encrypted video and large document uploads). No specialized laboratory space required.

3. Process Safety Engineer (ATEX & Hazard Analysis)

Contract Type: independent_contractor

Contract Type Justification: Process Safety Engineer (ATEX specialist) is required for a defined, episodic deliverable: the formal HAZOP/LOPA analysis (Months 1–3 = 2026-11-09 to 2027-01-09), estimated 300–400 hours, with independent third-party review of interlocks before construction. This is specialist, front-loaded work that is not continuous. An internal safety engineer (full-time employee, separately) oversees design implementation. The external ATEX consultant is procured for the specific hazard-analysis and certification task, not ongoing operations; this is typical external safety-review engagement.

Explanation: Manages the hydrogen-oxygen explosion hazard—the highest-consequence safety risk. Conducts formal HAZOP/LOPA analysis (Month 1–3 = 2026-11-09 to 2027-01-09), establishes Design Basis for Safety (gas composition and inventory limits, overpressure interlocks, safe shutdown on power loss), defines the Adopter Change Boundary so replicators know what is safe to modify. Independently reviews safety interlocks and emergency shutdown design before construction. Works throughout all phases ensuring safety constraints are met.

Consequences: Hydrogen-oxygen hazard inadequately analyzed; interlocks and shutdown logic not independently reviewed; unsafe design buried in complexity until Kenyan replication or deployment; safety incident causes fatalities, site closure and legal liability; ATEX compliance fails late, forcing design re-certification and cost overrun (EUR 0.5–1.5M); project credibility destroyed.

People Count: 1 ATEX-certified safety consultant (independent of host institution for Phase One HAZOP); 1 internal safety engineer overseeing design implementation and Phase Three verification. ATEX consultant: 300–400 hours (Month 1–3 = 2026-11-09 to 2027-01-09 estimate). Internal engineer: 50% FTE in Phase One, 30% in Phase Two–Three. Total 0.5 FTE internal, 0.1 FTE external consultant surge.

Typical Activities: Ingrid leads the formal Process Hazard and Operability Analysis (HAZOP) or Layers of Protection Analysis (LOPA) of the hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria fermentation process, identifying all failure modes (electrolyzer malfunction, gas-line rupture, overpressure, seal failure, backflow during power loss, operator error). She ranks failures by severity and likelihood and specifies design responses (inherent limits, design changes, or layered instrumented controls). She works with the lead process engineer to establish the Design Basis for Safety: gas composition limits (e.g., <4% O₂ in H₂-rich streams or >60% inert), gas-inventory limits (<0.5 m³ H₂ and <0.2 m³ O₂), pressure limits and safe-shutdown logic that apply consistently across all three reactor concepts. She defines the Adopter Change Boundary in writing, explicitly listing which components and parameters replicators may change without re-certification and which require full safety re-analysis. She independently reviews the safety interlocks and emergency-shutdown design before any pressurized equipment is built or ordered.

Background Story: Dr. Ingrid Sørensen is a 48-year-old Danish process safety engineer and ATEX-certified consultant based in Aarhus, with 22 years' experience in hazardous-process design and industrial safety. She holds an M.Sc. in chemical engineering and an ATEX certification from TÜV Nord. She spent 15 years at a major chemical engineering firm designing and certifying pressurized reactors, gas-handling systems and hydrogen production facilities for industrial clients. For the past seven years, she has worked as an independent consultant for small biotech and alternative-energy companies, specializing in formal hazard analysis (HAZOP/LOPA) and safety interlocks for novel processes. Ingrid is recognized for her ability to identify safety blind spots early and work with designers to embed inherent safety principles. She has testified as an expert witness on process-safety design.

Equipment Needs: Computer for HAZOP/LOPA documentation and formal hazard-analysis reports, access to ATEX-certification databases and standards (ISO 80079 series, DIRECTIVE 2014/34/EU), pressure-relief and interlock testing equipment (pressure gauges, flow meters, gas analyzers) if independent verification of design is conducted on a small-scale mockup; estimated cost EUR 15,000–25,000 for mockup if built. Most of the HAZOP work is desk-based analysis and document review.

Facility Needs: Office space for HAZOP facilitation and document production. Access to a small pressurized test cell or laboratory fume hood if a safety-design mockup is built to verify interlock logic and emergency-shutdown design before large-scale hardware commitment. Access to the Danish host's laboratory for on-site ATEX design verification during Phase One (Month 1–3 = 2026-11-09 to 2027-01-09). No continuous facility need; work is primarily independent consultant engagement (300–400 hours total, estimated 8–10 weeks).

4. Techno-Economic Modeler & Cost Analyst

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Techno-Economic Modeler is a continuous core function across all phases (50% Phase One, 40% Phase Two, 30% Phase Three, 0.4 FTE average), maintaining the cost and energy model, analyzing scale-up assumptions, and translating technical results into deployment feasibility for gates. This is integrated technical work that underpins all hypothesis testing and gate decisions. The modeler interprets disproof-experiment results and adjusts deployment-scenario feasibility, requiring deep continuity and accountability. Not a phase-specific or episodic task.

Explanation: Builds and maintains the cost and energy model connecting bench productivity to deployment scenarios. Defines material and energy balance, calculates production cost per kilogram (electrolyzer + fermenter + downstream + capex + overhead), identifies scale-up cost drivers, conducts sensitivity analysis against locked adoption thresholds. Runs disproof experiments: pre-registers failure thresholds, analyzes scale-up assumptions (mass-transfer coefficient, energy per kg, downstream yield). Gives gates meaning by translating technical results into deployment feasibility.

Consequences: Cost model is weak; deployment thresholds are not anchored in measured data; scale-up cost surprises arise late (Phase III productivity 30% lower than model, cost jumps from EUR 12 to EUR 19/kg); gates cannot distinguish pass from fail on economic grounds; adopters distrust cost claims; adoption rates fall 30–50%; project conclusion is Research Only despite viable technology.

People Count: 1 specialist (engineer or economist with bioprocess modeling experience). 50% FTE in Phase One (model build, sensitivity analysis), 40% in Phase Two (scale-up data integration, gate evidence), 30% in Phase Three (final cost accounting). Total 0.4 FTE average.

Typical Activities: Jacob builds and maintains the techno-economic model connecting bench-scale productivity to deployment scenarios, calculating production cost per kilogram (electrolyzer + fermenter + downstream + capex amortized + overhead). He develops the material and energy balance, breaking down inputs (nitrogen source, minerals, water treatment, cooling, spares like electrolyzer membranes) into local, regional and imported categories and quantifying days of production without resupply. He conducts sensitivity analysis on cost against locked adopter thresholds, identifying which parameters (gas-transfer efficiency, downstream yield, energy per kg, capital cost) have the highest cost impact. He pre-registers failure thresholds for disproof experiments (e.g., if kLa declines by >25% bench to pilot scale, what is the cost impact?) and analyzes Phase II scale-up results against these pre-set thresholds. He produces the cost and deployment-feasibility section of each gate review, translating technical results into whether scenarios are likely to be met.

Background Story: Dr. Jacob Møller is a 39-year-old Danish bioprocess techno-economic analyst with 14 years' experience in biotechnology cost modeling and scale-up economics. He holds an M.Sc. in engineering and an MBA from Copenhagen Business School, and spent ten years in the biofuels and alternative-protein sector building detailed cost and energy models for fermentation-based processes. He has published on the uncertainty ranges in scale-up assumptions and has worked closely with venture-backed biotech companies translating pilot results into deployment feasibility. Jacob is skilled in sensitivity analysis, identifying which cost drivers have the highest impact on viability thresholds. He has worked with adopter organizations to understand real cost constraints. He brings familiarity with material and energy balances and can rapidly iterate models as Phase Two data emerge.

Equipment Needs: High-performance computer for cost-model development, sensitivity analysis and data visualization (spreadsheet software, Python or R for modeling, Monte Carlo simulation tools). Access to published cost data on alternative proteins, fermentation equipment vendors and deployment scenarios (estimated database subscriptions EUR 5,000–10,000/year). Laboratory data from Phase One and Two (biomass yield, energy consumption, downstream costs) must be made available promptly. Capital cost database for electrolyzer membranes, reactor equipment and infrastructure.

Facility Needs: Dedicated desk and computer with secure network access to experimental data systems (Phase One bench, Phase Two pilot, Phase Three reference unit), allowing timely cost-model updates as Phase Two and Three data emerge. Access to a shared spreadsheet or data-warehouse system linking to the lead process engineer and downstream specialist for rapid feedback on cost assumptions. Occasional (quarterly) office space for face-to-face meetings with the process engineer and gate-review panel to validate model assumptions and disproof thresholds.

5. Kenyan Co-Development Partner & Site Operations Lead

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Kenyan Co-Development Partner and Site Operations Lead is the organizational and operational owner of the replication—hypothesis B evidence and independence credibility. This role requires sustained institutional presence, staff recruitment and training, site infrastructure management, and six months of continuous reference-unit operation (Months 48–54 = 2030-10-09 to 2031-04-09), with fault-injection testing and weekly reporting. This is a permanent, core accountability role within the Kenyan partner organization, not a consultant or temporary assignment. Independence and credibility depend on stable, embedded leadership.

Explanation: Owns the replication in Kenya—the credibility evidence for hypothesis B and local operation. Manages the Kenyan site (infrastructure, utilities, logistics), recruits and trains local technicians, runs fault-injection and component-substitution tests, maintains the audited assistance log, operates the reference unit through six months of production. Reports weekly to the Danish team and independently to the gate-review panel. Ensures the Kenyan team is genuinely separate organizationally and functionally.

Consequences: Replication is weak, undocumented or not truly independent; site is chosen for convenience rather than envelope realism; documentation defects are hidden or worked around without logging; hypothesis B remains untested; independence claim is not credible; adopters and regulators lose confidence; adoption rates fall 40–60%; project conclusion is Modify (incomplete evidence) or Research Only (technology works but not deployable).

People Count: 1 Kenyan partner organization with institutional capacity, credible track record and signed co-development agreement. Within that partner: 1 full-time site manager (recruited by Month 6 = 2027-04-09 for Phase Three start at Month 30 = 2029-04-09); 1 lead technician (trained by Month 36 = 2029-10-09); 3–4 technician cohort (trained and competency-verified by Month 48 = 2030-10-09). Total 5–6 FTE on-site by Phase Three, plus remote support from Denmark (technical troubleshooting, safety review) capped at 4 hours/month average.

Typical Activities: Samuel leads organizational and operational setup for the Kenyan replication, securing the site that genuinely tests the defined operating envelope (grid outages, water quality, local skills) rather than a showcase location. He recruits and manages a core technician team (5–6 people by Phase Three), conducts intensive hands-on training in hydrogen safety, culture maintenance, fermentation operation and troubleshooting, and implements competency verification before full-scale commissioning. He manages the Kenyan site's quarterly monitoring protocol (power-outage logs, water-quality sampling, spare-part availability), flags any drift >20% from baseline and coordinates contingency actions (e.g., adding controlled outage stressors if power becomes more reliable). He oversees the six-month Phase III reference-unit operation, collecting weekly samples, recording biomass composition and production uptime. He maintains the audited assistance log, recording all external help (safety reviews, regulatory consultation, developer troubleshooting) and ensuring that hands-on developer involvement does not exceed ~4 hours per month average. He reports weekly to the Danish team and independently to the gate-review panel.

Background Story: Dr. Samuel Kipchoge Kimani is a 41-year-old Kenyan bioprocess engineer and co-founder of a Nairobi-based research organization focused on appropriate-technology biotechnology for East Africa. He holds a Ph.D. in microbial engineering from the University of Nairobi and a postdoctoral fellowship in fermentation engineering from a Norwegian university. Samuel has 16 years of experience in laboratory and small-scale bioprocess work, including work on alternative proteins and local production capacity building. He has trained technicians in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania and has strong relationships with the Kenya Bureau of Standards and the National Biosafety Authority. Samuel is deeply embedded in Kenyan research and industrial networks and has successfully navigated permitting and equipment procurement in resource-constrained settings. He speaks English, Swahili and French and understands the real operational challenges of Kenya's power, water and supply-chain infrastructure.

Equipment Needs: Laptop and secure communications for remote support to the Kenyan site (encrypted email, video conferencing, file-transfer tools), access to laboratory-data systems (sharing experimental results, composition data, outage logs). On-site during Phase Three commissioning and initial operation (~Months 40–48 = 2030-02-09 to 2030-10-09): laptop, field instruments (multimeter, pressure gauge, thermometer, water-quality testing kit for baseline confirmation), vehicle for local logistics and supplier visits. Estimated field equipment cost EUR 5,000–10,000.

Facility Needs: Office and coordination space at the Kenyan site (40–60 m²) for the Site Manager, lead technician and administrative functions: desk space, secure file storage, secure document storage for permits and agreements, team meeting room, vehicle parking. Access to utilities including reliable internet (for communication with Denmark team), telephone and mobile coverage. Housing or accommodation support for the Site Manager (this is a relocation to Kenya, typically 3–5 years). Training facilities for the technician cohort (classroom space, hands-on fermentation and safety training). Proximity to water supply (for baseline testing and process water), electrical supply (for monitoring outage patterns and site infrastructure), and local suppliers (for parts sourcing and logistics).

6. Independent Gate-Review Panel Chair & Panel Members

Contract Type: independent_contractor

Contract Type Justification: Independent Gate-Review Panel Members are external subject-matter experts (3–5 people) recruited for defined gate-review milestones (Phase One Month 10 = 2027-08-09, Phase Two Month 30 = 2029-04-09, Phase Three Month 60 = 2031-10-09). Each gate review is an episodic engagement (estimated 40 hours per member per gate, ~120 hours over the 5-year project). Panel members are deliberately kept external and independent of the host institution and funder operations. They are specialist reviewers procured on a gate-by-gate basis, not embedded team members. Funding is ring-fenced (EUR 0.30M) and managed separately to maintain independence.

Explanation: Three to five independent experts with no employment ties to the host institution or funder, recruited and funded separately to ensure true independence. Panel examines evidence against pre-locked gate criteria at Phase One (Month 10 = 2027-08-09), Phase Two (Month 30 = 2029-04-09) and Phase Three (Month 60 = 2031-10-09) gates. Produces written continue/modify/research-only/stop recommendations binding in the sense that funder deviations require published written justification. Protects the EUR 50M investment from momentum-driven continuation despite weak evidence.

Consequences: Gate review becomes advisory or rubber-stamped; panel members lack independence (conflicts of interest, funding pressure); recommendations lack credibility; funder ignores unfavorable recommendations without accountability; weak Phase One or Two evidence is not surfaced; project continues on momentum alone; EUR 20–30M Phase Three spend occurs without justified evidence; final Go decision is rationalization, not evidence-based; adopter and public trust collapses.

People Count: 3–5 panel members (process engineer, ATEX safety specialist, biotech regulatory consultant, adoption economist, optional product expert); 1 panel chair to organize deliberations and author joint recommendation. Minimum 40 hours per member per gate (3 gates × 40 hours = 120 hours per member × 3–5 members = 360–600 hours total). Funded separately: EUR 0.30M over 5 years (funder-managed, not host-institution budget). Average ~EUR 10,000–20,000 per gate.

Typical Activities: Michael recruits, charters and coordinates the independent gate-review panel (3–5 members, separately funded by the funder). He schedules panel meetings at each gate (Phase One Month 10 = 2027-08-09, Phase Two Month 30 = 2029-04-09, Phase Three Month 60 = 2031-10-09), typically 1–2 days in person or virtual. He ensures each panel member receives comprehensive briefing materials (technical reports, safety analyses, cost models, regulatory correspondence) at least 4–6 weeks before each gate meeting and allocates sufficient review time (estimated 40 hours per member per gate). During deliberations, Michael facilitates discussion of evidence against pre-locked gate criteria (productivity target, strain-rights documentation, Kenyan biosafety feasibility, safety design basis completion, scenario lock-in, regulatory pathway, and blueprint readiness at Phase One gate; disproof thresholds, strain stability, documentation defects and downstream validation at Phase Two gate; replication success, uptime, fault-injection results, operator competence and scenario achievement at Phase Three gate). He ensures the panel produces a written joint recommendation (continue, modify, research-only or stop) with detailed rationale, signed by all members and published within 5 working days. He alerts the funder to any deviation from the panel's recommendation and records the funder's published written justification.

Background Story: Prof. Michael Hoffmann is a 55-year-old German process engineer and independent safety expert, chair of the gate-review panel, with 28 years in industrial biotechnology, ATEX compliance and research-programme governance. He holds a Ph.D. in chemical engineering and has led or reviewed safety work on dozen large infrastructure projects in pharma and industrial biotech. He is an ATEX-certified reviewer and has published on independent oversight in high-uncertainty R&D. Michael is respected across Europe for his intellectual rigor and skepticism of optimistic technical claims. He has no institutional affiliations that depend on this project's continuation and no prior involvement in alternative-protein or hydrogen-fermentation research. He is fluent in Danish, German, English and Dutch. The panel members are recruited to complement Michael's expertise: Dr. Yuki Tanaka (Japanese biotech regulatory expert with EU and Kenya experience), Dr. Elena Sánchez (Spanish adoption-economy specialist) and Dr. Kwame Adekunle (Nigerian ATEX safety engineer).

Equipment Needs: Computer and secure video-conferencing system for gate-review meetings (3 gates × 1–2 days in-person or virtual = estimated 40 hours per panelist per gate). No specialized equipment required; panel members work independently using existing professional tools. Gate briefing materials (technical reports, data files) delivered digitally. Optional: recording and transcription services for gate meetings to ensure accurate documentation of panel discussions (EUR 3,000–5,000 estimate).

Facility Needs: Meeting facilities for in-person gate reviews (3 gates, Month 10 = 2027-08-09, Month 30 = 2029-04-09, Month 60 = 2031-10-09): conference room with video conferencing, whiteboard/screen for technical discussion, secure meeting space for confidential deliberations. Alternatively, fully virtual meetings with secure platform and recorded sessions. No office or laboratory space required. Panel members are external; the funder and host institution must provide meeting space and administrative support (scheduling, preparation of briefing materials, publication of recommendations).

7. Downstream Bioprocessing Engineer (Harvest, Nucleic Acid Reduction, Drying)

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Downstream Bioprocessing Engineer is a continuous technical specialist (40% Phase One, 60% Phase Two, 40% Phase Three, 0.5 FTE average) designing and validating the processing train (harvest, nucleic acid reduction, drying). This work is integrated into the core hypothesis-testing roadmap: bench-scale method selection (Phase One), pilot-scale validation (Phase Two), and full-scale commissioning and quality assurance (Phase Three). Product composition and regulatory compliance depend on this engineer's continuity. This is not externally procurable as a one-off project; it requires ongoing integration with the fermenter design and regulatory strategy.

Explanation: Designs and validates the processing train (harvesting, cell disruption, nucleic acid reduction, drying) that turns raw biomass into usable, on-spec protein product. Conducts bench-scale tests on nucleic acid-reduction methods (thermal, enzymatic, or passive), pilots the selected method at 1–10 L scale, validates product composition (protein, nucleic acid, moisture, digestibility) against regulatory and scenario thresholds. Downstream cost and energy often exceeds fermenter cost; this role prevents cost surprises and regulator rejection of final product.

Consequences: Nucleic acid removal underestimated; product fails composition spec in Phase III; regulator rejection or product-category pivot required; EUR 0.2–0.5M redesign cost and 2–4 month delay; downstream energy and cost not integrated into total-system benchmark; cost model fails (e.g., EUR 12/kg target becomes EUR 15–20/kg on actual downstream); deployment case invalidated; adoption scenarios fail to meet thresholds.

People Count: 1 specialist (bioprocess or food engineer with downstream purification experience). 40% FTE in Phase One (method selection, bench tests), 60% in Phase Two (pilot-scale validation, product composition analysis), 40% in Phase Three (full-scale commissioning and quality assurance). Total 0.5 FTE average.

Typical Activities: Sophia designs and validates the downstream-processing train (harvesting, cell disruption, nucleic-acid reduction, drying) in parallel with fermenter optimization. She conducts bench-scale method selection experiments on nucleic-acid reduction (thermal, enzymatic, passive) on biomass from the reference strain, measuring efficiency, product yield and final composition (protein, nucleic acid, moisture). She specifies a fixed processing boundary (harvest method, disruption if any, nucleic-acid reduction step, drying method) that is used consistently in all cost and energy benchmarks throughout the project. She pilots the selected downstream method at 1–10 L scale during Phase Two, validating product composition against regulatory limits (nucleic acid ≤2% of dry matter, protein ≥60%, moisture ≤8%) and calculating cost and energy per kilogram of usable protein. During Phase III, she oversees full-scale downstream commissioning on the Danish reference unit, verifies product meets composition spec weekly, and trains the Kenyan team on downstream operation. She flags any significant deviation from Phase II composition or energy data and investigates root causes (temperature drift, reagent degradation, equipment fouling).

Background Story: Dr. Sophia Volkov is a 37-year-old Russian-Danish bioprocess engineer specializing in downstream processing and protein purification, with 13 years' experience in single-cell protein harvesting, cell disruption and nucleic-acid removal. She holds a Ph.D. in bioengineering from KTH in Sweden and spent eight years at a Nordic biotechnology firm optimizing harvest and purification trains for industrial fermentation. She has published on nucleic-acid reduction in microbial biomass and has worked on regulatory dossiers for novel protein-product composition and digestibility. Sophia brings deep knowledge of cost and energy trade-offs in downstream steps and has practical experience with both thermal, enzymatic and mechanical nucleic-acid reduction methods. She is detail-oriented and has identified cost surprises in previous bioprocess projects that were hidden in downstream complexity.

Equipment Needs: Bench-scale laboratory equipment for downstream-processing method selection: centrifuge (5,000–10,000 g capacity), filtration apparatus, thermal treatment oven (30–100°C range), basic enzyme reagents and analytical standards, water-quality testing kit. Pilot-scale equipment (Phase Two): 5–10 L harvest volume capacity, including cell-recovery equipment (centrifuge or filter press), nucleic-acid reduction apparatus (thermal bath or enzymatic digestion flask), drying equipment (freeze-dryer or spray-dryer pilot unit). Estimated bench and pilot equipment cost: EUR 40,000–80,000. Analytical instruments (HPLC, amino-acid analyzer, moisture analyzer) shared with the fermenter team.

Facility Needs: Dedicated downstream-processing laboratory space (30–50 m²) separate from the fermenter area, with utility connections (electricity, cooling water, compressed air, waste disposal), fume hood or chemical exhaust for enzymatic digestion and thermal treatment, temperature-controlled storage for intermediates and reagents (4°C and room temperature), secure documentation storage for product-composition data and regulatory specifications. Access to high-temperature oven and freeze-dry or spray-dry equipment (may be shared or outsourced to a pilot-scale facility if not available in-house). Equipment for nucleic-acid quantification (qPCR or UV absorption, shared with the microbiologist).

8. Project Manager & Governance Administrator (Phase Gate Coordination & Documentation)

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Project Manager and Governance Administrator is a core administrative and governance role (50% Phase One, 40% Phase Two–Three, 0.45 FTE average) managing steering committees, milestone tracking, gate-panel coordination, documentation-defect tracking, and compliance with partner agreements. This is a persistent, non-technical core function that underpins governance credibility and transparency. Gate independence and defect-tracking accountability depend on this role's continuity and neutrality. Not externally procurable; must be embedded in the project team and directly accountable to the funder.

Explanation: Coordinates quarterly steering-committee meetings, tracks milestones and spending against phase budgets, manages the independent gate-review panel (scheduling, briefing materials, published decisions), maintains the documentation-defect tracker and audited assistance log, ensures funder approvals and partner agreements stay current, produces monthly progress and financial reports. Acts as the single point of contact for the gate-review panel and funder. Ensures gates have teeth: criteria are locked before experiments, defects are tracked transparently, and decisions are documented.

Consequences: Gate criteria are not locked or enforced; documentation defects are not tracked; assistance log is incomplete; funder and panel do not receive timely, accurate reports; milestone slippages are not caught early; partners miss renewal dates; steering committee becomes reactive rather than proactive; gate decisions are delayed or lack supporting evidence; EUR 50M investment is not transparently managed; funder and public trust erodes.

People Count: 1 dedicated project manager (50% FTE minimum in Phase One due to charter and panel setup, 40% FTE in Phase Two–Three). Total 0.45 FTE average. Must have project-governance experience and familiarity with research-programme administration. Cannot be delegated to a technician or part-time administrator.

Typical Activities: Emilie coordinates quarterly steering-committee meetings (Danish team, Kenyan partner, funder, gate-panel chair) and produces written summaries of decisions, action items and risk escalations. She maintains a live project-milestone tracker showing progress against Phase One, Two and Three schedules and milestones (strain feasibility report, HAZOP completion, reactor selection, Phase II gate evidence lock, etc.). She manages the gate-review panel: recruits members by Month 1.5 (2026-11-24), prepares briefing materials, schedules meetings, ensures payment of honoraria from the separate panel-funding budget line, and publishes recommendations and any funder deviations. She establishes and monitors the documentation-defect tracker during Phase II early replication, ensuring every ambiguity is logged with location, description, severity and resolution, and that the independent auditor reviews findings monthly. She maintains the audited assistance log, ensuring all external help to the Kenyan team (safety reviews, regulatory consultation, developer troubleshooting) is recorded with date, duration, outcome and auditor sign-off. She produces monthly progress reports and quarterly financial statements, tracking spending against phase budgets and flagging any cost or schedule variance >10% for steering-committee escalation. She also manages partner agreements, ensuring renewal dates stay current and contingency plans are activated if partners face challenges.

Background Story: Dr. Emilie Rasmussen is a 34-year-old Danish project manager and governance specialist with 11 years' experience managing large research programmes and infrastructure projects, including a EUR 15M+ EU-funded collaborative initiative. She holds an M.Sc. in project management and environmental science and has worked in both university research administration and private consulting. Emilie is skilled at building steering-committee processes, managing milestone tracking, coordinating independent reviewers and ensuring transparency of progress and financial spending. She has implemented documentation-defect tracking systems for complex hardware projects and is familiar with the governance challenges of independent replication and gate-review credibility. She is detail-oriented, diplomatic and has experience escalating issues to decision-makers without blame.

Equipment Needs: Computer and project-management software (Asana, Monday.com, or similar for milestone tracking and risk management), spreadsheet software for budget tracking and financial reports, secure file-storage system (shared drive or cloud repository) for gate-review materials, partner agreements and compliance documentation, video-conferencing system for steering-committee meetings, document-management and version-control system for the documentation-defect tracker and audited assistance log. Estimated software subscriptions and tools: EUR 5,000–10,000/year.

Facility Needs: Dedicated office desk and workspace for project manager in the Danish host institution, with secure access to all project systems (budget data, partner agreements, regulatory correspondence, gate-review documents). Access to a conference room for monthly or quarterly steering-committee meetings (in-person or hybrid, with video conferencing). Access to a document-management system where all project records are stored, versioned and accessible to stakeholders under appropriate security controls. No specialized laboratory or hazardous-work facilities required.

Omissions

1. Steward Entity Governance and Long-Term Licensing Stewardship

The plan mandates publishing a complete open-source package under open licences but provides no detail on who holds the licences, enforces terms, manages the source repository, or ensures the core remains open long-term after the EUR 50M programme ends. The Open Licence Stack decision (Decision 12) discusses licence choices but not stewardship continuity. Without a named, funded steward entity with sustainable revenue, the open package risks being forked, closed or abandoned post-2031.

Recommendation: By Month 2 (2026-12-09), define the steward entity (non-profit foundation, university consortium spin-off, or open-source collective) that will hold licences and enforce terms. Commit steward-entity startup and three-year operational funding (EUR 0.2M estimated) within the EUR 50M ceiling. Name the steward in the Phase One gate report and secure its formal legal charter before Phase Two begins. Include steward duties in annual project reports (licence enforcement, fork prevention, repository maintenance, patent monitoring).

2. Adopter and Deployment Site Engagement Beyond Threshold-Locking

The plan locks deployment scenarios with named adopters by Month 9 (2027-07-09) but does not specify ongoing engagement during Phase Two and Three. Adopters may withdraw, change priorities, or face budget cuts mid-programme. No mechanism is defined for validating that locked scenarios remain credible, for handling adopter withdrawal, or for testing prototype acceptance by named adopters before the Phase Three gate. Hypothesis B success depends on actual adopters being willing to operate the Kenyan replication unit.

Recommendation: Establish a quarterly Adopter Engagement Protocol starting Month 6 (2027-04-09): semi-annual updates to named adopters on progress, Phase Two data, cost and capacity forecasts. Document any adopter withdrawal or threshold changes publicly within 30 days of notification. By Month 54 (2031-04-09), conduct a pre-Phase Three gate 'Adopter Readiness Assessment' in which each named adopter confirms they remain committed to the locked thresholds and their readiness to begin deployment planning if the technology passes. If an adopter withdraws and remaining scenarios fall below a minimum viability threshold (defined by the panel), trigger a gate-review escalation before the Phase Three gate meets.

3. Staff Turnover, Knowledge Retention and Succession Planning

The plan identifies key roles (Lead Process Engineer, Strain Rights Specialist, Kenyan Site Manager, Project Manager) requiring 3–5 year tenure, but does not specify turnover-risk monitoring, knowledge-transfer protocols, or succession-planning procedures. Loss of a critical staff member (e.g., the Site Manager or Lead Engineer) mid-Phase Three could disrupt commissioning, delay operations or compromise independence evidence. No redundancy is planned for specialist roles.

Recommendation: Establish a Staffing and Continuity Protocol by Month 3 (2027-01-09): assign dual accountability (outgoing and incoming staff) for critical roles; require 4–6 weeks overlap and signed-off competency assessment for departures; document all design decisions and technical rationale in a living 'Design Rationale' wiki updated monthly. Monitor staff turnover quarterly; flag any key role with >6 months vacancy or >50% turnover rate as a risk requiring escalation. For critical roles (Lead Process Engineer, Site Manager, Safety Engineer, Strain Rights Specialist), maintain a pre-identified internal or external backup candidate with a standing offer and retention agreement.

4. Post-Deployment Phase: Long-Term Sustainability and Adoption Support

The plan ends at Month 60 (2031-10-09) with a Go/Modify/Research Only/Stop decision and publication of the open package. However, it does not address what happens after: (1) Does the project team remain available for early-adopter support or training? (2) Who funds ongoing steward-entity operations beyond Year 1? (3) What is the commercial or donor route for deploying the first units at Scenarios A, B and C? (4) How does the open design compete against proprietary systems (e.g., Solar Foods, Calysta) in a commercial marketplace if no one is actively marketing or supporting the open version? An open design with no adoption pathway is not a public good.

Recommendation: Before the Phase Three gate, develop a Post-Deployment Support and Adoption Strategy (Month 54 = 2031-04-09): (1) Specify a 12–24 month post-gate 'transition phase' in which key project staff remain available for early-adopter training, regulatory support and troubleshooting (0.5–1.0 FTE, funding source TBD); (2) Identify a sustainable funding route for the steward entity (endowment, membership fees, licensing platform, or donor commitment); (3) Partner with at least one named adopter to demonstrate the first deployment case, bridging the gap between research completion and commercial/field operation; (4) Publish an 'Adoption Playbook' for prospective deployers, covering regulatory pathway, procurement checklist, training plan and cost-of-capital assumptions. Without a post-gate adoption strategy, the open package may remain a research artifact rather than a deployable public good.

5. Independent Auditor for Replication Defect Tracking and Assistance Log

The plan mandates an independent third-party auditor to review the documentation-defect tracker and audited assistance log during Phase II and III. However, no detail is provided on auditor selection criteria, funding source (estimated EUR 50,000–100,000 over 3 years, not explicitly budgeted), authority to recommend rework, or escalation path if the auditor identifies systematic documentation gaps late in Phase III. If the auditor is underfunded or lacks enforcement authority, the defect log becomes a compliance exercise rather than a credibility tool.

Recommendation: By Month 3 (2027-01-09), recruit and fund the independent auditor through the funder's budget (separate from project spend), with a signed charter specifying: monthly review of defects, authority to flag inadequate resolutions and request re-work, direct reporting to the gate-review panel (not the project manager), and escalation triggers (e.g., if critical defects remain unresolved at Month 22 = 2028-08-09, recommend extending Phase II documentation work). Budget EUR 50,000–100,000 for auditor fees and allocate from the Phase One contingency or programme reserve. Require the auditor to produce a formal 'Replication Readiness Report' at the Phase II-to-Phase III gate with explicit sign-off: 'We find documentation sufficiently clear for independent replication, with residual defects not exceeding [threshold].' Do not release Phase III funding without this sign-off.

6. Allergenicity and Toxicology Safety Data for the Product Category

The plan specifies product composition (protein ≥60%, nucleic acid ≤2%, moisture ≤8%) and requires digestibility data for the selected product category by the Phase Two gate. However, it does not explicitly mandate allergenicity testing, acute or repeated-dose toxicology studies, or microbiological safety (absence of pathogens or endotoxins) for the novel protein product. Different product categories (animal feed, food ingredient, emergency nutrition) have different safety-data requirements. Regulatory rejection due to missing safety data discovered late in Phase III could force redesign or category pivot.

Recommendation: By Month 6 (2027-04-09), commission a regulatory pre-submission consultation with the Danish EPA and EFSA (or Kenya's equivalent) to obtain written specification of the minimum safety-data package required for the provisional product category. Define a Safety Testing Roadmap by Month 9 (2027-07-09) listing: allergenicity testing (if food ingredient or emergency nutrition), acute toxicity (LD50 if required), 28-day oral toxicity (if novel protein), microbiological safety limits, and the laboratory and timeline needed for each. Allocate a dedicated EUR 0.2–0.4M work package in Phase II to generate safety data in parallel with product-composition and digestibility work. Before the Phase Two gate, require independent review of generated safety data against regulatory requirements to confirm the product category remains credible.

7. Kenyan Technician Training Content and Competency Framework

The plan requires 'locally trained technicians after a short, competency-verified training programme' (hypothesis A) and specifies general training topics (hydrogen safety, culture maintenance, fermentation operation, troubleshooting) but does not detail training content, duration, teaching methods, assessment criteria or pass thresholds. Risk: technicians may appear competent after training but fail during real operation under stress (power outages, equipment failures).
