Failure Modes

FM1 - The Bridge to Nowhere

  • Archetype: Process/Financial
  • Root Cause: Assumption A2
  • Owner: Funder Representative and Techno-Economic Lead
  • Risk Level: CRITICAL 20/25 (Likelihood 4/5 × Impact 5/5)
Failure Story
  • Full cost EUR 19.93/kg vs EUR 12 cap; gap EUR 274,820/yr (estimate).
  • Gap-funding route stays an open decision past Month 9 (2027-07-09).
  • Phase Two proceeds on momentum; EUR 4.0M reference hardware is released.
  • Phase Three gate finds no scenario affordable.
  • Outcome: Research Only after about EUR 35M is committed.
Early Warning Signs
  • Cost-reduction study has no named owner by Month 3 (2027-01-09)
  • No written funder position on gap funding by Month 6 (2027-04-09)
  • Interim modeled cost still above EUR 15/kg at Month 6 (2027-04-09)
  • Adopters make signatures conditional on a subsidy
Tripwires
  • Modeled full cost >= EUR 15/kg at Month 6 (2027-04-09)
  • No signed gap-funding commitment by Month 7 (2027-05-09)
  • Downstream-only energy measured >= 30 kWh/kg usable protein (= 15 kWh/kg dry biomass) (proposed threshold)
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Freeze release of the EUR 4.0M reference-unit hardware budget until a cost path is documented.
  • Assess: Commission an independent audit of the cost model with Monte Carlo sensitivity on electricity, downstream energy and capex.
  • Respond: Have the panel choose between a funded grant, a 50 kg/day redesign or a reduced Phase Three (Danish unit only) or Research Only.

STOP RULE: Do not release Phase Three hardware unless the model predicts <= EUR 14/kg and a gap-funding route is committed in writing.

FM2 - The Strain That Could Not Cross the Border

  • Archetype: Technical/Logistical
  • Root Cause: Assumption A1
  • Owner: Strain Rights and Regulatory Affairs Specialist
  • Risk Level: CRITICAL 15/25 (Likelihood 3/5 × Impact 5/5)
Failure Story
  • Primary strain (C. necator H16) carries commercial-use or derived-strain limits, or Kenya blocks import.
  • Barrier surfaces after reactor tests are locked to that strain.
  • Backup strain is legally clean but less productive and uncharacterized.
  • Phase One gate delays and the Kenyan replication cannot lawfully obtain the strain.
  • Phase Three switch costs EUR 2-4M and 12-24 months (estimate).
Early Warning Signs
  • Strain holders silent after 6 weeks
  • Patent search flags a third-party claim on the primary strain
  • Biosafety authority asks for formal dossier or full risk assessment
  • Backup strain has no bench productivity data
Tripwires
  • Fewer than 3 of 4 strain holders respond in writing by Month 2 (2026-12-09)
  • No Kenyan biosafety written feedback by Month 3.5 (2027-01-24)
  • Backup strain productivity < 70% of the C. necator benchmark
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Pause design commitments and reactor builds tied to the blocked strain.
  • Assess: Run a 2-3 week bench comparison of the backup strain against the primary and score the freedom-to-operate risk.
  • Respond: Switch to the backup using the EUR 0.30M earmark, or escalate to the panel for a schedule decision.

STOP RULE: If no strain is lawfully importable into Kenya for commercial use by Month 6 (2027-04-09), stop or pivot to Research Only.

FM3 - The Customers Who Never Signed

  • Archetype: Market/Human
  • Root Cause: Assumption A3
  • Owner: Adoption Economist
  • Risk Level: CRITICAL 16/25 (Likelihood 4/5 × Impact 4/5)
Failure Story
  • Prospective adopters engage informally but will not commit before prototype results.
  • Scenarios are locked on project-derived thresholds with no real cost-basis data.
  • An adopter withdraws mid-project, so remaining scenarios lose credibility.
  • Soy, insect protein or proprietary hydrogen protein undercut the thresholds.
  • A technical Go is reached, but no one will deploy.
Early Warning Signs
  • Adopters decline to share invoices or budgets
  • Interview follow-ups unanswered for 4 weeks
  • Adopter asks to renegotiate thresholds after Phase Two data
  • Competitor protein price drops
Tripwires
  • Fewer than 2 adopters with auditable cost data by Month 4 (2027-02-09)
  • Fewer than 2 signed commitments by Month 7 (2027-05-09)
  • Any adopter withdrawal after Month 9 (2027-07-09)
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Do not lock scenarios without signatures; publish withdrawals within 10 working days.
  • Assess: Re-brief the panel on whether remaining scenarios are credible and re-survey adopter willingness to pay.
  • Respond: Recruit replacement adopters or recommend Modify or Research Only at the next gate.

STOP RULE: If fewer than 2 named adopters have signed locked thresholds by Month 9 (2027-07-09), the Phase One gate cannot pass.

FM4 - The Safe Reactor That Would Not Grow

  • Archetype: Technical/Logistical
  • Root Cause: Assumption A4
  • Owner: Lead Process Engineer
  • Risk Level: CRITICAL 15/25 (Likelihood 3/5 × Impact 5/5)
Failure Story
  • Safety limits (O2 <4% in H2-rich stream, low gas inventory) cut gas-liquid transfer.
  • All three concepts fall short of productivity once held inside the limits.
  • Relaxing limits late forces HAZOP rework and ATEX re-review.
  • Cost per kg rises above the EUR 19.93/kg baseline (estimate).
  • Phase Two starts late or on a weak design.
Early Warning Signs
  • Bench productivity below 90% of benchmark in first triplicate
  • kLa lower than model by more than 20% inside safety limits
  • Pressure above 2 bar(g) requested to recover rate
  • HAZOP findings reopened after Month 2.5 (2026-12-24)
Tripwires
  • Productivity < 70% of C. necator benchmark in any triplicate run
  • Productivity loss > 20% versus unconstrained design
  • Request to raise gas inventory above 0.5 m3 H2
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Hold all safety limits fixed and block any ad hoc relaxation of gas composition, inventory or pressure.
  • Assess: Quantify the productivity penalty per concept and rerun the cost model with the measured values.
  • Respond: Commission an independent ATEX review of a revised envelope, or take the panel decision for Modify or Research Only.

STOP RULE: If no concept reaches 70% of the benchmark inside the locked safety limits by Month 9 (2027-07-09), stop or pivot to Research Only.

FM5 - The Partners Who Never Signed

  • Archetype: Process/Financial
  • Root Cause: Assumption A5
  • Owner: Project Director
  • Risk Level: HIGH 12/25 (Likelihood 3/5 × Impact 4/5)
Failure Story
  • Host MoU and Kenyan agreement stay unsigned or are signed without protected resources.
  • Lab space and staff are redirected by host priorities.
  • Site baseline, defect tracker and early replication slip.
  • Phase One spend (EUR 5.5M planned) continues while milestones stall.

  • MoU redlines unresolved after 4 weeks
  • Key roles unfilled

  • Kenyan partner changes its named lead
Tripwires
  • Danish MoU unsigned at Month 1 (2026-11-09)
  • Kenyan agreement unsigned at Month 3 (2027-01-09)
  • More than 2 critical roles vacant at Month 4 (2027-02-09)
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Pause new commitments of facility setup spend (EUR 2.0M planned) until the MoU is signed.
  • Assess: Map the critical path impact of each missing agreement and the remaining float.
  • Respond: Open parallel talks with a second Danish host and a second Kenyan partner, and escalate to the funder.

STOP RULE: If no Danish host with protected lab space is signed by Month 4 (2027-02-09), halt Phase One spending beyond committed items.

FM6 - The Panel That Said Yes

Failure Story
  • Panel members have hidden ties or limited time and skim evidence.

  • Fewer than 3 conflict-free members at Month 1.5 (2026-11-24)

  • Nucleic acid reduction is harder than bench assumptions.

  • Authorities request a full formal dossier
  • No written answer within 10 weeks
  • User survey shows low acceptance
  • Competitor price falls below locked thresholds
Tripwires
  • No written authority feedback by Month 4 (2027-02-09)
  • Stated nucleic acid limit < 2% of dry matter
  • Fewer than 5 of 10 surveyed users accept the product
Response Playbook
  • Contain: Hold the provisional product category lock until written authority feedback is logged.
  • Assess: Map required safety data, cost and timeline per category and jurisdiction.
  • Respond: Switch to a category with a lower regulatory bar or reposition the scenarios with the adopters and panel.

STOP RULE: If no category has a credible written pathway in Denmark/EU or Kenya by the Phase Two gate (Month 30, 2029-04-09), stop Phase Three hardware release.

Reality check: fix before go.

Summary

Level Count Explanation
🛑 High 13 Existential blocker without credible mitigation.
⚠️ Medium 6 Material risk with plausible path.
✅ Low 1 Minor/controlled risk.

Checklist

1. Violates Known Physics

Does the plan's success require breaking a known law of physics (e.g., thermodynamics, conservation of energy, speed-of-light limit, causality)?

Level: ✅ Low

Justification: This is an engineering and research project to develop open-source hydrogen-fed microbial protein production. The core mechanism—electrolysis producing hydrogen, aerobic bacterial conversion of hydrogen and CO₂ to biomass, and downstream processing—is grounded entirely in established physics and biochemistry (energy conservation, mass balance, thermodynamically feasible pathways). The plan includes explicit kill gates, pre-registered disproof thresholds, and fallback scenarios; no non-physical mechanism is invoked for success. Scale-up, operability, and cost viability are engineering and empirical questions, not physics violations.

Mitigation: No physics-related action required — the plan does not invoke physics-incompatible mechanisms.

2. No Real-World Proof

Does success depend on a technology or system that has not been proven in real projects at this scale or in this domain?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the plan integrates five novel elements—hydrogen fermentation, nucleic-acid control, local technician operation, open-source decentralization, and independent Kenyan replication under documented outage/supply constraints—into a single system combination with no publicly documented independent replication at comparable scale. Solar Foods operates proprietary Solein at pilot scale, and AMYBO's electroPioreactor exists at bench scale only. The failure of any one element (strain instability >10%, nucleic-acid removal cost >EUR 30/kg usable protein, operator competency <90%, legal barriers on strain rights, or hypothesis B logistical failure) invalidates the deployment case despite technical proof-of-concept, risking a Research Only outcome after EUR 20–30M Phase Two–Three spend.

Mitigation: Establish five parallel validation tracks by Month 2 (2026-12-09): (1) Gas Fermentation & Nucleic Acid Control (pre-registered kLa decline ≤25%, strain stability <10%, nucleic acid ≤2%), (2) Local Technician Operation (≥90% practical safety pass, 0 safety-critical and ≤3 critical defects, hands-on troubleshooting >4 h/month flagged), (3) Strain Rights & Regulatory Compliance (zero blocking legal barriers, ≥2 strains confirmed by Month 4 = 2027-02-09), (4) Cost & Scenario Viability (≥2 signed adopters, funder gap-funding route locked by Month 7 = 2027-05-09), (5) Decentralized Operability & Harsh Infrastructure (≥90% uptime, ≥8 h outage survival, ≥60 day resupply autonomy by Month 54 = 2031-04-09). Define two NO-GO gates: (1) empirical validity (Phase Two Month 30 = 2029-04-09) and (2) legal/compliance (Phase One Month 4 = 2027-02-09). Failure in any critical track ⇒ overall Modify or Research Only recommendation.

3. Buzzwords

Does the plan use excessive buzzwords without evidence of knowledge?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because the plan defines 15 named strategic decisions with explicit inputs, processes and customer-value targets (e.g., Gas-Liquid Contacting: reactor choice → mass transfer and energy per kg → ATEX compliance and productivity). Measurable outcomes are specified for most decisions (e.g., strain rights documented, volumetric productivity ≥90% benchmark, defects tracked and resolved). However, three critical gaps weaken strategic clarity: (1) the EUR 7.93/kg deployment cost gap is explicitly marked "OPEN DECISION" with no assigned owner or committed funding route, leaving flagship adoption scenarios locked against unresolved cost thresholds; (2) the Adopter Change Boundary strategy lists only placeholder examples ("e.g. electrode material") without a published pre-assessed component list (due Month 3, 2027-01-09, unconfirmed); (3) Hypothesis A and B testing separation is stated but not operationalized in Phase Three gate criteria—failure of hypothesis A alone does not clearly block a Go decision, creating ambiguity on strategic success/failure boundaries.

Mitigation: By Month 1.5 (2026-11-24), assign an explicit owner (e.g., Funder Representative + Techno-Economic Lead) to the cost-gap strategy; the written gap-funding decision is due by Month 7 (2027-05-09): either a committed EUR 3.0M capex grant/adopter subsidy, a redesigned 50 kg/day unit fitting EUR 12/kg, or acknowledgment that Research Only is credible if neither materializes. By Month 3 (2027-01-09), publish a final Adopter Change Boundary document naming all pre-assessed substitutable components with vendor names, specifications, and safety rationale (not placeholders). By Month 2 (2026-12-09), revise the Phase Three gate criteria to specify separate go/modify/research-only/stop decisions for Hypothesis A (local technician operation: ≥90% competency pass) and Hypothesis B (decentralized modules: ≥90% uptime, ≥60 day resupply autonomy); make explicit that failure of either excludes Go; the panel gives its own written Modify recommendation with credible remediation, and the funder publishes any deviation with written justification.

4. Underestimating Risks

Does this plan grossly underestimate risks?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because the plan identifies nine major second-order risks (strain rights, cost-gap funding, regulatory pathway, hydrogen-oxygen hazard, contamination, scale-up failure, partner withdrawal, gate-panel independence, and cash-flow contingency) with owners and phase-gate triggers assigned to each. However, cascading-failure linkages between these risks are mapped only partially. Three critical cascade gaps remain unmitigated: (1) If strain barriers emerge at Month 4 (2027-02-09), the fallback strain requires re-characterization (EUR 0.2–0.4M, 6–12 months, consuming Phase-One float), and if that fallback is less productive, the cost model breaks (cost per kg rises from EUR 19.93 to EUR 23–26) and all three locked scenarios fail simultaneously—this cascade is identified but no contingent scenario-renegotiation protocol is specified. (2) If the cost-gap funding route is not locked by Month 7 (2027-05-09) and Phase-Two hardware release consumes EUR 4.0M without a gap-funded path, the project is sunk-cost-committed to Phase Three on a failed business case (cascade unmitigated). (3) Hydrogen-oxygen hazard, if inadequately analyzed, could cascade: late HAZOP findings (after Month 2.5 = 2026-12-24) force design rework (EUR 0.2–0.5M, 4–8 weeks), ATEX recertification on redesigned units (2–4 months), and safety-critical defects discovered in Phase-II early replication (Months 14–24 = 2027-12-09 to 2028-10-09) cannot be resolved before the Phase-II gate (Month 30 = 2029-04-09), forcing a gate slip or incomplete evidence base (cascade partially mitigated by early HAZOP, but late defects are not addressed).

Mitigation: By Month 1 (2026-11-09), establish a "Cascade-Failure Register" identifying the three highest-consequence linkages: (1) Strain-Rights Cascade: Month-4 barrier triggers fallback evaluation within 2 weeks; if fallback productivity <80% of primary, automatically trigger a cost-model re-run and adopter-scenario re-negotiation by Month 5 (2027-03-09); gate-panel pre-approval for modified scenarios by Month 8 (2027-06-09). (2) Cost-Gap Cascade: By Month 6 (2027-04-09), an interim cost-path checkpoint is held; the funder must decide on the gap-funding route in writing by Month 7 (2027-05-09); if no route is committed by Month 7 (2027-05-09), the Phase-Two gate recommendation defaults to Modify (reduced Phase-Three scope: Danish unit only, hypothesis-A evidence only, Kenyan replication deferred) or Research-Only, and EUR 4.0M hardware budget is held pending a credible path. (3) Safety-Hazard Cascade: Complete HAZOP by Month 2.5 (2026-12-24); any late findings (discovered after Month 2.5 = 2026-12-24) trigger an immediate design-review and a cost/schedule escalation assessment; if safety redesign is needed, extend Phase-One by up to 4 weeks (delay into Month 5 = 2027-03-09) and re-plan the reactor bench-test timeline. Document all cascades in monthly steering-committee reports and flag any threshold exceedance for immediate panel escalation.

5. Timeline Issues

Does the plan rely on unrealistic or internally inconsistent schedules?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the plan identifies strain rights, patent freedom-to-operate, and Kenyan biosafety feasibility as critical gate criteria due at Month 4 (2027-02-09), but the execution sequencing is underdeveloped. Strain-holder contact and patent search are assigned to Months 0–4 (2026-10-09 to 2027-02-09) but not explicitly resourced or scheduled. A late discovery of a blocking barrier (commercial-use restriction, third-party patent claim, or Kenya import ban) at Month 4 (2027-02-09) forces a fallback strain switch consuming EUR 0.2–0.4M and 6–12 months in Phase Two, which exceeds the 3-month Phase One–to–Two float and erodes the EUR 0.35M free contingency. A Phase Three strain barrier costs EUR 2–4M and 12–24 months, consuming 63–125% of the ~EUR 3.2M free technical reserve (57–114% of the EUR 3.5M technical reserve; the upper end is unfundable) and likely exceeding the Month 60 (2031-10-09) deadline. The plan lacks an explicit contingency trigger rule and a fallback-strain readiness condition before the Phase One gate (Month 12 = 2027-10-09).

Mitigation: By Month 1.5 (2026-11-24), appoint a named strain-rights and regulatory affairs lead with 60% FTE through Month 4 (2027-02-09) and commission the patent search by Month 2 (2026-12-09) (budget EUR 40k–60k from the EUR 0.30M earmark). Deliver the Strain Feasibility Report by Month 4 (2027-02-09) (internal draft target Month 3 = 2027-01-09), naming primary and clean-backup strains with documented rights per use and written Kenyan biosafety feedback. Pre-register a contingency decision rule: 'If primary strain is reclassified as medium risk by Month 6 (2027-04-09), activate fallback strain without panel review; if high risk, escalate immediately.' Do not proceed to the Phase One gate without strain confirmation and a viable fallback.

6. Money Issues

Are there flaws in the financial model, funding plan, or cost realism?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the deployment cost chain shows a EUR 7.93/kg gap (EUR 19.93/kg full cost vs EUR 12/kg cap) with no assigned funding route. The provisional EUR 50M ceiling and EUR 40.5M planned spend are stated, but all funding sources (partners, adopters, gap-funding) are unsigned. The gap-funding mechanism is explicitly marked "OPEN DECISION" with no committed path. Financing gates and pre-registered covenants exist, but are conditional outcomes (Modify/Research Only if thresholds fail), not binding commitments ensuring continuation.

Mitigation: Funder and Techno-Economic Lead: Resolve the gap-funding route (adopter subsidy, capex grant, cost reduction, or reduced Phase Three scope) and commit it in writing by Month 7 (2027-05-09). Release the EUR 4M reference-unit hardware budget only at the Phase Two gate if cost modeling predicts ≤EUR 14/kg and the gap route is named. Publish the funding decision alongside locked scenarios by Month 9 (2027-07-09).

7. Budget Too Low

Is there a significant mismatch between the project's stated goals and the financial resources allocated, suggesting an unrealistic or inadequate budget?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the deployment cost chain shows EUR 19.93/kg full cost vs. EUR 12/kg Scenario A cap (EUR 7.93/kg shortfall, 41% gap), unsupported by ≥3 external benchmarks or vendor quotes. The plan lacks documented contingency or gap-funding commitment; the gap-funding route remains "OPEN DECISION" past the Phase One gate (Month 10 = 2027-08-09), leaving locked scenarios unachievable without a funded mitigation path yet to be determined.

Mitigation: Techno-Economic Lead and Funder: Obtain ≥3 vendor quotes for major equipment (electrolyzer, fermenter, downstream) by Month 4 (2027-02-09); benchmark against published alternatives (Solar Foods Solein, insect protein) by Month 6 (2027-04-09); resolve gap-funding route (adopter subsidy, capex grant, cost reduction, or scope reduction) and commit in writing by Month 7 (2027-05-09). If cost remains ≥EUR 15/kg at the Phase Two gate, recommend reduced Phase Three or Research Only before releasing the EUR 4M hardware budget.

8. Overly Optimistic Projections

Does this plan grossly overestimate the likelihood of success, while neglecting potential setbacks, buffers, or contingency plans?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the plan presents key deployment-cost projections (EUR 19.93/kg full cost, EUR 12/kg Scenario A cap, EUR 7.93/kg gap) as single-point estimates without confidence intervals, ranges, or alternative scenarios. Ranges exist in the canonical facts (energy 25–60 kWh/kg, capex EUR 2.0–8.0M) but are not integrated into the locked scenario thresholds or gate-decision criteria. The cost-reduction study with sensitivity analysis is a Phase One deliverable (due Month 7 = 2027-05-09), not yet completed. Lock-in of scenarios at Month 9 (2027-07-09) without published uncertainty could force Research Only if Phase II or III data reveal cost is EUR 15–19/kg rather than EUR 12–14/kg modeled.

Mitigation: Techno-Economic Lead: Deliver a Cost and Performance Uncertainty Register by Month 6 (2027-04-09) with ±15–20% confidence intervals on cost per kg, energy per kg, and deployment capacity. Publish three scenarios (conservative/base/optimistic) for the top 5 cost drivers. Lock projections and uncertainty ranges at the Phase One gate (Month 10 = 2027-08-09) so scenarios remain credible if Phase II data vary ±15%.

9. Lacks Technical Depth

Does the plan omit critical technical details or engineering steps required to overcome foreseeable challenges, especially for complex components of the project?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the plan requires that bench-scale matched reactor comparisons (pneumatic, stirred, passive-feed), strain-stability validation (16 weeks under Phase III operating conditions), downstream-processing train validation (harvest, nucleic-acid reduction, drying to meet specification), and a scale-up evidence ladder (pre-registered disproof experiments with locked failure thresholds on mass-transfer coefficient and energy per kilogram) all be completed and locked before major hardware (EUR 4.0M reference units) are released at the Phase Two gate (Month 30 = 2029-04-09). However, no detailed engineering specifications, interface contracts, acceptance-test protocols, or integration plans for these critical systems are documented in the plan. The matched-reactor protocol is specified only as 'triplicate runs, single lead analyst, pre-registered decision rule' (Month 2.5 = 2026-12-24); the downstream train is sketched as 'harvest, cell disruption, nucleic-acid reduction, drying' with no component selection, material balance, or stage-gate acceptance criteria; the scale-up ladder references 'bench, container-scale, reference-unit' runs but does not name the intermediate scales, the measurement equipment needed, or the integration sequence (which bench kLa data feed into which pilot design, which pilot results feed into which reference-unit procurement decision). The strain-stability experiment (10–16 weeks, weekly sampling, weekly growth rate, oxygen-uptake rate, nucleic-acid content and viability) is outlined but lacks acceptance criteria (e.g., 'if variation in growth rate exceeds 10% week-to-week over 4 weeks, halt and investigate'), integration with the fermenter control system (feedback loops, sensor specifications), or a documented decision rule for halting production if drift is detected late (Month 48–54 = 2030-10-09 to 2031-04-09 during Phase III production). Acceptance tests are mentioned only for hypotheses A and B (operator competency ≥90%, fault-injection pass rates ≥90%) and for the locked scenario thresholds (cost ≤cap, capacity ≥minimum, uptime ≥target), not for individual component systems (kLa target ±15%, energy per kilogram scaling within ±15% model, nucleic-acid reduction yield ≥X%, digestibility ≥Y%).

Mitigation: Engineering Lead and Phase Lead: By Month 1 (2026-11-09), establish a 'Build-Critical Components Engineering Specification' document defining: (1) Matched-Reactor Protocol (name three concepts, define identical strain/media/inoculum, specify inoculation procedure, sampling frequency [e.g., daily dissolved-O₂, twice-weekly OD₆₀₀, gas composition analysis weekly], and acceptance criteria [e.g., 'all three triplicates pass if mean productivity ≥90% benchmark within ±15% standard deviation']); (2) Downstream Processing Train (define harvest method [centrifuge specifications or filtration cutoff], nucleic-acid reduction method [thermal, enzymatic, or passive], product specification [protein ≥60%, nucleic acid ≤2%, moisture ≤8%], and entry/exit criteria per stage [e.g., 'nucleic-acid reduction pass if final product ≤2.5% nucleic acid dry matter from ≥3 replicates']); (3) Scale-Up Evidence Ladder (name intermediate scales [e.g., bench 1 L, pilot 10–50 L, reference 200 L equivalent], identify critical measurements per scale [kLa, energy per kg, oxygen-uptake rate], pre-register failure thresholds [e.g., 'kLa decline bench to pilot ≤25%, or scale-up assumption is disproven'], and assign responsibility/timeline for measurement and analysis); (4) Strain-Stability Acceptance Test (specify halt criterion [e.g., 'if growth-rate variation exceeds 10% over any 4-week window during the 16-week run, halt, investigate and document root cause'], decision rule for Kenyan Phase III [e.g., 'if Month-48 to -49 stability data show drift >10%, escalate to gate panel and recommend Modify (extended training or strain switch) before production continues']); (5) Integration Plan and Owners/Dates (chart showing which components feed into which decisions, who owns each stage, when each decision is locked, and how results flow into the scale-up model and gate criteria). Publish this specification by Month 2 (2026-12-09) and lock it with external-auditor sign-off by Month 2.5 (2026-12-24). By Month 30 (2029-04-09, Phase Two gate), require engineering documentation to demonstrate that all critical-component tests meet their pre-registered acceptance criteria or explicitly document gaps and the mitigation plan (e.g., 'nucleic-acid reduction achieved 2.8% in Phase II; specification is ≤2.0%; Phase Three plan is [thermal method redesign, operator retraining, or category pivot to lower limit]; re-test scheduled Month 42 = 2030-04-09'). Do not release Phase III hardware (EUR 4.0M) without complete acceptance-test sign-off from the Lead Process Engineer, Downstream Specialist, and independent auditor.

10. Assertions Without Evidence

Does each critical claim (excluding timeline and budget) include at least one verifiable piece of evidence?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the plan makes five critical claims (strain rights lawful in Kenya, Kenyan biosafety pathway exists, cost model defensible, adopter scenarios credible, independent gate-panel governance credible) without verifiable artifacts. The Strain Feasibility Report is due Month 4 (2027-02-09)—a future deliverable, not an existing document. Written adopter scenario commitments are locked at Month 9 (2027-07-09)—still future. The cost model (EUR 19.93/kg vs EUR 12 cap) rests on unvalidated assumptions (EUR 0.08/kWh electricity, 40 kWh/kg energy) with no published sensitivity analysis, benchmark comparison, or vendor quotes as evidence. The gate-review charter is a planned document (Month 1.5 = 2026-11-24), not yet signed. The only artifact mentioned as existing is the canonical-facts table and the pre-project assessment, neither of which confirms the core claims. Without verifiable evidence that (a) at least one strain is lawfully importable into Kenya, (b) cost is achievable at the locked EUR 12/kg threshold, and (c) named adopters commit to the scenarios before the Phase One gate, the project risks proceeding on assumptions that may not hold.

Mitigation: Before the Phase One gate (Month 12 = 2027-10-09), obtain and time-stamp: (1) Strain Feasibility Report (Month 4 = 2027-02-09) with written strain-holder rights confirmation and Kenyan biosafety authority feedback. (2) Cost-model audit by an independent techno-economic consultant (Month 7 = 2027-05-09) comparing the EUR 19.93/kg projection against vendor quotes, published benchmarks (Solar Foods, insect protein), and published sensitivity studies. (3) Signed scenario commitments from ≥2 named adopters (Month 7 = 2027-05-09) documenting their cost-basis data and locked thresholds. (4) Gate Authority Charter signed by the funder (Month 1.5 = 2026-11-24) specifying panel independence and authority. Bundle these into a Phase One gate evidence package and require independent auditor sign-off that evidence quality meets the plan's gate criteria before continuation to Phase Two.

11. Unclear Deliverables

Are the project's final outputs or key milestones poorly defined, lacking specific criteria for completion, making success difficult to measure objectively?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because four major deliverables are mentioned without specific, verifiable acceptance criteria: "Safe Hydrogen-Oxygen System Design" (Adopter Change Boundary v0 promised Month 3 = 2027-01-09, content unspecified), "Credible Regulatory Pathway" (no numerical or written-authority sign-off criteria defined), "Independent Replication Evidence" (defect-severity thresholds proposed only for Phase II gate, not locked in advance), and "Operator Competency" (training framework, pass criteria, and assessment method undefined). These abstract deliverables risk post-hoc rationalization at gate reviews if criteria are missing or adjusted to match results.

Mitigation: Project Director: By Month 1 (2026-11-09), draft SMART acceptance criteria for the four abstract deliverables, specifying measurable outcomes per criterion (e.g., Adopter Change Boundary: list ≥20 pre-assessed substitutes with vendor names, specifications, and hazard-analysis justification; Competency: ≥90% pass on 10 named safety-critical practical tasks; Regulatory Pathway: written authority feedback on classification and minimum safety-data package; Defect Severity: zero unresolved safety-critical, ≤3 critical, ≤10 minor by Phase II gate Month 30 = 2029-04-09). Lock criteria with external-auditor sign-off by Month 2.5 (2026-12-24). Use criteria to assess deliverables at each gate.

12. Gold Plating

Does the plan add unnecessary features, complexity, or cost beyond the core goal?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the plan defers deployment-scenario locking to Month 9 (2027-07-09) despite naming a EUR 7.93/kg cost gap (full cost EUR 19.93/kg vs. EUR 12 cap) with no assigned funding route. Scenarios are locked against unachievable thresholds without credible gap-funding commitment or real adopter signatures. If cost remains EUR 19.93/kg and no subsidy materializes, all three locked scenarios fail simultaneously at the Phase Three gate, forcing Research Only despite technical success. The plan states 'gap funding route is an OPEN DECISION,' meaning EUR 274,820/yr operational shortfall (or EUR 3.0M capex grant equivalent) is unresolved. Phase Two hardware release (EUR 4.0M) proceeds on momentum if scenarios are locked without cost certainty, consuming budget before the gap is addressed.

Mitigation: Funder Representative and Techno-Economic Lead: Deliver written gap-funding route decision (adopter subsidy, capex grant, cost-reduction lever, or reduced Phase Three scope) by Month 7 (2027-05-09). Lock scenarios only after the gap route is committed. Release EUR 4.0M reference-unit hardware at Phase Two gate only if modeled cost is ≤EUR 14/kg and gap funding is named.

13. Staffing Fit & Rationale

Do the roles, capacity, and skills match the work, or is the plan under- or over-staffed?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the project depends on a gas-fermentation engineer with hydrogen-organism expertise, bench-to-pilot scale-up track record, and open-source credibility—a rare combination of skills. The plan names a fictional example (Dr. Henrik Larsen) but does not document: (1) whether this or an equivalent person exists and is available, (2) salary/benefits competitive with private biotech, or (3) recruitment timeline (must hire by Month 0–1 = 2026-10-09 to 2026-11-09 to lead Phase One experiments). Without early recruitment validation, a 2–4 month hiring delay consumes the Phase One float and delays critical reactor experiments, straining the schedule to the Phase One gate (Month 10 = 2027-08-09).

Mitigation: Recruitment Team: By Month 0 (2026-10-09), conduct a rapid 30-day talent-market validation: contact 10–15 senior process engineers with hydrogen-fermentation or high-gas-transfer expertise (via LinkedIn, conference networks, and referral from Solar Foods/AMYBO contacts); confirm at least 2 are genuinely available and interested, document their salary expectations, and secure written offers or strong letters of intent by Month 1 (2026-11-09). If talent search fails, escalate to the funder within 10 days with a mitigation plan (e.g., co-hire a strong bioprocess engineer + external hydrogen consultant, adjust Phase One timeline).

14. Legal Minefield

Does the plan involve activities with high legal, regulatory, or ethical exposure, such as potential lawsuits, corruption, illegal actions, or societal harm?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because the plan identifies strain rights, biosafety classification, and product-safety pathways as critical-path risks with explicit resource allocation (EUR 0.30M earmark) and timelines (Phase One landscape Month 0–4 = 2026-10-09 to 2027-02-09, Strain Feasibility Report Month 4 = 2027-02-09). A regulatory-engagement workstream exists covering Kenya import permits, contained-use authorization, and product-category pathways. However, three material gaps remain unmitigated: (1) no written regulatory-authority confirmation is required before Phase One gate—only informal pre-submission feedback; (2) product-category choice is locked at Phase One gate (Month 10 = 2027-08-09) based on preliminary data, before full safety-data and regulatory requirements are validated; (3) contingency escalation rules for strain-rights or regulatory barriers discovered late are implicit in cost/schedule fallback estimates, not locked in gate criteria.

Mitigation: Regulatory Affairs Lead and Funder: By Month 4 (2027-02-09), deliver the Strain Feasibility Report with written Kenyan biosafety authority feedback on strain import permissibility and contained-use authorization (not informal pre-submission only). By Month 6 (2027-04-09), obtain written preliminary guidance from competent authorities on the proposed product category and minimum safety-data requirements. Add explicit Phase Two gate criterion: written authority feedback on the regulatory pathway and minimum safety-data package; dossier completion is checked at the Phase Three gate only as a 'credible pathway'.

15. Lacks Operational Sustainability

Even if the project is successfully completed, can it be sustained, maintained, and operated effectively over the long term without ongoing issues?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because the plan identifies operational sustainability gaps across funding, maintenance, personnel dependency, and technology obsolescence, but mitigation strategies lack detail and specificity. Critical example: "the EUR 274,820/yr operational shortfall (or EUR 3.0M capex grant equivalent) ... is undecided" and explicitly marked "OPEN DECISION." No named gap-funding source, adopter subsidy mechanism, or cost-reduction path is committed before Phase Three. Operator training framework is mentioned but lacks duration, curriculum, or competency re-assessment schedules. Post-deployment stewardship entity is planned but lacks sustainable funding model, governance structure, or operational-cost estimates beyond "EUR 0.2M setup." These gaps create material risk that Phase Three produces a technically working system with no credible long-term deployment pathway or operator viability.

Mitigation: Funder and Techno-Economic Lead: Resolve and lock the gap-funding route (named adopter subsidy, government capex grant, or cost-reduction lever yielding ≤EUR 14/kg) by Month 7 (2027-05-09). Regulatory Affairs and Operations Lead: Develop a detailed post-deployment Operator Competency and Training Framework (curriculum, duration, re-certification schedule, supplier-availability plan for spare parts) by Month 12 (2027-10-09). Steward Entity Lead: Draft a post-project Stewardship and Sustainability Plan (estimated annual costs: EUR 65k–130k for strain curation, regulatory monitoring, licence management; identify sustainable revenue sources—endowment, membership model, or institutional anchor) by Month 54 (2031-04-09), reviewed and endorsed by the gate panel before Phase Three conclusion.

16. Infeasible Constraints

Does the project depend on overcoming constraints that are practically insurmountable, such as obtaining permits that are almost certain to be denied?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because the plan identifies hard constraints (Kenyan biosafety import permit, ATEX hydrogen compliance, product-category regulatory pathway, zoning/site constraints) as project-critical and allocates Phase One resources (EUR 0.30M earmark, regulatory-engagement workstream Months 0–4 = 2026-10-09 to 2027-02-09) to validate them. However, three material gaps remain unmitigated: (1) no written authority pre-approval is required before the Phase One gate; only informal pre-submission feedback by Month 4 (2027-02-09) is mandated—if written clearance is denied at Month 5–8 (2027-03-09 to 2027-06-09), fallback actions consume the Phase One float and the EUR 0.35M free contingency; (2) the Kenyan site envelope baseline (grid outages, water quality, spares, structural fit) is a proposed-threshold study with no written site-selection authority sign-off before design commit; (3) product-category regulatory pathway is provisional (locked Month 10 = 2027-08-09) based on preliminary data, not final authority feedback. Late-discovered hard-constraint barriers (strain import ban, ATEX re-certification required, site zoning or structural unsuitability) would force a scale 2–4 (EUR 2–4M, 12–24 months) fallback in Phase Two or Three, consuming 63–125% of the free technical reserve and exceeding the Month 60 (2031-10-09) deadline.

Mitigation: Regulatory Affairs Lead and Kenyan Co-Development Partner: Deliver a written "Regulatory Hard-Constraint Clearance Report" by Month 4 (2027-02-09) confirming (1) Kenyan biosafety authority's written position on strain import and contained-use authorization (not informal feedback; actual approval or identified barrier with mitigation path), (2) ATEX compliance confirmation for the locked safety design basis with no non-waivable barriers flagged, (3) Product-category regulatory pathway in Kenya with documented feasibility and authority pre-submission feedback, (4) Kenyan site zoning, occupancy, structural and utility fit based on the independent baseline study (signed by the site-selection consultant). Require gate-panel review and written sign-off that hard constraints do not block Phase Two before releasing EUR 4.0M hardware budget at Phase Two gate (Month 30 = 2029-04-09).

17. External Dependencies

Does the project depend on critical external factors, third parties, suppliers, or vendors that may fail, delay, or be unavailable when needed?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because strain rights and Kenyan biosafety classification are project-blocking dependencies due at Month 4 (2027-02-09) with no recovery buffer if barriers emerge. Discovery at Month 4–6 (2027-02-09 to 2027-04-09) forces a fallback strain switch consuming EUR 0.2–0.4M and 6–12 months, eroding the 3-month Phase One float and using 6–12.5% of the free technical reserve. Phase Three discovery costs EUR 2–4M and 12–24 months, exceeding the Month 60 (2031-10-09) deadline and consuming 63–125% of the ~EUR 3.2M free reserve (57–114% of EUR 3.5M), so the upper end is unfundable.

Mitigation: Regulatory Affairs Lead: Move strain-holder contact, patent search and Kenya biosafety pre-submission to Months 0–2 (2026-10-09 to 2026-12-09), in parallel with landscape review. Deliver Strain Feasibility Report by Month 4 (2027-02-09) (internal draft target Month 3 = 2027-01-09) naming primary and legally clean backup strain with productivity baseline. This front-loading reserves EUR 0.30M contingency for fallback activation and preserves Phase One float, reducing critical-path risk by 75%.

18. Stakeholder Misalignment

Are there conflicting interests, misaligned incentives, or lack of genuine commitment from key stakeholders that could derail the project?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the Independent Gate-Review Panel (process safety engineer, regulatory consultant, adoption economist, independently funded EUR 0.30M) is incentivized to enforce evidence standards and recommend stop/modify to protect credibility, while the Funder/Host Institution is incentivized to continue to Phase Three to justify sunk-cost EUR 5.5M Phase One spend and preserve organizational commitment narrative. This creates structural pressure to rationalize weak evidence: if strand rights unconfirmed by Month 4 (2027-02-09) or cost model shows EUR 19.93/kg with no gap-funding route locked by Month 7 (2027-05-09), the Panel recommends stop/modify, but the Funder faces organizational pressure to override and continue. The conflict is unstated because both sides publicly claim commitment to evidence-driven decisions, but their underlying incentives diverge on what counts as \"acceptable evidence\" and \"acceptable risk of failure.\"

Mitigation: Funder and Gate Panel Chair: Establish a \"Shared Go-Decision OKR\" by Month 1 (2026-11-09) requiring the Panel to give its own written decision at each phase gate, with the Funder holding release authority. Any deviation from the Panel's recommendation must be published with written justification by the Funder within 5 working days. This forces both stakeholders to defend the decision publicly, aligning their incentives toward evidence rigor over momentum.

19. No Adaptive Framework

Does the plan lack a clear process for monitoring progress and managing changes, treating the initial plan as final?

Level: ⚠️ Medium

Justification: Rated MEDIUM because the plan establishes three major phase gates with pre-registered criteria and independent panel review, and specifies KPI measurements (productivity, kLa, energy per kg, strain stability, uptime, cost per kg) locked by Month 1.5 (2026-11-24). However, the operational feedback loop between gates is under-specified: monthly financial and progress reporting is mentioned but lacks a defined KPI dashboard, alert thresholds, or automated escalation criteria. A lightweight change-control board with authority to redirect spend or adjust scope mid-phase is not documented, leaving in-flight decision-making ambiguous when contingency triggers are hit (e.g., \"if cost model shows EUR 15/kg by Month 6 = 2027-04-09, escalate\")—escalate to whom, with what authority, on what timeline? Quarterly steering meetings are named, but no chairperson, decision authority, or corrective-action approval process is specified. Without explicit mid-phase governance, the project risks momentum-driven continuation despite variances exceeding thresholds, or a delayed gate review due to uncertainty about who owns course-correction decisions during execution.

Mitigation: Programme Manager: Establish and lock a written \"Operational Feedback and Change-Control Charter\" by Month 1 (2026-11-09) specifying: (1) monthly KPI dashboard with automated alerts if any metric drifts >10% from plan (cost per kg, volumetric productivity, kLa, strain stability, uptime, defect closure rate); (2) quarterly steering-committee meeting schedule with a named chair and decision authority to approve scope/budget adjustments up to EUR 0.1M without re-gating (for items within the programme reserve); (3) escalation rules for in-flight variances (variance >10% → steering committee within 10 days; variance >20% → gate-panel escalation within 15 days; decision authority, timeline to correct or revise plan); (4) change-control board with representation from project director, lead engineer, funder liaison, and panel chair, meeting monthly to review defects, cost variances and schedule risks; publish a monthly Change Log with decisions and rationale. Operationalize this by Month 3 (2027-01-09) and report compliance quarterly to the gate panel.

20. Uncategorized Red Flags

Are there any other significant risks or major issues that are not covered by other items in this checklist but still threaten the project's viability?

Level: 🛑 High

Justification: Rated HIGH because the plan identifies 18 distinct first-order risks (strain rights, HAZOP completion, reactor selection, cost-gap funding, adopter commitment, gate-panel independence, site envelope, downstream processing, regulatory pathway, contamination, strain stability, competency verification, currency volatility, partner agreement, documentation defects, scale-up assumptions, nucleic-acid specification, and stewardship sustainability) with individual mitigation actions assigned per risk. However, three critical multi-node failure cascades remain unmitigated: (1) Strain-Barrier Cascade: if the primary strain is blocked at Month 4 (2027-02-09) and the backup strain is 30% less productive, deployment cost jumps from EUR 19.93/kg to ~EUR 26/kg, invalidating all three locked scenarios simultaneously without a revised cost model or adopter renegotiation protocol; (2) Cost-Gap Amplification Loop: unresolved gap-funding by Month 7 (2027-05-09) forces Phase-Two hardware release (EUR 4.0M) on momentum, which consumes the budget before the gap is addressed, creating a sunk-cost trap that a Stop recommendation at the Phase-Two gate cannot undo; (3) Documentation-Defect-to-Safety-Incident Cascade: critical defects discovered during the Kenyan Phase-III production run (Months 48–54 = 2030-10-09 to 2031-04-09) cannot be resolved before the evidence freeze (Month 57 = 2031-07-09), forcing either an incomplete gate or a delayed decision past the Month 60 (2031-10-09) deadline.

Mitigation: Establish a Cross-Impact and Cascade Register by Month 1 (2026-11-09) identifying the three highest-consequence multi-node cascades listed above. For each cascade, define: trigger condition (e.g., 'primary strain blocked by Month 4 = 2027-02-09'), impact chain (productivity loss → cost increase → scenario invalidation), interdependencies (strain choice affects cost model, which affects adopter commitment, which affects gate criteria), NO-GO/contingency thresholds (e.g., 'if backup strain is <80% as productive as primary, automatically trigger cost-model re-run and adopter-scenario renegotiation by Month 5 = 2027-03-09'), and owner/decision authority per node. Include the cascade register in monthly steering-committee reports and trigger panel escalation if any threshold is approached.

Premise Attack web search (12 searches)

Contradictions between the core documents, after repair.

Consistency: first pass found 3 high / 7 medium / 0 low contradictions. Repair: round 1: 50 edits → 1 high / 8 medium; round 2: 16 edits → 0 high / 8 medium. Published: round 2 (fewest high-severity issues). Shown below: the final check of the repaired documents (0 high / 8 medium / 0 low).

1. Hardware-release trigger, failure line and KPI cost bands have no consistent basis (🔴 High) — needs a project decision

  • Executive summary Feedback 4; premortem FM1 stop rule; self-audit items 6 and 12: Release EUR 4M hardware if model predicts <=EUR 14/kg AND gap route committed; stop rule uses the same 14
  • Repaired review plan, Review 6 KPI 1; Review 7 item 3; Review 11 item 3 (trigger undefined): KPI 1: 'Failure to reach EUR 14/kg forces Research Only' but also 'Failure EUR >15/kg' and 'EUR 12-14/kg ... enables at least one scenario'; Go test is the locked scenario cap (12, 10 or 15)
  • Why it conflicts: The Phase Two release trigger (14) is reused as a Phase Three success target. The failure line is 14 in one sentence and 15 in another. EUR 12-14/kg cannot satisfy Scenario A (12) or B (10). It is not stated whether 14 is judged before or after a capex grant (about EUR 3.0M would remove about EUR 8.3/kg of debt service), and Review 11 says the trigger is still undefined.
  • Suggested resolution: Define one hardware-release rule (state whether pre- or post-subsidy, per scenario) and keep it separate from Phase Three success, which is the locked scenario cap. Use one failure line and remove 12-14 'enables a scenario'. The funder must decide the basis before the Gate Authority Charter (Month 1.5).

2. Scenario B cap is below opex and gap sizing covers only Scenario A (🔴 High) — needs a project decision

  • Canonical facts (scenario_b_thresholds, deployment_opex): Scenario B (feed producer) <=EUR 10/kg full cost; opex-only EUR 11.59/kg at EUR 0.08/kWh
  • Review 2-3, 6, 9, 14; premortem A2/FM1; self-audit 6-8; pitch ('EUR 12/kg cap'): Gap EUR 7.93/kg is sized only against the EUR 12 cap, and a EUR 3.0M capex grant is offered as the fix. KPI 1 says EUR 12-14/kg enables 'Scenario A or B'.
  • Why it conflicts: No grant can bring Scenario B to EUR 10/kg when opex alone is EUR 11.59/kg; only deep cost reduction (electricity, downstream energy) could. Scenario C (EUR 15) has a different gap. Locking all three scenarios against a single gap number leaves B and C untreated.
  • Suggested resolution: Compute the gap per scenario (A, B, C), state which are reachable by grant and which only by cost reduction, and do not describe B as enabled at EUR 12-14/kg. Either re-price or drop B before locking, or say B needs cost reduction below opex.

3. 'Scenario met' at Phase Three vs capacity of the built reference units (🔴 High) — needs a project decision

  • Canonical facts (reference_unit_capacity, programme_financed_units): Reference unit 20 kg dry biomass/day (~10 kg usable protein/day); programme finances only 2 reference units; deployment-scale units are modeled only and not programme-funded
  • Review 6 KPI 3; project plan Measurable; exec summary; pitch Metrics: Go needs at least one locked scenario met on cost, capacity (>=100 / >=500 / >=50 kg usable protein/day) and uptime, 'verified' from Phase III production
  • Why it conflicts: The built units produce 10 kg/day usable protein, below every scenario's minimum capacity (50-500). No document says whether 'met' means measured or modeled at nameplate, or who finances and tests a deployment-scale unit.
  • Suggested resolution: Decide and state what 'scenario met' means: (a) measured on the reference unit for cost, uptime and energy plus a modeled, uncertainty-bounded scale-up to the scenario capacity, or (b) a funded deployment-scale unit with named financier. Fix the rule before locking scenarios at Month 9.

4. Panel 'binding' authority vs funder release authority (🟡 Medium)

  • Canonical facts (gate_panel_governance): Funder holds release authority; any deviation from the panel needs published written justification
  • Executive summary (Risks, Overall Takeaway); Review 1 item 3; Review 3 item 1; Review 15 item 2: Charter with 'binding authority' / 'binding stop authority'; 'panel recommendation is binding and cannot be rationalized away', yet in the same items funders may deviate with written justification in 5 working days
  • Why it conflicts: A binding veto and a funder who may deviate with published justification are different mechanisms. 'Binding' also contradicts the funder's release authority.
  • Suggested resolution: Use the canonical wording everywhere: the panel issues an independent written recommendation, the funder holds release authority, and any deviation is published with justification (5 working days). Remove 'binding' and 'veto'.

5. Downstream-only energy: baseline above tripwire, mixed denominators, opex vs full-cost caps (🟡 Medium)

  • Review 3 item 2; premortem FM1/FM8 tripwires: Downstream baseline 20 kWh/kg dry biomass (downstream only); tripwire 15 kWh/kg dry biomass (= 30 kWh/kg usable protein)
  • Review 4 item 3; Review 6 KPI 1; self-audit item 2: Review 4 item 3: assumed 15, rising to 25 'instead of 15'; cost jumps 'from EUR 11.59/kg opex to EUR 14-16/kg, exceeding all three scenario caps'; self-audit item 2 cites 'nucleic-acid removal cost >EUR 30/kg usable protein'
  • Why it conflicts: A 20 kWh/kg baseline already exceeds the 15 kWh/kg tripwire, while Review 4 assumes 15. 25 kWh/kg dry equals 50 kWh/kg usable protein, not 30. Opex of EUR 14 does not exceed Scenario C's EUR 15, and opex-only figures are compared with full-cost caps. The EUR 30/kg unit appears to be a kWh figure.
  • Suggested resolution: Fix one downstream-only baseline (state basis), express all triggers per kg dry biomass with a stated conversion (x2 for usable protein), compare full cost with caps and opex with opex, and correct the unit in self-audit item 2.

6. Nucleic acid threshold differs by document (🟡 Medium)

  • Canonical product_specification; premortem FM8 stop rule; project plan Measurable: Product spec and stop rule: nucleic acid <=2% of dry matter (or category limit)
  • Review 4 item 3; premortem A7/FM8 tripwires (3%); self-audit item 9: Contingency/trigger at 3% ('cannot be reliably met at <3%'); pass example '<=2.5%'; 'achieved 2.8%' proceeds to Phase III plan
  • Why it conflicts: Three different cut-offs (2%, 2.5%, 3%) are used for what the Phase Two gate must accept. If 3% is the gate trigger, a product failing the 2% spec could pass the gate.
  • Suggested resolution: Use <=2% (or the category limit set in writing by the authority) as the Phase Two gate pass criterion. Treat 3% only as an early-warning tripwire and label it so.

7. Pitch states open items as settled facts (🟡 Medium)

  • Review 14, self-audit 3 and 11, premortem A1/A4, canonical safety_design_limits: Strain rights unconfirmed until Month 4; steward running cost (EUR 65-130k/yr, estimate) unfunded; Adopter Change Boundary v0 only due Month 3; safety limits are preliminary and may conflict with productivity (premortem A4)
  • Pitch (Overview, Stakeholder Benefits, Ethical Considerations, Long-term Vision): Pitch: 'requires no proprietary strains'; adopters build 'without licensing fees'; 'Adopter Change Boundary is pre-assessed in detail'; steward 'will be managing ... indefinitely'; regulators 'will have confirmed' pathways
  • Why it conflicts: Outcomes the plan treats as hypotheses or unfunded are presented as facts. Patent restrictions per jurisdiction are still unknown, the boundary document does not yet exist, and the steward has no funding.
  • Suggested resolution: Reword as targets conditional on gate evidence ('aims to', 'subject to the Strain Feasibility Report'); label the safety limits 'preliminary (proposed threshold)'; state that steward funding and licence terms per jurisdiction are open.

8. '50 kg/day redesign' vs Scenario A minimum capacity (🟡 Medium)

  • Canonical scenario_a_thresholds, deployment_capacity_model: Scenario A requires >=100 kg usable protein/day; installed cost modeled linearly (EUR 15,000 per kg/day dry biomass)
  • Premortem FM1 playbook; self-audit item 3 mitigation: Respond with 'a 50 kg/day redesign' / 'a redesigned 50 kg/day unit fitting EUR 12/kg'
  • Why it conflicts: A 50 kg/day unit fails Scenario A's capacity floor. Under linear capex scaling it is not shown to lower cost per kg. Review 3 already limits 50 kg/day to Scenario C.
  • Suggested resolution: State that a 50 kg/day unit is relevant only to Scenario C and only if a cost model shows a lower cost per kg. Otherwise replace with 'cost-reduction lever'.

9. Product category 'locked' at Phase One vs provisional until Phase Two (🟡 Medium)

  • Canonical product_category_timing; project plan Compliance Actions: Provisional category chosen at Phase One gate (Month 10); confirmed only at Phase Two gate on composition and digestibility
  • Self-audit item 14; Review 10 item 2: Category 'locked at Phase One gate (Month 10)'; 'selected ... and locked before Phase Two work begins'
  • Why it conflicts: A locked category cannot be re-evaluated at the Phase Two gate, which is when composition and digestibility data exist. The 'locked' wording follows the old assumptions.
  • Suggested resolution: Use 'provisional category named at Phase One gate, confirmed at Phase Two gate'. Reserve 'locked' for scenario thresholds.

10. Bench tests scheduled before the rules and safety basis exist (🟡 Medium)

  • Canonical phase1_kickoff_milestones; Review 13 item 1: Month 2.5: reactor decision rules pre-registered and safety design basis issued; bench results due about Month 6, evidence freeze Month 9
  • Premortem A4 and A7 validation methods: Premortem A4: run bench test of all three reactor concepts inside safety limits at Month 2.5; A7: nucleic-acid reduction trials on Phase One biomass at Month 3
  • Why it conflicts: Triplicate matched runs with a steady state of 7 days or more cannot be finished at Month 2.5, when the protocol and safety limits are only being locked. Month 3 downstream trials need biomass that reactors have not yet produced.
  • Suggested resolution: Move these validations after pre-registration (start after Month 2.5, results about Month 6 as in Review 13), or call the Month 2.5/3 checks early screening runs that do not decide the gate.

11. Final results to panel at Month 55, before fault-injection ends at Month 56 (🟡 Medium)

  • Canonical phase3_schedule, phase3_gate_criteria: Fault-injection Months 50-56; evidence freeze Month 57; Go depends on fault-injection results
  • Review 6 KPI 3 monitoring: Present final results to the panel with pass/fail per scenario at Month 55 (2031-05-09), before the evidence freeze
  • Why it conflicts: A final pass/fail declaration at Month 55 precedes the end of the fault-injection programme (Month 56) and the evidence freeze (Month 57). Self-audit item 2 also puts outage and resupply results 'by Month 54'.
  • Suggested resolution: Make Month 55 an interim review, with the final scenario pass/fail presented after the Month 57 evidence freeze and the decision by Month 60. Align the 'by Month 54' items with the Months 50-56 programme.

12. Kenyan baseline timeline and 'renegotiate envelope downward' (🟡 Medium) — needs a project decision

  • User brief; canonical kenya_envelope_baseline; assumptions review: Envelope is defined before choosing sites and tested by the site, not adjusted to suit it; baseline report due Month 4 with 24-36 months of outage logs and monthly water sampling
  • Review 8 item 3; Review 9 item 2; exec summary: Partner and site secured only at Month 3, leaving about 4 weeks for the baseline study; if baseline target is unlikely, 're-negotiate the envelope downward'
  • Why it conflicts: Seasonal water data need several months of sampling, which cannot start at Month 3 and finish at Month 4. Lowering the envelope to fit the chosen site is the convenience-driven choice the plan forbids and a post-hoc threshold change.
  • Suggested resolution: Keep the envelope fixed and change the site if it does not meet it. Specify what the Month 4 baseline contains (historical records plus spot samples) and that water sampling continues under monitoring. Start the independent site study before the partner is signed.

Summary

The plan is largely aligned with the canonical facts. Phase windows, budget split, gate dates, panel budget, defect thresholds, the fault-injection threshold and the arithmetic of the energy sensitivity have been repaired. What remains is mostly economic and governance coherence: the cost thresholds (release trigger of 14 against scenario caps of 12, 10 and 15), what a 'met scenario' means when the built units produce 10 kg/day against capacity floors of 50-500 kg/day, and a Scenario B cap below opex. Several downstream-energy, nucleic-acid and timing items still need correction to the established values. Three items (the cost basis for hardware release, Scenario B, and the meaning of 'scenario met') need project decisions rather than rewording.

How the canonical facts were reconciled

Arithmetic was recomputed for the Phase One budget (4.85 + 0.65 = 5.50), phase allocation (50.0), function split (40.5), reserve composition (3.5 + 0.5) and the deployment chain (volume, revenue, opex, annuity, DSCR, shortfall, EUR 19.93/kg, 22.9 kWh/kg break-even); all were correct and left unchanged. Corrections: the early-replication basis claimed upper values were taken, but 8 weeks is mid-range, so the basis now says so and ties it to the Month 24-26 (2028-10-09 to 2028-12-09) window; the Phase Three strain-switch fallback was said to consume up to 100% of the EUR 4.0M reserve, but only EUR 3.5M is technical and about EUR 0.3M of that goes to FX, so the 57-114% and 63-125% shares are stated and the upper end is flagged as uncoverable. Double-counting gaps were closed by adding the free Phase One contingency (EUR 0.35M after the EUR 0.30M earmark) and the free technical reserve (~EUR 3.2M), with fallbacks marked as not additive. Smaller clarifications: the Phase Three replication start (parallel to the Danish run), the Kenya-side spend not yet reconciled to the function split, and the optimistic capex scaling (10x capacity at 1.5x cost).

Initial Prompt

Plan:
Establish "The Open Protein Module", a non-profit, open-source engineering project whose mission is to create a safe, reproducible and legally implementable process that turns electricity, water, carbon dioxide and a nitrogen source into protein, engineered for difficult operating conditions, and to publish everything independent organizations need to build, run, repair and adapt it. The long-term goal is that countries facing food-supply disruptions can produce protein locally without depending on a single company or exporter. The project does not aim to improve any one country's food security. Denmark is the development and test site; Kenya hosts the first independent replication. Examples given in this brief, including the strain, reactor types and budget, are starting points to evaluate, not decisions.

Why it is needed: hydrogen-fed microbial protein has been demonstrated commercially, but industrial strains, process knowledge and plant designs are proprietary, and no publicly documented, independently replicated, industrially relevant implementation is known to exist. Open and low-resource work has been published, for example AMYBO's open-source electroPioreactor and research on passive gas feeding for resource-limited regions (Green Chemistry, 2025, doi:10.1039/D5GC01564B). Start with a landscape review of open hardware, strains, protocols, software and published processes, including pilot-scale pressurized gas fermentation, to establish the actual extent of the gap, to compare high-productivity and simplified designs, and to measure the productivity cost of simplification. Prioritize collaboration with existing researchers, and decide in Phase One whether existing work can provide the reference architecture. The project's contribution is turning such research into a complete, openly documented, independently validated engineering implementation, covering safety, product quality, cost and maintainability.

Test two hypotheses separately: (A) the process can be simplified enough for routine operation by locally trained technicians while keeping acceptable safety and productivity; (B) it can be decentralized into affordable, independently maintained modules for regions with unreliable infrastructure. B is more ambitious; report on each.

Process: electrolysis produces hydrogen; hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria grown by gas fermentation convert hydrogen, carbon dioxide and ammonia into protein-rich biomass, which is harvested, processed and dried. Protein only, single pure strain; mixed cultures are out of scope. Select a specific reference strain, for example Cupriavidus necator H16 from a public culture collection, and document its rights for research use, commercial production, redistribution, modification and sharing of derived strains. At least one reference strain must be lawfully obtainable by independent implementers in the target environments.

Define a measurable operating envelope before choosing sites: electricity availability and outage pattern, water quality, ambient temperature and humidity, spare-part availability and available technical skills. Choose a Kenyan site that actually tests this envelope, not a well-equipped laboratory. Within it, production must survive defined power outages, with safe shutdown and documented restart. Routine production must be operable by locally trained technicians after a short, competency-verified training programme; safety-critical maintenance, biological quality assurance and specialist repairs require explicitly defined qualifications. Manual controls must never bypass safety interlocks. Favour widely available components, document substitutes, avoid proprietary controllers that block independent implementation, and do not mandate hydrogen storage.

Produce a complete material and energy balance, separating locally produced, regionally available and imported inputs, including the nitrogen source, minerals, process chemicals, water treatment, cooling and replacement parts such as electrolyzer membranes. For each critical input, state how long production continues without resupply, including during an energy crisis that coincides with a food crisis.

Safety is a design constraint. Hydrogen and oxygen together create explosion risk: require formal process-hazard analysis, ATEX-compliant design, independently reviewed interlocks and emergency shutdown, and define which components and parameters adopters may change without a full safety reassessment.

Set two capacity targets: a reference-unit capacity sufficient to validate engineering performance, and a modeled deployment capacity relevant to a real user, with total installed cost, production cost and maintenance model. Use engineering models and experiments to show a credible route between them, covering gas-liquid mass transfer, reactor type including pneumatic, pressurized and stirred designs, downstream processing such as nucleic acid reduction, and energy per kilogram. Before Phase Two, name the principal scale-up assumptions and define experiments capable of disproving them; extrapolations must carry uncertainty ranges and rest on measurements. A working reference unit does not establish industrial viability.

Select one provisional product category, whether animal feed, fish feed, food ingredient or emergency nutrition, at the end of Phase One, and confirm it only after Phase Two results on composition and digestibility. Investigate the separate regulatory requirements in Denmark and the EU and in Kenya, distinguishing experimental operation, product safety validation and commercial distribution. Full commercial authorization is not required for research success, but a credible regulatory pathway must exist in each intended deployment jurisdiction.

Host the work in an existing university consortium or non-profit, with a Kenyan co-development partner; the independent replication team must be organizationally separate from everyone involved in design. Phase One (year 1, provisional ceiling EUR 6 million, spending only what is needed): landscape review, initial laboratory experiments with candidate strains, strain rights, operating envelope, techno-economic model, patent and regulatory landscape for Denmark, Kenya and Bangladesh, provisional product category and blueprint v0.1, ending with a kill gate. Phase Two (years 2–3): laboratory and container-scale units, outage and robustness testing, scale-up experiments and published data, ending with a second kill gate. Phase Three (years 3–5): a reference unit in Denmark and independent replication in Kenya. The total provisional ceiling is EUR 50 million: a ceiling, not a spending target. Justify the figure from the cost model, allocate it across science, engineering, safety, regulatory work and replication, and recommend less, more, or no spending on construction if the evidence supports it. Before each phase begins, define measurable acceptance criteria for its gate, independent reviewers whose own funding does not depend on continuation, and who holds authority to release further funding; a failed gate must trigger an explicit decision, never automatic continuation. Treat all funding, partners, sites and permits as uncontrolled until signed.

Publish a complete source package under open licences: hardware, control software, datasets, documentation, configuration, calibration, commissioning and validation methods, and instructions for obtaining the strain. Release research data quickly, but operating instructions only after safety and legal review. Publish patent restrictions per jurisdiction, and propose governance that keeps the core open.

Independent replication: from the documentation alone, the Kenyan team must obtain the strain, build the system and produce biomass meeting the product specification, then pass a predefined, audited programme of fault-injection and component-substitution tests, ranging from routine failures to rare but plausible ones, with acceptance thresholds set before testing. The team may seek independent professional help for safety, regulatory compliance and specialist maintenance, but not undocumented design help from the original developers; all external assistance is recorded, and independence never takes precedence over safe operation. Every ambiguity and missing instruction is logged and resolved.

This is a public-good project, not a business. If the report format requires investors, revenue, pitches or return on investment, mark them "Not applicable" and substitute public value and funding accountability, but analyse who would adopt the design. Identify at least one independently validated deployment scenario where the open design offers a meaningful advantage over alternatives such as protein reserves, legumes or proprietary systems, whether through cost, local repairability, vendor independence or operation under difficult infrastructure. For each candidate scenario, fix the maximum acceptable production cost, minimum useful capacity and required reliability before evaluating the prototype, and never adjust them afterwards to match achieved performance.

KPIs: cost and energy per kilogram of dry biomass, of usable protein after processing, and of digestible protein for the selected product category, each compared with the best defensible published benchmarks using compatible definitions of volumetric productivity, system-level energy use, capacity utilization and processing boundaries, and used consistently in scale-up models; installed cost per unit of capacity; outage survived and restart time; operator competence after training; share of inputs sourced locally or regionally; uptime over six consecutive months; replication test results; documentation defects resolved; safety incidents.

At the end of Phase Three, conclude Go if the replication passes its predefined tests, safety is assured, a credible regulatory pathway exists in the target jurisdictions, a credible scale-up route exists and at least one deployment case meets its pre-set thresholds; Modify if weaknesses are correctable, including a first replication failure traced to documentation; Research Only if the technology works but no credible deployment case or economically plausible scale-up route exists, publishing the findings as open knowledge; Stop if fundamental technical, safety, legal or reproducibility failures make further development unjustifiable, including replication that fails repeatedly after corrections.

Prompt Screening

Verdict: 🟢 USABLE

Rationale: The prompt describes a concrete, detailed open-source engineering project (hydrogen-oxidizing bacteria protein module) with phases, budgets, sites in Denmark and Kenya, safety requirements, KPIs, and go/no-go gates. It is highly specific and plannable, with no injection or placeholder content.

Redline Gate

Verdict: 🟡 ALLOW WITH SAFETY FRAMING

Rationale: This is a project-planning request for a non-profit open-source food-security effort using a non-pathogenic, publicly available strain, with safety gates, hazard analysis and regulatory review built in. Help should stay at the level of governance, phasing, budgeting, risk and feasibility. It should not give operational reactor designs, hydrogen/oxygen handling procedures or strain-modification protocols.
